For the center's 50th anniversary (2009–10), Diller Scofidio + Renfro and other architects gave the complex a much-needed and critically acclaimed freshening up.

fact_check.omission_check: Lincoln Center opened 1962 on the site of San Juan Hill, a predominantly Black/Latino neighborhood razed under Robert Moses; West Side Story exteriors filmed there; widely criticized for fortresslike conservative design. script_body: This compelling little museum, housed in a three-story town house from 1898, is one of Manhattan's best-kept secrets. It displays 150 paintings by the prolific Nicholas Konstantinovich Roerich, a Russian-born poet, philosopher and painter who lived from 1874 to 1947. His most remarkable works are his stunning depictions of the Himalayas, where he and his family settled in 1928 — icy Tibetan peaks in shades of blue, white, green and purple.

poi_name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
script_body: The largest place of worship in America has yet to be completed — and probably won't be anytime soon. But this glorious Episcopal cathedral commands attention with its ornate Gothic-style facade, booming vintage organ, and extravagantly scaled nave — twice as wide as London's Westminster Abbey. The first cornerstone was laid on St John's Day in 1892, but construction was hardly smooth. Engineers had to dig 70 feet in order to find bedrock to anchor the building. Architects died or were fired, and in 1911, the initial Romanesque design was exchanged for a bigger, Gothic-inspired plan. Depleted funds have seen construction regularly halted. The north tower remains unbuilt, and a 'temporary' domed roof constructed out of terracotta tile in 1909 still rises above the epicenter of the church. If it is ever completed, the 601-foot-long cathedral will rank as the world's third-largest church, behind Rome's St Peter's Basilica and Côte d'Ivoire's Basilica of Our Lady of Peace at Yamoussoukro.

script_body: For more than 40 years, this treasured museum has showcased influential African American artists. The permanent collection is rich, holding nearly 9000 works. The Studio Museum has been an important patron to African American artists, and the collection features work by more than 800 of them. This includes important pieces by painter Jacob Lawrence, photographer Gordon Parks, and collagist Romare Bearden — all represented in major museum collections in the US. Additional works include those by a new generation of artists, such as Nigeria-born Njideka Akunyili Crosby, who was awarded a MacArthur Genius Award in 2017 for her large-scale collage and photo transfer-based paintings.

script_body: Among the Cloisters' many rare treasures is the beguiling tapestry series The Hunt of the Unicorn, dating from 1495 to 1505. Also worth seeking out is the remarkably well-preserved 15th-century Annunciation Triptych, also called the Merode Altarpiece. Then there's the stunning French 12th-century Saint-Guilhem and Bonnefant cloisters, the latter featuring plants used in medieval medicine, magic, ceremony, and the arts, with views over the Hudson River.

source_passage: Among its many rare treasures is the beguiling tapestry series The Hunt of the Unicorn (1495–1505). Also worth seeking out is the remarkably well-preserved 15th-century Annunciation Triptych (Merode Altarpiece). Then there's the stunning French 12th-century Saint-Guilhem and Bonnefant cloisters, the latter featuring plants used in medieval medicine, magic, ceremony and the arts, and with views over the Hudson River.

fact_check.omission_check: Unicorn tapestries, Merode Altarpiece, and Bonnefont cloister garden all remain on display. Note: 'Bonnefant' in script is the book's spelling of the cloister normally rendered 'Bonnefont'; the fact (medieval medicinal-plant garden) is correct, so no edit.

script_body: Founded in Lower Manhattan in 1754 as King's College, the oldest university in New York is now one of the world's premier research institutions. In 1897, the Ivy League school moved to its current location — the site of a former asylum — where its stately, gated campus offers plenty of cultural happenings. The principal point of interest is the main courtyard on either side of College Walk at 116th Street, surrounded by Italian Renaissance-style buildings. In the northern half, you'll find the statue of the open-armed Alma Mater seated before the Low Memorial Library.

source_passage: Founded in Lower Manhattan in 1754 as King's College, the oldest university in New York is now one of the world's premier research institutions. In 1897 the Ivy League school moved to its current location (the site of a former asylum), where its stately, gated campus offers plenty of cultural happenings. The principal point of interest is the main courtyard (located on either side of College Walk, at 116th St), which is surrounded by various Italian Renaissance–style buildings. In the northern half, you'll find the statue of the open-armed Alma Mater seated before the Low Memorial Library.

fact_check.omission_check: Founded 1754 as King's College in Lower Manhattan (oldest in NY State); moved 1897 to Morningside Heights on the former Bloomingdale Insane Asylum site; Alma Mater statue still before Low Memorial Library. No change.

poi_name: General Ulysses S Grant National Memorial
script_body: Popularly known as Grant's Tomb — 'Who's buried in Grant's Tomb? Who? Grant, stupid!' goes a classic joke — this landmark holds the remains of Civil War hero and 18th president Ulysses S Grant and his wife, Julia. Completed in 1897, twelve years after Grant's death, the imposing granite structure is the largest mausoleum in America. A gallery covers key events in Grant's life, and rangers lead guided tours throughout the day.

source_passage: Popularly known as Grant's Tomb ('Who's buried in Grant's Tomb?' 'Who?' 'Grant, stupid!' goes a classic joke), this landmark holds the remains of Civil War hero and 18th president Ulysses S Grant and his wife, Julia. Completed in 1897 – 12 years after his death – the imposing granite structure is the largest mausoleum in America. A gallery covers key events in Grant's life. Rangers lead guided tours at various times throughout the day and answer questions about the general and statesman.

fact_check.omission_check: Grant's Tomb (General Grant National Memorial) holds Ulysses (d.1885) and Julia Grant; dedicated 1897, twelve years after his death; largest mausoleum in North America. Still open on Riverside Dr at 122nd. No change.

script_body: This imposing neo-Gothic beauty was built by the Rockefeller family in 1930. While the sparseness of the interior evokes an Italian Gothic style, the stained-glass windows in the narthex are actually Flemish, dating back to the 16th century. The church rings its 74 carillon bells with an extraordinary 20-ton bass bell — the world's largest — at 10:30am and 3pm on Sunday.

poi_name: Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture
script_body: The nation's largest collection of documents, rare books and photographs relating to the African American experience resides at this scholarly center run by the New York Public Library. It's named after Arthur Schomburg, a Black Puerto Rican activist who amassed a singular collection of manuscripts, slave narratives and other important artifacts.

Named after Arthur Schomburg, a Black Puerto Rican activist and collector
Run by the New York Public Library
source_passage: The nation's largest collection of documents, rare books and photographs relating to the African American experience resides at this scholarly center run by the New York Public Library. It's named after Arthur Schomburg, a Black Puerto Rican activist who amassed a singular collection of manuscripts, slave narratives and other important artifacts.

fact_check.omission_check: Schomburg Center remains an active NYPL research center (celebrated centennial in 2025); named for Arturo (Arthur) Schomburg, Afro-Puerto Rican collector. No closure or rename.
unverified_claims: Superlative 'nation's largest collection' relating to the African American experience — NYPL describes it as 'one of the world's leading' institutions with 11M+ items; the 'nation's largest' framing is plausible and not contradicted, but not stated verbatim by the primary source.

script_body: When completed in 1916, this brick beaux-arts giant at 555 Edgecombe Avenue was Washington Heights' first luxury apartment complex, with a concierge, a separate workers' entrance, and no fewer than three elevators. It was initially available only to whites, but the neighborhood's transformation from predominantly Irish and Jewish to African American saw the building's residents become mostly Black by the 1940s. Its tenants would include some of New York's most prominent African Americans, among them boxer Joe Louis and music heavyweights Lena Horne, Count Basie, Duke Ellington, and Billy Strayhorn.

Its tenants would include some of New York's most prominent African Americans, among them boxer Joe Louis and music heavyweights Lena Horne, Count Basie, Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn.

fact_check.omission_check: 555 Edgecombe Ave (built 1914-16, also Paul Robeson Residence, National Historic Landmark 1976) still stands. Tenant roster of Joe Louis, Lena Horne, Count Basie, Duke Ellington, Billy Strayhorn confirmed.
unverified_claims: Superlative 'Washington Heights' first luxury apartment complex' — repeated by Lonely Planet and corroborating sources; plausible and uncontradicted but not anchored to a primary registry document.

script_body: One of New York's premier Latino cultural institutions, El Museo del Barrio presents thoughtful rotating exhibitions spanning all media, from painting and photography to video and site-specific installations. The shows often highlight the museum's strong permanent collection, which includes pre-Columbian artifacts, traditional folk works, and a stellar array of postwar art by a wide range of Latino artists — including Chilean surrealist Roberto Matta and established contemporary artists such as Félix González-Torres and Pepón Osorio.
key_claims: Permanent collection includes pre-Columbian artifacts, traditional folk works, and postwar Latino art
Collection includes works by Roberto Matta, Félix González-Torres, Pepón Osorio
source_passage: Bienvenido to one of New York's premier Latino cultural institutions, with thoughtful rotating exhibitions that span all media, from painting and photography to video and site-specific installations. The shows often highlight El Museo's strong permanent collection, which includes pre-Columbian artifacts, traditional folk works and a stellar array of postwar art made by a wide range of Latino artists. The museum includes pieces by well-known historical figures such as Chilean surrealist Roberto Matta and established contemporary artists such as Félix González-Torres and Pepón Osorio.

fact_check.omission_check: El Museo del Barrio remains open; permanent collection (8,500+ works) spans pre-Columbian Taíno artifacts to contemporary Latino art. González-Torres and Pepón Osorio confirmed in collection; Roberto Matta association consistent with museum holdings and not contradicted.
unverified_claims: Specific presence of a Roberto Matta work in the permanent collection — confirmed by Lonely Planet text; museum's holdings include postwar Latino art and Matta is a documented Chilean surrealist, but a primary catalog entry was not located. Not contradicted.

script_body: This Federal-style retreat belonged to Founding Father Alexander Hamilton, who owned a 32-acre country estate here in the early 1800s. Unfortunately, Hamilton was able to enjoy his abode for only two years before his life was cut short in a fatal duel with political rival Aaron Burr. The building was moved from Convent Avenue to its present location in 2008, and has seen a visitor surge of some 75% thanks to Lin-Manuel Miranda's musical Hamilton.

script_body: What started as an occasional pilgrimage has turned into a tourist-industry spectacle: entire busloads of travelers now make their way to Harlem every Sunday to attend a gospel service. The volume of visitors is so high that some churches turn away people due to space constraints. In some cases, tourists have been known to outnumber congregants. Naturally, this has led to friction — many locals are upset by visitors who chat during sermons, leave in the middle of services, or show up in skimpy attire. If you do attend, be respectful: dress modestly, don't take pictures, and remain for the duration. The most famous services are the soulful Sunday gospel services at Abyssinian Baptist Church, running mid-September through July. Arrive at least an hour before the 10am Sunday service to queue up.

Some churches turn away visitors due to space; tourists sometimes outnumber congregants
Abyssinian Baptist Church tourist gospel service at 11:30am Sunday, mid-Sep through July

source_passage: What started as an occasional pilgrimage has turned into a tourist-industry spectacle: entire busloads of travelers now make their way to Harlem every Sunday to attend a gospel service. The volume of visitors is so high that some churches turn away people due to space constraints. In some cases, tourists have been known to outnumber congregants. Naturally, this has led to friction. Many locals are upset by visitors who chat during sermons, leave in the middle of services or show up in skimpy attire. Plus, for some, there's the uncomfortable sense that African American spirituality is something to be consumed like a Broadway show. The churches, to their credit, remain welcoming spaces. But if you do decide to attend, be respectful: dress modestly (Sunday best!), don't take pictures and remain present for the duration of the service. The soulful Sunday gospel services at Abyssinian Baptist Church are the city's most famous. Arrive at least an hour before the service to queue up, and abide by the strict entry rules: no tank tops, flip-flops, shorts, leggings or backpacks.

fact_check.omission_check: Church active; tourist gospel access continues. Service time has changed since the 2022 edition: official site now lists Sunday worship at 10:00am, not 11:30am. (Note: Rev. Calvin Butts died Oct 2022; current senior pastor Dr. Kevin R. Johnson — not named in script.)

corrections.original_text: the 11:30am tourist service
corrections.corrected_text: the 10am Sunday service
corrections.reasoning: Abyssinian's official site lists current Sunday worship at 10:00am (in-person and virtual); the church no longer runs a separate 11:30am tourist service. Tourists are directed to the regular Sunday service and asked to arrive ~1hr early. The 11:30am time would send visitors at the wrong hour.

disputes.claim: running mid-September through July
disputes.issue: Church now publishes a year-round Sunday worship schedule (including summer/August worship schedules); the implied mid-Sep–July seasonal window may no longer hold, but the current official calendar does not state a tourist-specific seasonal range, so the exact replacement is non-obvious.
disputes.recommendation: Verify the current visitor-season policy by phone (212-862-7474) before relying on the mid-Sep–July window; consider neutral phrasing ('most Sundays year-round').

script_body: When the Brooklyn Bridge opened in 1883, its span of 1,596 feet was then-unequalled, and it became the first land connection between Brooklyn and Manhattan as well as the world's first steel suspension bridge. This timeless example of urban design has inspired poets, writers and painters; even today, it never fails to dazzle. An engineering masterpiece, it remains one of New York City's most-photographed sights.

fact_check.omission_check: Bridge open and intact; pedestrian walkway present. Opened May 24, 1883; first steel-wire suspension bridge; first fixed Brooklyn-Manhattan connection. No closure.

script_body: German-born engineer John Roebling designed the bridge, but after contracting tetanus when his foot was crushed by a ferry at Fulton Landing, he died before construction even began. His son, Washington Roebling, took over the project, which lasted 14 years. Roebling junior also became a victim, contracting 'the bends' from working underwater in a pressurized caisson. Bedridden within sight of the bridge for many years, he relied on his wife, Emily Warren Roebling, herself a mathematician and engineer, to oversee construction in his stead; she also had to deal with budget overruns and unhappy politicians. Aside from the Roeblings, at least 27 workers died during the bridge's construction.

Washington Roebling took over; project lasted 14 years
Washington got 'the bends' from caisson work
Emily Warren Roebling, a mathematician and engineer, oversaw construction

source_passage: German-born engineer John Roebling designed the bridge, but after contracting tetanus when his foot was crushed by a ferry at Fulton Landing, he died before construction even began. His son, Washington Roebling, assumed responsibility for the project, which lasted 14 years. However, Roebling junior also became a victim, contracting 'the bends' from working underwater in a pressurized caisson. Bedridden within sight of the bridge for many years, he relied on his wife, Emily Warren Roebling, herself a mathematician and engineer, to oversee construction in his stead. She also had to deal with budget overruns and unhappy politicians. Aside from the Roeblings, at least 27 workers died during the bridge's construction.

fact_check.omission_check: John Roebling died of tetanus (foot crushed by ferry at Fulton slip, 1869); Washington Roebling took over and was disabled by caisson disease ('the bends'); Emily Warren Roebling, recognized as engineer, oversaw construction; ~14-year project. 'At least 27 workers died' is within the commonly cited 20-27+ range. All confirmed.

script_body: There was one final tragedy to come. In 1883, six days after the official opening, a massive crowd of pedestrians was bottlenecked at a stairway when rumours of a collapse, possibly started in jest, set off a stampede in which dozens were injured and 12 were crushed to death.

fact_check.omission_check: No omission. Bridge opened May 24, 1883; stampede May 30, 1883 (Memorial Day) = six days after. 12 killed, dozens injured confirmed. Collapse-rumor trigger confirmed.

script_body: A stunning example of industrial regeneration, this 85-acre, multi-use waterfront park skirts the East River for 1.3 miles, from Jay St in Dumbo to the west end of Atlantic Ave in Cobble Hill. It has revitalized a barren shore and its once-decaying piers into a scenic playground for all-comers: local amblers, camera-toting tourists and families with kids in tow. There's running, cycling, lounging, skating, bouldering and more across its multifarious parkland.

script_body: In the northern section of Dumbo, between the Brooklyn and Manhattan Bridges, the Empire Fulton Ferry section of the park spreads a sweeping grassy lawn with stunning views of the East River. Alongside the lovingly restored 1922 Jane's Carousel, there are shrubby landscaped gardens and walking tracks leading to the best vantage point for that essential Brooklyn Bridge photograph. The section is bordered by the Empire Stores, a cluster of Civil War-era warehouses that now house restaurants, shops and the acclaimed avant-garde theater St Ann's Warehouse.

script_body: Main Street Park, just south of the Manhattan Bridge, has a bouldering wall, a dog run, a nautical-themed playground, a pebble beach and the Park Authority's Environmental Education Center. Among the piers, Pier 2 is all about sweat — a roller rink, an outdoor gym, courts for bocce, handball, basketball and shuffleboard, and free kayaking. Pier 3 has lawns and granite steps for sitting; Pier 4 has a small beach for launching a paddle boat; and Pier 5 has sports fields, cycling paths, a 'picnic peninsula' with shade umbrellas and barbecues, and an OddFellows ice-cream kiosk.

Pier 3 has more lawns and granite steps for sitting and contemplating, while Pier 4 has a small beach where you can launch a paddle boat or dip your toes in the East River. Main Street Park amenities, Pier 2 roller rink (still open, 2025/2026 seasons) and other pier features remain accurate.

script_body: Though Central Park is New York's most storied green space, its 19th-century architects, Frederick Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, considered Prospect Park their true chef d'œuvre — their crowning achievement. Between its looping bridges, scenic lake, broad meadow and the only swath of forest in Brooklyn, you might agree. Opened in 1867, the 585-acre park today receives roughly 10 million visitors a year.

script_body: Carrying a distinctly Parisian feel, the monumental Grand Army Plaza, with its dominant ceremonial arch, sits at the intersection of Flatbush Ave and Prospect Park West, marking the beginning of Eastern Pkwy and the entrance to Prospect Park. The arch was built in the 1890s as a memorial to Union soldiers who fought in the Civil War; there's also a bust of John F Kennedy nearby. The Greenmarket is held here on Saturdays from 8am to 4pm year-round.

On its south end is the Picnic House, with a snack stand and public bathrooms.

From the boathouse there's a trailhead for more than 2.5 miles of woodsy nature trails. The mile-long route along Lullwater Creek is very scenic, while a slightly shorter trail plunges into the Midwood, offering views of the park's oldest trees.

script_body: This five-story, 560,000-sq-ft beaux-arts building was designed in the early 1890s by McKim, Mead & White, a leading architectural powerhouse. It was conceived as the largest single-site museum in the world — though it was significantly scaled back when Brooklyn was incorporated into NYC, and it's now one of New York's largest museums. Inside there is ancient art, lavish 19th-century interiors and cutting-edge contemporary work.

It includes bas-reliefs and Roman-era portraits, some drawn from the museum's ongoing excavations in Egypt, and a mummy chamber holds sarcophagi and ritual objects. Seek out the Wilbour Plaque, a limestone fragment showing the vivid profile of Queen Nefertiti facing a male figure, likely Akhenaten — father of Tutankhamun — dating to 1352–1336 BCE.

script_body: The Brooklyn Museum is one of the few mainstream arts institutions to devote permanent space to women artists. The 8,300-sq-ft Elizabeth Sackler Center for Feminist Art on the 4th floor shows a mix of one-person and historical exhibitions, from radical Black women artists to video installations and photography. At its core is Judy Chicago's absorbing 1979 installation, The Dinner Party, with place settings for 39 mythical and historical women; it somehow succeeds in being both imposing and intimate.

script_body: Coney Island — a name synonymous in American culture with antique seaside fun and frolicking — achieved worldwide fame as a working-class amusement park and beach-resort area at the turn of the 20th century. After decades of decline, its kitschy charms have experienced a 21st-century revival. Though it's no longer the booming attraction it once was, it still draws crowds of tourists and locals alike for legendary roller-coaster rides, hot dogs and beer on the beachside boardwalk.

script_body: For a sense of the city as it was, wander around Brighton Beach. Under the elevated tracks on Brighton Beach Ave, the bustling Russian district known as 'Little Odessa' is packed with greengrocers and emporiums dispensing smoked fish and pierogi. On the street you'll find a cross-section of humanity — from grandmas to sulky teens — chattering in dozens of different languages as the trains rumble overhead. It's unmistakably New York. Directly east along the boardwalk from Coney Island, Brighton Beach is dubbed 'Little Odessa' for its large population of Ukrainian and Russian families.

Hands-on Discovery Garden for kids
Washington Ave entrance has eco-designed visitor center with a living roof
source_passage: A network of trails runs throughout the gardens, connecting popular sections devoted to native flora, bonsai trees, a wood covered in bluebells and a rose garden. The Discovery Garden is a hands-on, immersive space for kids, with regular family activities. ... The Washington Ave entrance around the corner (at President St) leads to a striking eco-designed visitor center with a 'living roof' covered in a thriving diversity of plants.

fact_check.omission_check: No adverse change. Steinberg Visitor Center (990 Washington Ave) with 10,000 sf living roof of 40,000+ grasses/bulbs/wildflowers confirmed present; Discovery Garden and native flora/bonsai/rose garden trails confirmed.

script_body: When Brooklyn ferry services started in the early 1800s, well-to-do Manhattanites began building beautiful houses in Brooklyn Heights. The piers are now recreational areas with lawns gazing towards Manhattan's skyscrapers, while east lies cobblestone Dumbo — short for 'Down Under the Manhattan Bridge Overpass.'
key_claims: When Brooklyn ferry services started in the early 1800s, well-to-do Manhattanites built houses in Brooklyn Heights
Dumbo means 'Down Under the Manhattan Bridge Overpass'
source_passage: When Brooklyn ferry services started in the early 1800s, well-to-do Manhattanites began building beautiful houses in Brooklyn Heights. The piers are now recreational areas with lawns gazing towards Manhattan's skyscrapers. East lies cobblestone Dumbo ('Down under the Manhattan Bridge overpass'), beyond which Vinegar Hill hoards a few special restaurants.

fact_check.omission_check: No adverse change. Brooklyn ferry service early 1800s (Fulton's steam ferry 1814) drove well-to-do Manhattanites to build in Brooklyn Heights; Dumbo = 'Down Under the Manhattan Bridge Overpass' confirmed (acronym coined 1970s). No physical cues.

script_body: Occupying an old subway station built in 1936 — out of service since 1946 — this kid-friendly museum takes on 100-plus years of getting around town. The best part is the downstairs platform area, where you can climb aboard 20 original subway and elevated train cars dating to 1907.

physical_cues.cue: The downstairs platform with 20 original subway and elevated train cars from 1907

key_claims: Museum occupies a subway station built in 1936, out of service since 1946
Downstairs platform has 20 original subway and elevated train cars dating to 1907
source_passage: Occupying an old subway station built in 1936 (and out of service since 1946), this kid-friendly museum takes on 100-plus years of getting around town. The best part is the downstairs area, on the platform, where you can climb aboard 20 original subway and elevated train cars dating to 1907.

fact_check.omission_check: No adverse change. Court Street station opened April 9 1936, closed to passengers 1946; museum holds ~20 vintage subway/elevated cars dating from 1907 on the downstairs platform. All confirmed.

script_body: Inside an 1899 brick building in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, Kings County Distillery makes craft spirits from New York grain. Its tour touches on a bit of history — the 19th-century Whiskey Wars, which erupted in nearby Vinegar Hill and devastated Brooklyn.
key_claims: Kings County Distillery is in an 1899 brick building in the Navy Yard
Tour touches on the 19th-century Whiskey Wars, which erupted in nearby Vinegar Hill
source_passage: Set in an 1899 brick building in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, this distillery uses New York grain to create some mighty smooth craft spirits. Come on a 45minute guided tour ... with a bit of a history thrown in – the 19thcentury Whiskey Wars, which erupted in nearby Vinegar Hill, devastated Brooklyn.

fact_check.omission_check: No adverse change. Kings County Distillery operates in the Navy Yard's 1899 Paymaster Building (brick); the 19th-century Whiskey Wars (1860s) centered on nearby Vinegar Hill / Irishtown. NYC grain spirits confirmed. No physical cues.

script_body: BLDG 92, a museum and gallery built into the Brooklyn Navy Yard, tells Brooklyn's living history from the navy yards to its present-day innovators. Three floors of exhibition rooms showcase the shipbuilding history that made Brooklyn, with gripping testimony from women welders who worked 10-hour days while fighting for equal pay with the men.
key_claims: BLDG 92 is a museum in the Navy Yard telling Brooklyn's living history
Three floors of shipbuilding exhibits
Testimony from women welders working 10-hour days fighting for equal pay
source_passage: A museum and gallery built in to the Brooklyn Navy Yard, BLDG 92 tells Brooklyn's living history, from the navy yards to its present-day innovators and designers. Three floors of exhibition rooms showcase the shipbuilding history that made Brooklyn, with some gripping testimony from characters of the time…women welders working 10-hour days while fighting for equal pay with the men, we salute you.

fact_check.omission_check: No adverse change. BLDG 92 is an operating Navy Yard museum/gallery (open Tue-Sat, free); permanent exhibit covers shipbuilding history including oral-history testimony from WWII women welders fighting for equal pay. No physical cues.
unverified_claims: Three floors of exhibition rooms (museum has 3 floors of exhibits, broadly corroborated but not pinned to a single primary count)

script_body: An international byword for beards, body art, bustling bars and fixed-wheel bikes, Williamsburg is now well and truly gentrified. Artists and students piled into the postindustrial neighborhood, then since the late 1990s its revitalized streets received a stampede of property developers sowing eye-watering rents. Street art, coffee joints and avant-garde nightspots remain, making this an exciting neighborhood to explore.

Artists and students piled in, then developers since the late 1990s drove up rents
Street art, coffee joints and avant-garde nightspots remain

Artists and students piled in to the postindustrial neighborhood, then since the late 1990s its revitalized streets received a stampede of property developers sowing eyewatering rents. Street art, coffee joints and avant-garde nightspots remain, making this an exciting neighborhood to explore.

fact_check.omission_check: No adverse change. Williamsburg's gentrification arc (artists/students from 1990s, developer influx, rising rents, surviving street art/coffee/nightlife) is well-documented and remains current. Characterization is interpretive but accurate. No physical cues.

script_body: This repository for New York-related ephemera tenderly curates objects from the recent past — seltzer bottles, postcards of Lady Liberty, decaying confetti. Push through the antique subway turnstile to learn about local character 'Little Egypt' in a peep-show-style booth, admire mosaic shrines out the back, and stick around for a drink.

Push through the antique subway turnstile to learn about local character 'Little Egypt' in a peep-show-style booth, admire mosaic shrines out the back, and stick around for a drink maybe.

script_body: Don't miss Battle Hill, the cemetery's highest point, where Washington's Continental Army lost to British and Hessian troops during the 1776 Battle of Long Island, also known as the Battle of Brooklyn. The event is commemorated by a 7ft statue of Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom, whose upright arm waves to the Statue of Liberty, facing back from a few miles across the harbor. The hill sits in the northeast sector of the cemetery, off Battle Ave.

fact_check.omission_check: No closure/removal. Minerva monument still present on Battle Hill; view toward Statue of Liberty is being protected.
unverified_claims: Minerva statue is exactly 7ft tall (sources confirm the statue exists and faces the Statue of Liberty but do not state a precise height; figure is uncontradicted)

script_body: Founded in 1838 as a rural cemetery with Manhattan views, Green-Wood has over 560,000 'permanent residents,' including notable personalities such as inventors Samuel Morse and Elias Howe, abolitionist Henry Ward Beecher, designer Louis Comfort Tiffany, artist Jean-Michel Basquiat and Susan Smith McKinney-Steward, the first African-American woman in New York state to gain a medical degree. Musical legend Leonard Bernstein and Brooklyn Dodgers owner Charles Ebbets are also buried here.

script_body: A bright-yellow, L-shaped structure houses this hands-on kids' favorite, founded in 1899 as the first children's museum in the US. The collection holds almost 30,000 cultural objects — musical instruments, masks and dolls — and natural-history specimens including rocks, minerals and a complete Asian-elephant skeleton. But Brooklyn is very much in the house, with a re-created bodega, a pizza joint, and a Caribbean market that kids can play-act in.

The collection contains almost 30,000 cultural objects (musical instruments, masks and dolls) and natural-history specimens (rocks, minerals and a complete Asianelephant skeleton). But Brooklyn is very much in the house, with a re-created bodega, a pizza joint, and a Caribbean market that kids can play-act in.

fact_check.omission_check: Museum open and operating. Founded 1899, first children's museum in the US (also cited as world's oldest) confirmed. ~30,000 objects, Asian-elephant skeleton, and World Brooklyn exhibit (bodega, pizza joint, Caribbean market) confirmed current.

script_body: Known for tree-lined streets and graceful brownstone houses, Park Slope is Brooklyn's answer to Manhattan's Upper West Side. This former working-class area is today filled with couples with toddlers and designer dogs, who stroll between brunch places, boutiques and 585-acre Prospect Park, Brooklyn's most beautiful green space.

script_body: The star attraction of the north end of Brooklyn Bridge Park is a vintage carousel built by the Philadelphia Toboggan Company back in 1922. In 1984 it was purchased by Dumbo artist Jane Walentas, who spent the next two decades faithfully restoring the vintage paint scheme on the ornate, carved-wood elements before it took up its current plum spot beneath New York's two most-photographed bridges. With 48 horses, two chariots and 1,200 lights, it is the first of its kind to be placed on the National Register of Historic Places, and is housed in a clear acrylic pavilion designed by Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel.

Housed in a clear acrylic pavilion by Jean Nouvel

In 1984 it was purchased by Dumbo artist Jane Walentas, who spent the next two decades faithfully restoring the vintage paint scheme on the ornate, carved-wood elements before the carousel took up its current plum spot beneath New York's two most photographed bridges. The carousel has 48 horses, two chariots and 1200 lights, and is the first of its kind to be placed on the National Register of Historic Places. The working treasure is housed in a clear acrylic pavilion designed by Pritzker Prize–winning architect Jean Nouvel.

fact_check.omission_check: Carousel open in Brooklyn Bridge Park. Built 1922 by Philadelphia Toboggan Company, 48 horses + 2 chariots + 1,200 lights, first carousel on the National Register of Historic Places, Jean Nouvel acrylic pavilion all confirmed. Walentas purchase 1984 and ~two-decade restoration confirmed (note: led by Jane Walentas with husband David).

script_body: Six of the east-west streets of well-to-do Brooklyn Heights, such as Montague and Clark Sts, lead to the neighborhood's number-one attraction: a narrow, paved walking strip with breathtaking views of Lower Manhattan and New York Harbor, blissfully removed from the busy Brooklyn-Queens Expressway over which it sits. This slice of urban beauty, over 1,800ft in length, is fiercely defended by locals against development proposals — a great spot for a sunset walk.

This little slice of urban beauty, over 1800ft in length, is fiercely defended by locals against development proposals. A great spot for a sunset walk.

fact_check.omission_check: Promenade open and unchanged; long-debated BQE rebuild that proposed temporarily replacing the Promenade was shelved, so the cantilevered strip still stands. No closure.

script_body: Built just after the Civil War, the Empire Stores are a vestige of Brooklyn's historic waterfront, which once supported 3 miles of brick warehouses stacked with coffee, sugar and tobacco. Retaining its original structure and features, it has been rehabilitated as an upscale hub of commerce and culture across 360,000 sq ft. Time Out's chic food market is the highlight; head to the 5th floor for remarkable views and alfresco tables.

Time Out's chic food market, complete with avocado toast, Mexican fusion and Michelin-star ramen, is the highlight; head to the 5th floor for remarkable views and alfresco tables.

fact_check.omission_check: Empire Stores built 1869 (just after the Civil War), rehabilitated; Time Out Market still open (hours confirmed 2025/2026) with a fifth-floor rooftop offering views and alfresco tables. No closure or demolition.
unverified_claims: '3 miles of brick warehouses' — descriptive historical figure for the old Brooklyn waterfront wall of stores; broadly supported but not pinned to an exact mileage by a primary source

script_body: At the center of Fort Greene Park stands the Prison Ship Martyrs' Monument, at the time of its construction the world's tallest Doric column, at 149ft. Designed by Stanford White of the prominent firm McKim, Mead & White, it was completed in 1908 to memorialize the 11,500 American prisoners of war who died in wretched conditions in British prison ships during the American Revolution. Some of their remains are interred in a crypt beneath its base.

script_body: War history and a hilly aspect make 30-acre Fort Greene Park a rewarding space to ramble. Forts from the Revolutionary War and War of 1812 were retired by 1847, when this tract became Brooklyn's first park — a measure championed by Walt Whitman, then editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle. By 1867, Calvert Vaux and Frederick Olmsted, designers of Central Park and Prospect Park, were resculpting its rugged expanse.
key_claims: 30-acre Fort Greene Park became Brooklyn's first park in 1847, championed by Walt Whitman (then editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle)
Forts from the Revolutionary War and War of 1812 retired by 1847
By 1896 Vaux and Olmsted resculpted it
source_passage: War history and a hilly aspect make 30-acre Fort Greene Park a rewarding space to ramble. Forts from the Revolutionary War and War of 1812 were retired by 1847 when this tract of land became Brooklyn's first park (a measure championed by Walt Whitman, then editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle). By 1896, Calvert Vaux and Frederick Olmsted – designers of Central Park and Prospect Park – were resculpting its rugged expanse.

fact_check.omission_check: Park open, 30 acres (30.2). Whitman (Brooklyn Daily Eagle editor) advocacy and 1847 designation confirmed. No closure.

corrections.original_text: By 1896, Calvert Vaux and Frederick Olmsted
corrections.corrected_text: By 1867, Calvert Vaux and Frederick Olmsted
corrections.reasoning: Olmsted and Vaux were engaged in 1867 and prepared their redesign in 1867-1868 (an extant 1867 Vaux-Olmsted plan map exists). 1896 is the year the park was RENAMED Fort Greene Park, not when Olmsted/Vaux resculpted it. The script attaches the wrong date (off by ~29 years) to their design work. Confirmed by 2+ sources (Wikipedia + Geographicus map + NYC Parks).

disputes.claim: this tract became Brooklyn's first park
disputes.issue: NYC Parks (official) and several guides call it 'Brooklyn's first park'; Wikipedia states it was Brooklyn's SECOND park, after City Park (today's Commodore Barry Park). Sources conflict.
disputes.recommendation: Leave as-is; the script matches the official NYC Parks position. Note the Wikipedia discrepancy. Not auto-corrected because the city's own authority supports 'first park.'

script_body: Built in 1903 to link Williamsburg and the Lower East Side at Delancey St, this steel-frame suspension bridge helped transform the area into a teeming industrial center. At the time it was the longest suspension bridge on earth, a behemoth with a 1,600ft span and all-steel towers. While the Brooklyn Bridge is the more attractive bridge, the Williamsburg Bridge's foot and bike paths offer excellent views of Manhattan and the East River.

At the time it was the longest suspension bridge on earth, a behemoth with its 1600ft span and all-steel towers. While the Brooklyn Bridge is the more attractive bridge, the Williamsburg Bridge's foot and bike paths offer excellent views of Manhattan and the East River, plus it connects two neighborhoods with numerous bars and restaurants.

fact_check.omission_check: Bridge open; 1903 opening, 1,600ft main span (longest in the world 1903-1924, surpassing Brooklyn Bridge), first major suspension bridge with all-steel towers. Foot/bike paths with East River views remain. No closure.

script_body: Harking back to when this area of New York was a beer-brewing center, the Brooklyn Brewery brews local suds and offers 45-minute tours of its facilities. Here's an interesting fact: the brewery's cursive logo was designed by none other than Milton Glaser, of 'I Heart New York' fame, who did the job in exchange for a share of the profits and free beer for life.

script_body: The grassy 35-acre McCarren Park makes a good picnic spot, where barbecues and bikinis define warm summer weekends. On sweltering days you might head to the free swimming pool — a huge, historic community spot that reopened in 2012 after being closed for almost three decades. Free movies and live-music nights are held on Wednesdays in July and August.

A working farm until 1901, this Dutch Colonial H-frame house has shingled walls and split doors, with a community vegetable garden outside. Guided tours explain the family's history and the additions made in the 18th and 19th centuries.

script_body: Extending from near JFK International Airport, the salty, marshy Jamaica Bay Wildlife Refuge covers the water north of the Rockaways' barrier island. As one of the most important migratory bird and wetland habitats along the eastern seaboard, it attracts more than 325 bird species in spring and fall. Spring features warblers and songbirds; in mid-August shorebirds start to move south from Canada, fueling up for the trip to Mexico. Fall brings migrating hawks and raptors, along with ducks, geese, monarch butterflies and thousands and thousands of dragonflies.

script_body: Before Queens was incorporated into New York City in 1898, it was a series of unrelated towns and villages each with their own street nomenclature — there were 40 Washington Streets alone. Something had to be done, but it didn't happen until 1911, a hundred years after Manhattan's grid system began. Today Queens has 167 avenues running east–west and 271 streets going north–south — Manhattan's total opposite. Those hyphenated addresses are the result: the two pre-dash numbers indicate the closest cross street, and the two post-dash numbers designate the building number.

source_passage: Before Queens was incorporated into New York City in 1898, it was a series of unrelated towns and villages each with their own street nomenclature (there were 40 Washington Streets alone!). Something had to be done but it didn't happen until 1911 – 100 years after Manhattan's grid system began. Today, the Queens grid system has 167 avenues that go east–west (Long Island City to Queens Village) and 271 streets that go north–south (Whitestone to Rockaway) – Manhattan's total opposite. But here's the most confusing bit: Addresses have two sets of double-digit numbers separated by a dash. The two pre-dash numbers indicate the closest cross street/avenue while the two post-dash numbers designate the building or house number (the lowest number starts nearest to that cross street).

fact_check.omission_check: Historical claims (1898 consolidation, ~40 Washington Streets, 1911 Powell numbering system, hyphenated-address logic) all corroborated. Manhattan's grid dates to the 1811 Commissioners' Plan, ~100 years before 1911. No issue.
unverified_claims: Exact current counts of 167 east-west avenues and 271 north-south streets (specific tallies not independently confirmed; not contradicted)

script_body: Long before European conquest, this island belonged to the Lenape, whose name means 'Original People.' They foraged, hunted and fished the regional bounty for some 11,000 years before the first Europeans sailed through the Narrows, leaving behind spear points, arrowheads, bone heaps and shell mounds. Some of their pathways still lie beneath streets such as Broadway. In their Munsee language the word Manhattan may have meant simply 'hilly island' — though others trace it to a more colorful phrase, 'place of general inebriation.'

His arrival was the opening move in several decades of European incursions that cultivated the Lenape's deep mistrust of outsiders.

script_body: In 1624 the Dutch West India Company sent 110 settlers to begin a trading post here in Lower Manhattan, calling their colony New Amsterdam. Their arrival touched off bloody battles with the unshakable Lenape. It all came to a head in 1626 when the colony's first governor, Peter Minuit, became the city's first — but certainly not the last — unscrupulous property developer, purchasing Manhattan's 14,000 acres for 60 guilders, about 24 dollars, plus some beads and various European tools.

script_body: The name Coney Island is a relic of Dutch New Amsterdam: it comes from Konijneneiland, meaning 'rabbits island.' Many New York place names carry the same Dutch fingerprints — Gramercy from Krom Moerasje, 'crooked lake,' and Bowery from bouwerij, an old word for 'farm.'

script_body: After Willem Kieft let the colony fall into disrepair, Peter Stuyvesant stepped in to fix the demoralized settlement — making peace with the Lenape, establishing markets and a night watch, repairing the fort and digging a canal under what is now Canal St. His vision of an orderly trading port drew on his time as governor of Curacao, and the booming Caribbean sugar economy inspired an investment in slave trading that pushed New Amsterdam's enslaved workforce to 20 percent of the population. By the 1650s, warehouses, workshops and gabled houses were spreading back from the river's edge on Pearl St.

The burgeoning sugar economy in the Caribbean inspired an investment in slave trading that soon boosted New Amsterdam's slave workforce to 20% of the population. By the 1650s, warehouses, workshops and gabled houses were spreading back from the dense establishments at the river's edge on Pearl St.

fact_check.omission_check: Stuyvesant's reforms, Curacao governorship link, and the ~20% enslaved share of New Amsterdam's population (roughly 300 enslaved Africans, almost 20% by the mid-1660s) are well-documented and stable.

script_body: In 1741 a spate of fires broke out across the city, including one at Fort George — then the home of Lieutenant Governor George Clarke and the colonial fort that stood here at the foot of the island. The blazes were blamed on African-American slaves, and rumors spread of a plot by rebellious Black New Yorkers and poorer white settlers to burn down the city. Despite contradictory accounts and a lack of solid evidence, the so-called Great Negro Plot led to the arrest and execution of numerous enslaved people and their alleged co-conspirators.

Despite contradictory accounts and a lack of solid evidence, the socalled Great Negro Plot led to the arrest and execution of numerous slaves and their alleged co-conspirators.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. The 1741 fires (first at Fort George, then-home of Lt Gov/Acting Gov George Clarke, on Mar 18, 1741) and the resulting 'Great Negro Plot' arrests and executions (~13 burned, ~17+ hanged) are accurately summarized; historians do dispute whether a real plot existed, which the script acknowledges ('contradictory accounts and a lack of solid evidence').

script_body: As war loomed, Patriots clashed in public spaces with Tories loyal to the king, while Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Hamilton became a fierce anti-British organizer. Revolutionary battle began in August 1776, when General George Washington's army lost about a quarter of its men in just a couple of days. He retreated, and fire engulfed much of the colony — but the British soon left and Washington's army reclaimed the city, celebrating with banquets and fireworks here at Bowling Green.

Citizens fled the city, sensing the oncoming war, and revolutionary battle began in August of 1776, when General George Washington's army lost about a quarter of its men in just a couple of days. He retreated, and fire encompassed much of the colony. But soon the British left and Washington's army reclaimed their city. After a series of celebrations, banquets and fireworks at Bowling Green, General Washington bade farewell to his officers at what is now the Fraunces Tavern Museum and retired as commander in chief.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. Battle of Brooklyn/Long Island began Aug 27, 1776; American losses (~300 killed, 650 wounded, ~1,100 captured of ~10,000 engaged) make 'about a quarter of his men' a defensible Lonely Planet approximation. Washington's overnight retreat (Aug 29-30) to Manhattan, the Great Fire of Sept 1776, and the British departure on Evacuation Day 1783 with Washington reclaiming the city are all accurate.
unverified_claims: The specific detail of banquets and fireworks celebrated 'here at Bowling Green' (local color from Lonely Planet; not independently corroborated, though consistent with 1783 Evacuation Day celebrations)

script_body: On December 16, 1835, a gas line broke in a dry-goods store near Hanover Square. The fire spread fast — south down Stone St and northeast toward Wall St — and raged for over a day, destroying much of what remained of the original Dutch and British colonial city.

It spread south down Stone St and northeast toward Wall St, raging over a day
It destroyed much of the original Dutch and British colonial city

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. The Great Fire of New York began the evening of Dec 16, 1835, from a ruptured gas pipe igniting in the Comstock & Andrews dry-goods store near Hanover Square (Beaver/Hanover/Wall area); it raged through the bitter-cold night into the next day, destroyed ~700 buildings across ~17 blocks, and leveled much of the old Dutch/British colonial core. The directional spread (south down Stone St, northeast toward Wall St) is consistent with the affected district.

It stood where Chinatown now lies

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. Five Points is widely described as the city's (and America's) first/most notorious slum, centered on the Baxter/Worth/Mosco intersection in what is today Chinatown / Columbus Park. Surrounding context (Great Fire of 1835, Draft Riots of 1863, cholera epidemics) is accurate.

script_body: Central Park was conceived as a grand project to boost the health of people crammed into tiny tenement apartments — an 843-acre public park. Work began in 1855 in an area so far uptown that some immigrants kept pigs, sheep and goats on the land. From the start the park was both a vision of green reform and a boon to real-estate speculation.
key_claims: Central Park was an 843-acre public park begun in 1855
The area was so far uptown some immigrants kept pigs, sheep and goats there
It was both green reform and a boon to real-estate speculation
source_passage: And there was yet another grand project afoot – one to boost the health of the people crammed into tiny tenement apartments – in the form of an 843acre public park. Begun in 1855 in an area so far uptown that some immigrants kept pigs, sheep and goats there, Central Park was both a vision of green reform and a boon to real-estate speculation.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. Central Park is 843 acres. The 'Work began in 1855' date is defensible: the city began the land-acquisition/eviction process for the park around 1853-1856, though physical construction proper began in 1857 (a ~2-year nuance, not a clear error). Pre-park land was occupied by ~1,600 residents including squatters who kept hogs/goats; the dual framing of green reform plus real-estate speculation is accurate.

script_body: German-born engineer John Roebling set out to solve the winter freezes that kept shutting down the ferry between downtown Manhattan and Brooklyn, then an independent city. He designed a soaring symphony of spun wire and Gothic arches to span the East River, and his Brooklyn Bridge accelerated the fusion of the neighboring cities.

physical_cues.cue: The spun-wire cables and Gothic arches spanning the East River

key_claims: Roebling sought to solve winter freezes that shut down the Manhattan-Brooklyn ferry
He designed a bridge of spun wire and Gothic arches over the East River
The bridge accelerated the fusion of the two cities
source_passage: Another vision was realized by German-born engineer John Roebling, who sought a solution to a series of winter freezes that had shut down the ferry system connecting downtown Manhattan to Brooklyn, then an independent city. He designed a soaring symphony of spun wire and Gothic arches to span the East River, and his Brooklyn Bridge accelerated the fusion of the neighboring cities.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. John A. Roebling was a German-born (Prussian) engineer and suspension-bridge/wire-rope pioneer who designed the Brooklyn Bridge over the East River, connecting Manhattan with Brooklyn (then an independent city until 1898 consolidation). The bridge's spun-wire cables and Gothic-arched stone towers still stand and span the East River. The 'winter freezes shutting down the ferry' motivation is the book's framing and is plausible (the East River was known to freeze in hard winters).

script_body: The Brooklyn Bridge opened with fanfare on May 24, 1883. After New York mayor Franklin Edson and Brooklyn mayor Seth Low led President Chester Arthur and Governor Grover Cleveland across, more than 150,000 members of the public followed — each paying a penny for the honor.
key_claims: The bridge opened May 24, 1883
Mayors Edson and Low led President Arthur and Governor Cleveland across
More than 150,000 people crossed, each paying a penny
source_passage: New York's Brooklyn Bridge opened with suitable fanfare on May 24, 1883. After New York mayor Franklin Edson and Brooklyn mayor Seth Low led President Chester Arthur and Governor Grover Cleveland across the structure, more than 150,000 members of the public followed suit, each paying a penny for the honor.

fact_check.omission_check: No misleading omission. The Brooklyn Bridge opened May 24, 1883. NY Mayor Franklin Edson and Brooklyn Mayor Seth Low led the ceremonial crossing with President Chester A. Arthur and NY Governor Grover Cleveland. More than 150,000 people streamed across in the first 24 hours; pedestrian toll was one penny (5c horse-and-rider, 10c horse-and-wagon).

script_body: By the turn of the 20th century, elevated trains carried a million people a day in and out of the city, and the metropolis overflowed with immigrants arriving from southern Italy and Eastern Europe — boosting the population to around three million. The journey from the immigrant landing stations at Castle Garden and Ellis Island led straight to the Lower East Side, where streets reflected these myriad origins with shop signs in Yiddish, Italian, German and Chinese.

Immigrants arrived from southern Italy and Eastern Europe via Castle Garden and Ellis Island
They settled the Lower East Side with shop signs in Yiddish, Italian, German and Chinese

At this point, the city was simply overflowing with the masses of immigrants arriving from southern Italy and Eastern Europe, who had boosted the metropolis's population to around three million. The journey from immigrant landing stations at Castle Garden and Ellis Island led straight to the Lower East Side. There, streets reflected these myriad origins with shop signs in Yiddish, Italian, German and Chinese.

fact_check.omission_check: Historical narrative; no post-2022 change affects it.

script_body: By the late 19th century all sorts of folks were living in squalor — crammed into packed tenements, shivering in soup lines and shoveling snow for nickels — while newly wealthy financiers built European-style chateaux on Fifth Ave. Reporter and photographer Jacob Riis exposed the widening gap between the classes in the New York Tribune and in his now-classic 1890 book, How the Other Half Lives, eventually forcing the city to pass much-needed housing reforms.
key_claims: Late-19th-century poor crammed into tenements while the wealthy built Fifth Ave chateaux
Jacob Riis exposed the class gap in the New York Tribune and his 1890 book How the Other Half Lives
His work forced the city to pass housing reforms

They crammed into packed tenements, shivered in soup lines and shoveled snow for nickels. Reporter and photographer Jacob Riis illuminated the widening gap between the classes by writing about it in the New York Tribune and in his now-classic 1890 book, How the Other Half Lives, eventually forcing the city to pass much-needed housing reforms.

fact_check.omission_check: Historical narrative; Riis dates and Tribune affiliation confirmed.

script_body: Alongside the suffragists holding street-corner rallies for the vote, nurse and midwife Margaret Sanger opened the first birth-control clinic in Brooklyn — where 'purity police' promptly arrested her. After her release from jail in 1921, she formed the American Birth Control League, now Planned Parenthood, which provided services for young women and researched safe methods of birth control.

After her release from jail in 1921 she formed the American Birth Control League (now Planned Parenthood), which provided services for young women and researched methods of safe birth control.

fact_check.omission_check: Sanger opened the first US birth control clinic in Brownsville, Brooklyn (Oct 1916), was arrested; founded American Birth Control League 1921 (precursor to Planned Parenthood). Confirmed.

script_body: The 1920s brought the Jazz Age, when Prohibition outlawed alcohol and fueled bootlegging, speakeasies and organized crime. As the Great Migration carried Black Americans north from the South, Harlem became the center of the Harlem Renaissance — a flowering of poetry, music and painting whose innovative spirit still inspires. Harlem's daring nightlife in the '20s and '30s drew the flappers and gin-soaked revelers who marked the complete failure of Prohibition and foreshadowed the liberated nightlife New Yorkers enjoy today.
key_claims: The 1920s Jazz Age and Prohibition fueled bootlegging and speakeasies
The Great Migration made Harlem the center of the Harlem Renaissance
Harlem's '20s-'30s nightlife marked Prohibition's failure

Babe Ruth reigned at Yankee Stadium and the Great Migration from the South led to the Harlem Renaissance, when the neighborhood became a center of African American culture and society. It produced poetry, music, painting and an innovative attitude that continues to influence and inspire. Harlem's daring nightlife in the 1920s and '30s attracted the flappers and gin-soaked revelers who marked the complete failure of Prohibition, and provided a foretaste of the liberated nightlife New Yorkers enjoy today.

fact_check.omission_check: Canonical history: Prohibition (1920-33), Great Migration, Harlem Renaissance. No issue.

script_body: When the stock market crashed in 1929, the Great Depression descended, and the once-grand Central Park blossomed with shacks derisively called Hoovervilles, after the president who refused to help the needy. The city scraped through on grit, rent parties and public-works projects, until Mayor Fiorello La Guardia found a friend in President Franklin Roosevelt and worked his Washington connections to bring relief money home.
key_claims: The 1929 crash brought the Great Depression
Central Park filled with shacks called Hoovervilles after President Hoover
Mayor La Guardia worked with FDR to bring relief money to the city
source_passage: The stock market crashed in 1929, beginning the Great Depression of the 1930s, which the city dealt with through a combination of grit, endurance, rent parties, militancy and a slew of public-works projects. The once-grand Central Park blossomed with shacks, derisively called Hoovervilles, after the president who refused to help the needy. But Mayor Fiorello La Guardia found a friend in President Franklin Roosevelt, and worked his Washington connections to great effect to bring relief money – and subsequent prosperity – home.

fact_check.omission_check: 1929 crash, Central Park Hooverville on the drained Lower Reservoir (Great Lawn), La Guardia-FDR relief ties all confirmed.

script_body: World War II brought troops galore to the city, ready to party down to their last dollar in Times Square before being shipped off to Europe. As the local factories converted to war industries and hummed — newly staffed by women and African American workers — the wartime boom created a housing crunch that gave New York its much-imitated, tenant-protecting Rent Control Law.
key_claims: WWII troops partied in Times Square before shipping to Europe
War factories were staffed by women and African American workers
The wartime housing crunch produced NYC's Rent Control Law

Converted to war industries, the local factories hummed, staffed by women and African American workers who had rarely had access to good, unionized jobs. The explosion of wartime activity led to a huge housing crunch that brought New York its much-imitated, tenant-protecting Rent Control Law.

fact_check.omission_check: NYC rent control originated 1943 from WWII housing shortage (Emergency Price Control Act); NY was the famed exception that retained it ('much-imitated'). Confirmed.

script_body: As Midtown bulked up with postwar skyscrapers and the financial center marched north, banker David Rockefeller and his brother, Governor Nelson Rockefeller, dreamed up the Twin Towers as a way to revitalize downtown.
key_claims: David Rockefeller and Governor Nelson Rockefeller dreamed up the Twin Towers to revitalize downtown

fact_check.omission_check: David Rockefeller (Chase chairman, DLMA) and brother Gov. Nelson Rockefeller championed the WTC to revitalize downtown; towers nicknamed 'David and Nelson'. Confirmed.

script_body: No one shaped the physical city of the 20th century more than urban planner Robert Moses — wonderfully or tragically, depending on whom you ask. He was the mastermind behind the Triborough Bridge, the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the West Side Hwy and the Long Island parkway system, plus endless highways, tunnels and bridges. His vision did away with intimate neighborhoods of brownstones and town houses in favor of sweeping parks and soaring towers — and his efforts to bulldoze neighborhoods so enraged preservationists that their pushback led to the Landmarks Preservation Commission being formed in 1965.
key_claims: Robert Moses shaped the 20th-century city more than anyone
He built the Triborough Bridge, Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, West Side Hwy and Long Island parkways
Preservationist pushback against his demolitions led to the 1965 Landmarks Preservation Commission
source_passage: Robert Moses, an urban planner who would influence the physical shape of the city more than anyone else in the 20th century – either wonderfully or tragically, depending on whom you ask. He was the mastermind behind the Triborough Bridge (now the Robert F Kennedy Bridge), Jones Beach State Park, the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge, the West Side Hwy and the Long Island parkway system – not to mention endless highways, tunnels and bridges. His vision was one of doing away with intimate neighborhoods of brownstones and town houses, and of creating sweeping parks and soaring towers. The approach got preservationists fired up and their efforts to stop him from bulldozing neighborhoods led to the Landmarks Preservation Commission being formed in 1965.

fact_check.omission_check: Moses built Triborough & Verrazzano-Narrows bridges, West Side Hwy, LI parkways; NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission created April 15, 1965 amid the preservation backlash (Penn Station). Confirmed.

script_body: The 1950s and '60s ushered in an era of legendary creativity and anti-establishment expression centered in Greenwich Village. One movement was abstract expressionism, a large-scale outbreak of American painters — Mark Rothko, Jackson Pollock and Helen Frankenthaler among them — who offended and intrigued with incomprehensible squiggles and exuberant energy. Then there were the writers: Beat poets Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac and novelist-playwright Jane Bowles, who gathered in Village coffeehouses to exchange ideas, often finding inspiration in the folk music of burgeoning names such as Bob Dylan.
key_claims: The 1950s-60s creative era centered in Greenwich Village
Abstract expressionists included Rothko, Pollock and Frankenthaler
Beat writers Ginsberg, Kerouac and Bowles gathered in Village coffeehouses, drawn to folk music like Bob Dylan's

One movement was abstract expressionism, a large-scale outbreak of American painters – Mark Rothko, Jackson Pollock and Helen Frankenthaler among them – who offended and intrigued with incomprehensible squiggles, blotches and exuberant energy. Then there were the writers, such as Beat poets Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac and novelist/playwright Jane Bowles. They gathered in Village coffeehouses to exchange ideas and find inspiration, which was often found in the form of folk music from burgeoning big names, such as Bob Dylan.

fact_check.omission_check: Historical 1950s-60s account; no superseding event affects accuracy.
unverified_claims: That Jane Bowles specifically gathered in Village coffeehouses with the Beats (Bowles spent the 1950s-60s mostly abroad in Tangier; she frequented Greenwich Village bohemia in the 1930s-40s). The book's grouping is loose but the figures and movements named are all correctly associated with the Village creative scene.

script_body: By the early 1970s, deficits had created a serious fiscal crisis that effectively demoted Mayor Abraham Beame to a figurehead. President Ford's refusal to lend federal aid — summed up by the Daily News headline 'Ford to City, Drop Dead' — marked the nadir of the relationship between the US and the city it loved to hate. Massive layoffs decimated the working class, and untended bridges, roads and parks reeked of hard times.

Ford refused federal aid; the Daily News ran 'Ford to City, Drop Dead'

President Ford's refusal to lend federal aid – summed up nicely by the Daily News headline 'Ford to City, Drop Dead' – marked the nadir of the relationship between the US and the city it loved to hate. As massive layoffs decimated the city's working class, untended bridges, roads and parks reeked of hard times.

fact_check.omission_check: Settled 1970s history; Daily News headline ran Oct 30, 1975 after Ford's Oct 29 speech. No omission.

script_body: The traumatic '70s — which hit bottom in 1977 with a citywide blackout and the terrorizing serial killer David Berkowitz — saw rents fall, which nourished an exciting alternative culture. Artists staged performances in abandoned schools, opened galleries in unused storefronts and revived the hair-dye industry with the punk-rock aesthetic. Ramones-loving punks turned former warehouses into pulsing meccas of nightlife, transforming the old industrial precincts of SoHo and Tribeca into America's center of tattooing and independent filmmaking.

Falling rents nourished an alternative punk culture
Punks transformed SoHo and Tribeca warehouses into nightlife and the center of tattooing and indie filmmaking
source_passage: The traumatic '70s – which reached a low point in 1977 with a citywide blackout and terrorizing serial killer David Berkowitz – saw rents fall, which helped nourish an exciting alternative culture that staged performances in abandoned schools, opened galleries in unused storefronts and breathed new life into the hair-dye industry with the advent of the punk-rock aesthetic. Ramones-loving punks turned former warehouses into pulsing meccas of nightlife, transforming the former industrial precincts of SoHo and Tribeca.

fact_check.omission_check: 1977 blackout and Son of Sam (David Berkowitz) are well-documented; cultural characterization is the book's own framing. No omission.

script_body: During the 1970s a wave of arson attacks reduced blocks of apartment houses in the South Bronx to cinders. Amid the smoke, an influential hip-hop culture was born, fueled by the percussive rhythms of Puerto Rican salsa. Rock Steady Crew, led by 'Crazy Legs' Richie Colon, pioneered athletic, competitive break dancing; DJ Kool Herc spun vinyl for all-night break-beat parties; and Afrika Bambaataa, another founding hip-hop DJ, formed Zulu Nation, bringing DJs, break dancers and graffiti writers together to end violence.

Hip-hop was born there, fueled by Puerto Rican salsa
Rock Steady Crew, DJ Kool Herc and Afrika Bambaataa's Zulu Nation were founding forces

Amid the smoke, an influential hiphop culture was born, fueled by the percussive rhythms of Puerto Rican salsa. script_body: Daring graffiti dazzled the public with train-long graphics. The best-known 'masterpiece' belied the writers' reputation as vandals: Lee 163, with the Fab 5 crew, painted a whole subway car with the message 'Merry Christmas, New York.' Some of these maestros of the spray can infiltrated the art world — most notably Jean-Michel Basquiat.

Some of these maestros of the spray can infiltrated the art world, most notably Jean-Michel Basquiat.

script_body: After the early-1990s real-estate crash, the dot-com market roared in, turning geeks into millionaires and the New York Stock Exchange into a speculator's fun park. Buoyed by tax receipts from IPO profits, the city launched a frenzy of building and partying unparalleled since the 1920s. With pro-business Mayor Rudy Giuliani targeting high-crime areas and using statistics to focus police, crime dropped, restaurants boomed and New York became America's safest big city — though things were faltering again as the new millennium dawned.

IPO tax receipts funded a 1920s-scale building and partying frenzy
Giuliani's statistics-driven policing made New York America's safest big city

Buoyed by tax receipts from IPO (initial public offering) profits, the city launched a frenzy of building, boutique-ing and partying unparalleled since the 1920s. The energetic mayor succeeded in making New York America's safest big city, by targeting highcrime areas and using statistics to focus police presence. Crime dropped, restaurants boomed, real-estate prices sizzled, and Sex & the City beamed a vision of sophisticated singles in Manolos around the world. Still, things were faltering in New York at the dawn of the new millennium.

fact_check.omission_check: Dot-com boom and Giuliani-era CompStat crime decline are documented; FBI recognized NYC as the safest large city in the late 1990s. Note Giuliani is a living person but the historical policy/crime claims here are factual, not contested character claims. No omission.

script_body: On September 11, 2001, terrorists flew two hijacked planes into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, turning the whole complex to dust and rubble and killing nearly 3000 people. Downtown Manhattan took months to recover from the ghastly fumes wafting from the ruins, as forlorn missing-person posters grew ragged on brick walls. While the city mourned its dead and recovery crews coughed through the debris, residents braved constant terrorist alerts and an anthrax scare — yet shock and grief drew people together, uniting the often fractious citizenry in a determined effort not to succumb to despair.

Downtown took months to recover from fumes; missing-person posters covered walls
Grief united the citizenry against despair

While the city mourned its dead and recovery crews coughed their way through the debris, residents braved constant terrorist alerts and an anthrax scare. Shock and grief drew people together, uniting the oft-fractious citizenry in a determined effort not to succumb to despair.

fact_check.omission_check: Sept 11, 2001 attacks and ~2,977 deaths at WTC/total are settled history. No omission.

script_body: In 2012, superstorm Hurricane Sandy struck New York. A prestorm surge on October 28 turned parts of Brooklyn and New Jersey into a New World Venice, but Sandy saved her ultimate blow for the next day — cyclonic winds and drenching rain caused severe flooding and property damage, including to the subway system, the Hugh L Carey Tunnel and the World Trade Center site. A major power blackout plunged much of Lower Manhattan into surreal darkness, and trading at the New York Stock Exchange was suspended for two days.

Sandy caused severe flooding to the subway, Hugh L Carey Tunnel and WTC site
A blackout darkened Lower Manhattan and the NYSE suspended trading for two days

While a prestorm surge on October 28 turned parts of Brooklyn and New Jersey into a New World Venice, Sandy saved her ultimate blow for the following day. Cyclonic winds and drenching rain pounded the city, causing severe flooding and property damage, including to the NYC subway system, Hugh L Carey Tunnel and the World Trade Center site. A major power blackout plunged much of Lower Manhattan into surreal darkness, while trading at the New York Stock Exchange was suspended for two days.

fact_check.omission_check: Sandy struck NYC Oct 29, 2012; NYSE closed Oct 29-30 (first consecutive weather closure since 1888); subway, Carey Tunnel and WTC site flooded; Lower Manhattan blackout. All confirmed. No omission.

script_body: Before Ellis Island, the immigrant landing station at Castle Garden — here at the foot of Manhattan — was one of the two gateways through which arriving newcomers passed on their way straight to the Lower East Side.

script_body: New York–style pizza is a very particular item, and the first pizzeria in America was Lombardi's, right here in Manhattan's Little Italy, which opened in 1905. Pizza made its way over to New York in the 1900s through Italian immigrants and its regional style soon developed — the thin crust allowing for faster cooking time in a city where everyone is always in a hurry.
key_claims: Lombardi's was the first pizzeria in America
Lombardi's opened in 1905 in Little Italy
Pizza arrived via Italian immigrants in the 1900s
source_passage: Pizza is certainly not indigenous to Gotham. But New York–style pizza is a very particular item, and the first pizzeria in America was Lombardi's in Manhattan's Little Italy, which opened in 1905. While Chicago–style pizza is 'deep dish' and Californian tends to be light and doughy, New York prides itself on pizza with a thin crust, an even thinner layer of sauce and triangular slices (unless they're Sicilian-style, in which case they're rectangular). Pizza made its way over to New York in the 1900s through Italian immigrants and its regional style soon developed, the thin crust allowing for faster cooking time in a city where everyone is always in a hurry.

script_body: Bagels may have been invented in Europe, but they were perfected around the turn of the 19th century in New York City — and once you've had one here, you'll have a hard time enjoying one anywhere else. It's a ring of plain-yeast dough that's first boiled and then baked, and bagel-makers claim it's the New York water that adds an elusive sweetness never found anywhere else. The most traditionally New York way to order is by asking for a 'bagel and a schmear' — said bagel with a small but thick swipe of cream cheese. Or splurge and add some lox — thinly sliced smoked salmon — as was originally sold from pushcarts on the Lower East Side by Jewish immigrants back in the early 1900s.

inline_foreign_phrases.gloss: a small but thick swipe of cream cheese

key_claims: Bagels perfected in NYC around turn of 19th century
NYC water adds elusive sweetness
Lox sold from pushcarts on Lower East Side by Jewish immigrants in early 1900s
source_passage: Bagels may have been invented in Europe, but they were perfected around the turn of the 19th century in NYC – and once you've had one here, you'll have a hard time enjoying one anywhere else. It's a straightforward masterpiece: a ring of plain-yeast dough that's first boiled and then baked, either left plain or topped with various finishing touches, from sesame seeds to chocolate chips. 'Bagels' made in other parts of the country are often just baked and not boiled, which makes them nothing more than a roll with a hole. And even if they do get boiled elsewhere, bagel-makers here claim that it's the New York water that adds an elusive sweetness never to be found anywhere else. The most traditionally New York way to order one is by asking for a 'bagel and a schmear,' which will yield you said bagel with a small but thick swipe of cream cheese. Or splurge and add some lox – thinly sliced smoked salmon – as was originally sold from pushcarts on the Lower East Side by Jewish immigrants back in the early 1900s.

script_body: The hot dog made its way to New York via various European butchers in the 1800s. One, Charles Feltman of Germany, was apparently the first to sell them from pushcarts along the Coney Island seashore. Nathan Handwerker, originally an employee of Feltman's, opened his own shop across the street, offering hot dogs at half the price of those at Feltman's, eventually eclipsing his former employer's empire. Today, the original and legendary Nathan's still stands in Coney Island, while its empire has expanded on an international scale.

Nathan's original stands in Coney Island

script_body: Don't go expecting eggs or cream in this frothy, old-school beverage — just milk, seltzer water and plenty of chocolate syrup, preferably the classic Fox's U-Bet brand, originally made in Brooklyn. The name stuck even though the ingredients were modified, and soon they were a staple of every soda fountain in New York. While Auster sold them for 3¢ apiece, today they'll cost anywhere from $2.50 to $5.

script_body: The key ingredient in New York–style cheesecake — cream cheese — came from a mistake. A botched attempt at making French Neufchâtel cheese by a 19th-century New York farmer resulted in a curious product. Enter James Kraft, founder of Kraft Foods, who picked it up in 1912, reformulated it, wrapped it in foil and introduced the country to cream cheese. Classic New York cheesecake was then immortalized at Lindy's restaurant in Midtown, opened by Leo Lindemann in 1921, where the particular confection — cream cheese, heavy cream, a dash of vanilla and a cookie crust — became wildly popular in the 1940s. Today, the most famous version is Junior's, right here in Downtown Brooklyn, whose well-known fans include Barack Obama.

script_body: Another New York classic was born in 1874 — the summer-centric Tom Collins. A mix of dry gin, sugar, lemon juice and club soda, the long drink's name stems from an elaborate hoax in which hundreds of locals were informed that a certain Tom Collins had been sullying their good names. While many set out to track him down, clued-in bartenders relished the joke by making the drink and naming it for the fictitious troublemaker. When the aggrieved stormed into the bars looking for a Tom Collins, they were served the drink to cool their tempers.
