script_body: Beer brewing was once a thriving industry in Brooklyn — by the 1870s, the borough boasted a belly-swelling 48 breweries. Most of these were based in Williamsburg, Bushwick and Greenpoint, neighborhoods packed with German immigrants with extensive brewing know-how. By the eve of Prohibition in 1919, the borough was one of the country's leading beer peddlers, famous for kids carrying growlers — beer jugs — as for its bridges. By the end of Prohibition in 1933, most breweries had shut shop. Fast-forward to today and Brooklyn is once more a catchword for craft beer, led by Brooklyn Brewery, brewing IPAs, lagers, non-alcoholic beers and limited-release offerings like raspberry sour ale.

By the eve of Prohibition in 1919, the borough was one of the country's leading beer peddlers, as famous for kids carrying growlers (beer jugs) as for its bridges. By the end of Prohibition in 1933, most breweries had shut shop. And while the industry rose from the ashes in WWII, local flavor gave in to big-gun Midwestern brands. Fast-forward to today and Brooklyn is once more a catchword for a decent brewski as a handful of craft breweries put integrity back on tap. Head of the pack is Brooklyn Brewery, brewing IPAs, lagers, non-alcoholic beers plus limited-release offerings like raspberry sour ale.

script_body: In the 1940s, an influx of cultural figures fleeing the carnage of WWII saturated New York City with fresh ideas. Peggy Guggenheim established the Art of this Century gallery on 57th St, a space that helped launch the careers of painters such as Jackson Pollock, Willem de Kooning and Robert Motherwell. These Manhattan-based artists, along with Elaine de Kooning, Joan Mitchell and Helen Frankenthaler, came to form the core of the abstract-expressionist movement — also known as the New York School — creating an explosive and rugged form of painting that changed the course of modern art.

script_body: By the 1960s and '70s, when New York's economy was in the dumps and much of SoHo lay in a state of decay, the city became a hotbed of conceptual and performance art. Carolee Schneemann organized performances that utilized the human body — at one famous 1964 event, she had a crew of nude dancers roll around in an unappetizing mix of paint, sausages and dead fish in the theater of a Greenwich Village church.

script_body: Contemporary graffiti as we know it was cultivated in NYC. In the 1970s, the graffiti-covered subway train became a potent symbol of the city and work by figures such as Dondi, Blade and Lady Pink became known around the world. Fine artists such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Kenny Scharf and Keith Haring began incorporating elements of graffiti into their work. The movement received new life in the late 1990s when a new generation of artists — many with art-school pedigrees — began using cut paper and sculptural elements. Less celebratory was the 2013 closure of the iconic 5Pointz, a cluster of Long Island City warehouses dripping with Technicolor graffiti — not even a plea from legendary British artist Banksy could save the veritable gallery, condemned to demolition. Today, spray-can and stencil hot spots include the Brooklyn side of the Williamsburg Bridge and the corner of Troutman St and St Nicholas Ave in Bushwick.

The movement received new life in the late 1990s when a new generation of artists – many with art-school pedigrees – began using materials such as cut paper and sculptural elements. Well-known New York City artists working in this vein include John Fekner, Stephen 'ESPO' Powers, Swoon, and the twin-brother duo Skewville and Shepard Fairey, who later went on to create the Obama 'Hope' poster. script_body: New York City has been a magnet for musicians across every genre. The city was where jazz players such as Ornette Coleman, Miles Davis and John Coltrane pushed the limits of improvisation in the 1950s; where folk singers Bob Dylan and Joan Baez crooned protest songs in coffeehouses; where bands such as the New York Dolls and the Ramones tore up the stage in Manhattan's gritty downtown; the nerve center of disco; and the cultural crucible where hip-hop was nurtured and grew. The local indie-rock scene is especially vibrant — groups including the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, LCD Soundsystem and Animal Collective all emerged in NYC, with Williamsburg at the heart of the action, packed with clubs, bars, indie record labels and internet radio stations.

It was the nerve center of disco. And it was the cultural crucible where hip-hop was nurtured and grew – and then exploded. The city remains a magnet for musicians. The local indie-rock scene is especially vibrant: groups including the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, LCD Soundsystem and Animal Collective all emerged in NYC. script_body: For nearly 100 years, New York City has been at the center of American dance. The American Ballet Theatre — founded by Lucia Chase and Richard Pleasant — was founded in 1939 and promoted the idea of cultivating American talent, hiring native-born dancers and putting on works by choreographers such as Jerome Robbins, Twyla Tharp and Alvin Ailey. NYC is also known for nurturing a generation of modern-dance choreographers such as Martha Graham, who challenged traditional notions of dance with boxy, industrial movements on bare, almost abstract sets. The boundaries were pushed further by Merce Cunningham, who disassociated dance from music.

script_body: The city that is home to the country's biggest publishing houses has also been home to some of its best-known writers. In the 19th century, Herman Melville (Moby Dick), Edith Wharton (The House of Mirth) and Walt Whitman (Leaves of Grass) all congregated here. Literary life became even more exciting in the early 20th century — there were the liquor-fueled literary salons of poet-communist John Reed in the 1910s, the acerbic wisecracks of the Algonquin Round Table in the 1920s, and the thinly veiled novels of Dawn Powell in the '40s, whose work often critiqued New York's media establishment.

There were the liquor-fueled literary salons of poet-communist John Reed in the 1910s, the acerbic wisecracks of the Algonquin Round Table in the 1920s and the thinly veiled novels of Dawn Powell in the '40s, whose work often critiqued New York's media establishment.

Later decades brought new voices from under-represented corners of the city, including Puerto Rican-Cuban writer Piri Thomas and Audre Lorde, a groundbreaking feminist poet and civil rights activist.

The city's passion for local and artisanal food continues, with organic tomatoes grown at Upper East Side delis and beehives on East Village tenement rooftops.

script_body: Today the arts scene in New York is mixed and wide-ranging. The major institutions — the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Guggenheim Museum, and the Brooklyn Museum — deliver major retrospectives covering everything from Renaissance portraiture to contemporary installation. The New Museum of Contemporary Art, on the Lower East Side, is more daring. New York remains the world's gallery capital, with well over 1000 spaces showcasing all kinds of art across the city.

New Museum of Contemporary Art is the more daring institution among NYC's major museums

The New Museum of Contemporary Art, on the Lower East Side, is more daring, while countless smaller institutions, among them the excellent Bronx Museum, El Museo del Barrio and the Studio Museum in Harlem, focus on more precise slices of art history. script_body: A number of gay-owned businesses once lined MacDougal St, among them the legendary Eve's Hangout at number 129, a tearoom run by Polish Jewish immigrant Eva Kotchever, known as Eve Addams. There she ran a bookstore and club in Paris, fought in the Spanish Civil War, and was eventually imprisoned and murdered in Auschwitz. Playwright Barbara Kahn wrote Unreachable Eden about Kotchever's life.

script_body: Harlem's drag balls became a hit with gay and straight New Yorkers in the roaring '20s. The biggest was the Hamilton Lodge Ball, run by Lodge #710 of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows and held annually at the swank Rockland Palace on 155th St. Commonly dubbed the Faggots Ball, it let men and women legally cross-dress and steal a same-sex dance, with a beauty pageant crowning the 'Queen of the Ball.' Langston Hughes called it the 'spectacles of color,' and the gay writer was one of many literati to attend; the papers covered the outrageous frocks as the talk of the town.

script_body: By the 1940s and '50s, the relative transgression of the early 20th century had given way to a new conservatism — the Great Depression, WWII and the Cold War took their toll, and Senator Joseph McCarthy declared that homosexuals in the State Department threatened America's security and children. Tougher policing forced the queer scene underground, and crackdowns on gay venues grew increasingly common. Yet on June 28, 1969, when police raided the Stonewall Inn — a gay-friendly watering hole in Greenwich Village — patrons did the unthinkable: they revolted. Fed up with harassment and with corrupt officers taking payoffs from the bars' mostly organized-crime owners, they bombarded the police with coins, bottles, bricks and chants of 'gay power' and 'we shall overcome.' They were met by a line of high-kicking drag queens and their now-legendary chant. The collective anger and solidarity was a turning point, igniting passionate debate about discrimination and forming the catalyst for the modern gay-rights movement — not just in New York but across the US and in countries from the Netherlands to Australia. On the one-year anniversary, the day was marked by the US's first LGBTIQ+ Pride march.

Conservatism was helped along by Senator Joseph 'Joe' McCarthy, who declared that homosexuals in the State Department threatened America's security and children. Tougher policing aimed to eradicate queer visibility in the public sphere, forcing the scene further underground in the 1940s and '50s. Yet on June 28, 1969, when police officers raided the Stonewall Inn – a gay-friendly watering hole in Greenwich Village – patrons did the unthinkable: they revolted. Fed up with both the harassment and corrupt officers receiving payoffs from the bars' owners (who were mostly organized-crime figures), they began bombarding the officers with coins, bottles, bricks and chants of 'gay power' and 'we shall overcome.' Their collective anger and solidarity was a turning point, igniting intense and passionate debate about discrimination and forming the catalyst for the modern gay-rights movement, not just in New York, but across the US and in countries from the Netherlands to Australia. On the one-year anniversary of the riots, the day was marked by the US's first LGBTIQ+ Pride march.

script_body: LGBTIQ+ activism intensified as AIDS hit headlines in the early 1980s. Writer Larry Kramer helped found ACT UP — the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power — in 1987 to fight perceived homophobia and the price-gouging of AIDS drugs. One of its boldest protests came on September 14, 1989, when seven ACT UP protesters chained themselves to the VIP balcony of the New York Stock Exchange, demanding that Burroughs Wellcome lower the price of the AIDS drug AZT from a prohibitive $10,000 per patient per year. Within days, the price was slashed to $6400.

script_body: In 2013, New Yorkers reeled when Mark Carson, a Brooklyn man, was fatally shot in Greenwich Village — one of Manhattan's most historically tolerant neighborhoods. Carson and a friend had been walking along 8th St in the early hours of May 18 when, after a short altercation with a group of men hurling homophobic abuse, the 32-year-old was shot at point-blank range. The attack was a sobering reminder that even in liberal New York City, not everyone is happy to live and let live.

script_body: The heart of New York's local film scene was Queens' still-kicking Kaufman Astoria Studios. Founded by Jesse Lasky and Adolph Zukor in 1916 as a one-stop-shop for their Famous Players–Lasky Corporation, the complex produced a string of silent-era hits, among them The Sheik (1921) and Monsieur Beaucaire (1924), both starring Italian-born heartthrob Rudolph Valentino, as well as Manhandled (1924), starring early silver-screen diva Gloria Swanson. Renamed Paramount Pictures in 1927, the studios became known for turning Broadway stars into big-screen icons — among them the Marx Brothers, Fred Astaire, and Ginger Rogers, the latter making her feature-film debut as a flapper in Young Man of Manhattan (1930).

script_body: Despite Paramount moving all of its feature film shoots to Hollywood in 1932, the complex — renamed Eastern Services Studio — remained the home of Paramount's newsreel division. Throughout the 1930s it was also known for its 'shorts,' which launched the careers of homegrown talents including George Burns, Bob Hope, and Danny Kaye. After a stint making propaganda and training films for the US Army between WWII and 1970, the studios were renamed Kaufman Astoria Studios by George S. Kaufman — the real-estate magnate, not the playwright — in 1982. It was here that the Huxtables lived out their middle-class Brooklyn lives in the '80s TV sitcom The Cosby Show, and it's still here that small-screen favorite Sesame Street is taped.

After a stint making propaganda and training films for the US Army between WWII and 1970, what had become known as the US Signal Corps Photographic Center was renamed the Kaufman Astoria Studios by George S Kaufman (the real-estate magnate, not the playwright) in 1983. It was here that the Huxtables lived out their middle-class Brooklyn lives in the '80s TV sitcom The Cosby Show, where the heroine of Nurse Jackie juggled addictions and work, and the inmates of Litchfield Penitentiary battled their demons in Orange is the New Black. script_body: In the cult musical Fame (1980), New York High School of Performing Arts students do little for the city's traffic woes by dancing on Midtown's streets. script_body: Up until the 19th century, life in New York City was primarily concentrated in what is now Lower Manhattan. Around 1700, the city barely extended beyond Fulton Street, and a hundred years later only a handful of additional apartment blocks had been built. When City Hall opened in 1812 it seemed unimaginable that the city might continue growing to the north.

script_body: At the end of the 19th century, Chinatown was often the scene for fighting street gangs, such as the Dead Rabbits and the Bowery Boys. Apartments in what is today Columbus Park garnered notorious nicknames such as Bone Alley, Kerosene Row, and Bandits' Roost. Chinatown has long since shaken off this reputation; today the dynamic neighborhood is a popular destination thanks to its plethora of stores and restaurants.

script_body: Jane's Carousel dates back to 1922. For years it operated in Youngstown, Ohio. The developer of the park where it currently stands bought it in 1983, together with his wife, Jane. After years of renovation it was restored to its original glory, and Jane's Carousel reopened in 2011. Now young and old can enjoy a ride for a fair price.

script_body: Castle Clinton was built on a man-made island and completed in 1811. Its initial purpose was to protect the harbor from the British. Later it functioned as a theater and then as a landing depot for immigrants — between 1855 and 1890, some 8 million immigrants passed through here. For a time after that, the castle was even home to the New York Aquarium. Today you can purchase tickets here for the ferry over to the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island.

script_body: On the site where Fort Amsterdam stood during the 17th century now stands the US Custom House, whose first three stories house the National Museum of the American Indian. The custom house was completed in 1907, at a time when the Port of New York was the most important port in the United States — sixty percent of all customs duties in the country were collected here.

script_body: Federal Hall National Memorial stands on the site where George Washington took the oath of office as the first U.S. president and where the first Congress convened. Today it is a museum about Washington's inauguration, freedom of the press, and Federal Hall — the first capitol, which stood on this spot.

script_body: The High Line opened in 2009 on an old train-line spur that runs through Chelsea and the Meatpacking District dozens of feet above street level. Until 1980 the line carried goods to and from the area's warehouses; after falling into disuse it was slated for demolition, until local residents came up with the idea of turning it into an elevated park. Because most of the surrounding buildings are relatively low, the High Line offers an amazing view out over the Hudson River and Chelsea.

script_body: A trip to the High Line feels like walking on a very long balcony that extends all the way through the city. The elevated park sits 30 feet above street level and stretches 1.45 miles from Gansevoort Street to West 34th Street, looking out over the Hudson River, old warehouses, and the streets of Manhattan.

physical_cues.cue: Elevated walkway 30 feet above the street, like a long balcony
Views over the Hudson River and old warehouses

key_claims: Park is 30 feet above street level
Stretches 1.45 miles from Gansevoort Street to West 34th Street
source_passage: A trip to the High Line, an elevated park built on a former train viaduct, feels like walking on a very long balcony that extends all the way through the city. The park is 30 feet above street level and stretches 1.45 miles (2.33 km) from Gansevoort Street to West 34th Street. From up here you can look out over the Hudson River, old warehouses, and the streets of Manhattan.

source_attribution.author: Moon Travel Guides
source_attribution.chapter: Walk 2: NoLIta, SoHo, West Village & High Line

script_body: The Bowery Mural is an open-air canvas — a wall where both well-known and lesser-known artists display their art. It's an initiative of Tony Goldman, Jeffrey Deitch, and Deitch Projects, who control the real estate the wall is part of. The first artist was Keith Haring, who added a piece here in 1982, kicking off nearly fifty years of urban graffiti art in the neighborhood.

physical_cues.cue: Large open-air mural wall at the corner of Houston and Bowery

key_claims: Bowery Mural is an open-air rotating mural wall
Initiative of Tony Goldman, Jeffrey Deitch, and Deitch Projects
First artist was Keith Haring
Started nearly 50 years of urban graffiti art in the neighborhood
source_passage: The Bowery Mural is actually an open-air canvas—a wall where both well-known and less well-known artists display their art. It’s an initiative from Tony Goldman, Jeffrey Deitch, and Deitch Projects that are responsible for the real estate of which the mural is a part. The first artist was Keith Haring, who added a piece on the wall in 1970 and started almost 50 years of Urban Graffiti Art in the neighborhood.

source_attribution.author: Moon Travel Guides
source_attribution.chapter: Walk 2: NoLIta, SoHo, West Village & High Line

corrections.claim: Keith Haring added the first piece in 1970
corrections.reason: The book's 1970 date is impossible (Haring was born in 1958). Multiple independent sources confirm Haring's Houston/Bowery mural was painted in 1982; it is described as his first large-scale public work.

script_body: The New Museum shows international exhibitions of contemporary art, giving emerging artists a platform that often leads to adventurous works — everything from sound installations to a simulated spaceship interior. In 2007 the museum moved to a bigger home on the Bowery, where you can easily spend hours taking in the art.
key_claims: Shows international contemporary art and supports emerging artists
Moved to a bigger Bowery home in 2007
source_passage: Visit the New Museum to see international exhibitions of contemporary art, featuring new art and new ideas. Emerging artists are given a platform for their work here, which often leads to exciting and adventurous works, including everything from sound installations to a simulated spaceship interior. In 2007 the museum moved to a bigger home on Bowery, where you can easily spend hours taking in all the artwork.

script_body: This small Little Italy museum began in 1999 as a temporary exhibit. It was met with overwhelming success, which led to the founding of the Italian American Museum in 2001. Here you can learn about the history of Italian Americans and see a variety of cultural exhibits.

Italian American Museum founded in 2001
Covers Italian-American history and culture

script_body: The Singer Building is an excellent place to start exploring SoHo's cast-iron architecture. It was erected in 1902 by the Singer Manufacturing Company, known primarily for sewing machines, and today houses offices and apartments.

Singer known primarily for sewing machines
A starting point for SoHo cast-iron architecture

script_body: The small, unassuming house at 105 Mercer Street has a remarkable history. One year after it was built in 1831, it became one of SoHo's most thriving brothels — a reminder that this neighborhood was once the city's red-light district.

key_claims: House at 105 Mercer Street built in 1831

SoHo was once the city's red-light district
source_passage: The small, unassuming house at 105 Mercer Street has a rather remarkable history. One year after it was built in 1831, it became one of SoHo’s most thriving brothels. It’s hard to imagine that, back in the day, SoHo was once the city’s red-light district.

script_body: Some of SoHo's most beautiful cast-iron buildings stand on Greene Street. The building at numbers 72-76, known as the "King of Greene Street," is one of the prime examples of the style in the neighborhood — take a step back to fully admire its tall windows and Corinthian columns.

The building at numbers 72-76, known as the “King of Greene Street,” is one of the prime examples of this type of architecture in the neighborhood. Take a step back to fully admire the tall windows and Corinthian columns.

script_body: For years the townhouse at 66 Perry Street was the backdrop for the series Sex and the City — the home of main character Carrie Bradshaw, set here in the West Village. Since then this quaint street has surged in popularity, and every day fans come to pose for a photo in front of the charming brownstone.

source_passage: For years the townhouse at 66 Perry Street was the backdrop for the series Sex and the City. The show’s main character, Carrie Bradshaw, lived here in the West Village, and since then this quaint street has seen a rise in popularity. Every day, countless fans come here to pose for a photo in front of the charming brownstone.

script_body: The Whitney Museum of American Art holds America's most diverse forms of artistic expression from the 20th and 21st centuries — Jasper Johns, Andy Warhol, paintings, sculptures, videos, and performance art. It was established in 1931 by the wealthy sculptor and art collector Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney with 700 works from her own collection; today the permanent collection holds around 18,000 pieces. Its well-known Whitney Biennial spotlights young, unknown talents.

Founded with 700 works from her own collection
Permanent collection now around 18,000 pieces
Whitney Biennial spotlights young talents
Holds works by Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol
source_passage: The Whitney Museum of American Art is a collection of America’s most diverse forms of artistic expression from the 20th and 21st centuries. See works from Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol, along with everything from paintings and sculptures to videos and performance art. The Whitney Biennial, which spotlights young, unknown talents, is particularly well known. The museum was established in 1931 by the wealthy sculptor and art collector Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney with 700 works from her own collection.

script_body: Fashion designer Marc Jacobs opened the bookshop Bookmarc in 2010 to celebrate his love of books, selling coffee-table books and other gems in a selection he curates himself. It's also a launch spot — Richard Hell, Grace Coddington, and Anjelica Huston all held their book launches here.

Richard Hell, Grace Coddington, and Anjelica Huston held book launches here

At Bookmarc they sell coffee table books and other gems in a selection curated by Marc Jacobs himself. And Bookmarc NYC is the place to be for book presentations. Richard Hell, Grace Coddington, and Anjelica Huston all held their book launches here.

script_body: You'll know you're close to Magnolia Bakery when you start seeing people carrying white boxes. Inside are the cupcakes made famous by the TV series Sex and the City — though if you're not in the mood for a cupcake, the banana pudding is the other thing to try.

script_body: In June 1969, a violent clash at the Stonewall Inn, near Christopher Park, sparked the fight for equal rights for gays and lesbians. Since then the park and its surroundings have become a symbol of gay liberation, and Christopher Street nearby is lined with LGBTQ bars and shops.

physical_cues.cue: Stonewall Inn near Christopher Park, with LGBTQ bars and shops along Christopher Street

key_claims: A violent clash at the Stonewall Inn in June 1969
Began the fight for equal rights for gays and lesbians
Christopher Park and area became a symbol of gay liberation
source_passage: In June of 1969, a violent clash at the Stonewall Inn near Christopher Park led to the start of the fight for equal rights for gays and lesbians. Since then, the park and its surrounding area have been the symbol of gay liberation. In the vicinity, especially on Christopher Street, there are a variety of LGBTQ bars and shops.

source_attribution.author: Moon Travel Guides
source_attribution.chapter: Walk 2: NoLIta, SoHo, West Village & High Line

script_body: Oreo cookies were once made in this old factory building. Today Chelsea Market is a place for food and shopping, with many options inside — the lobster roll at Lobster Place is highly recommended — and a hall where you can sit and people-watch, or take your food upstairs to the High Line.

physical_cues.cue: The old factory building now housing Chelsea Market's food hall

key_claims: Oreo cookies were once made in this factory building
Now a food and shopping hall
Connected upstairs to the High Line

There are many food options available here, but the lobster roll at Lobster Place is highly recommended. Look for a place to sit in the hall and enjoy people-watching as you eat. If there are no free tables, take your food outside and head upstairs to the High Line.

script_body: The Museum of Arts and Design, known as MAD, holds some 2,000 items in its permanent collection alone, including objects of fashion, design, and jewelry. There is more than enough here to give you a sense of how craft, ornament, and everyday objects become art.
key_claims: MAD holds about 2,000 items in its permanent collection

source_passage: The Museum of Arts and Design (MAD) has some 2,000 items in the permanent collection alone, including objects of fashion, design, and jewelry.

script_body: MAD is also known for its radical building renovation, which was not very well received in the architecture world. Particularly controversial were the windows, which appear to spell out the word "hi." Look up at the facade on Columbus Circle and judge for yourself. On the flip side, diners in the ninth-floor restaurant have an excellent view of Central Park.

Rooms on the north side of the hotel have a great view of Central Park, and if you're not dressed too shabbily you can probably steal a peek into the lobby.

script_body: The world-famous Museum of Modern Art, MoMA, holds an extensive and unique collection of contemporary and modern art. There is plenty to see, from a helicopter suspended from the ceiling and a collection of old computers to artwork by Picasso and modern video art. Don't forget to also visit the MoMA Design Store.

Don't forget to also visit the MoMA Design Store.

script_body: Learn all about the history of radio and television at the Paley Center for Media. Here you can watch and hear a Frank Sinatra concert, re-experience the first Star Trek episode, or settle in for a documentary, all drawn from the center's broadcasting archive.

script_body: 21 Club stands for all the history and stories that make New York so fantastic. Since 1930, "The 21" has been an institution for "everyone who is anyone," made clear by the enormous number of artifacts donated by famous people over the years. The jockey statues on the facade are proud gifts from Jay van Urk, the Vanderbilts, and many other notables.

The jockeys on the façade are proud gifts by Jay van Urk, the Vanderbilts, and many other notables.

script_body: The impressive St. Patrick's Cathedral, built in 1879, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the United States and can seat more than 2,000 people. Be sure to look for the Tiffany altars, the stained-glass windows, and the Pieta, the statue of Mary holding the body of Jesus.

script_body: In 1928, John D. Rockefeller bought a piece of property that he developed into office buildings and public promenades. He called it Rockefeller Center. Come here in winter to go ice skating next to the giant Christmas tree, and don't pass up a trip to 30 Rockefeller Plaza and the observation deck, Top of the Rock, with its unobstructed view of Central Park and the Empire State Building.

Come here in the winter to go ice skating next to the giant Christmas tree. script_body: One of the most popular events at Radio City Music Hall is the "Christmas Spectacular" with performances by the Rockettes. Radio City Music Hall is the largest covered theater in the world and a beautiful example of art deco style.

script_body: With its bright lights, enormous billboards, and constant crowds, Times Square is the pulse of New York City. Under the red stairs you'll find the TKTS Booth, where you can buy discounted tickets, sometimes up to 50 percent off, for shows on and off Broadway and for dance and music performances. Go early, because the lines can be long.

script_body: The largest branch of the New York Public Library opened in 1911 and is housed in the Stephen A. Schwarzman Building. In the 1930s, Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia gave the marble lions sitting outside the building the nicknames Patience and Fortitude. In doing so, he was emphasizing the very qualities New Yorkers needed to endure the Depression.

script_body: Head to Bryant Park for some rest and relaxation. Grab a coffee and a snack at one of the kiosks, then sit back and take in the tall buildings around you. At the east edge of the park is one of the city's most popular outdoor bars, and in summer there are open-air movies every Monday night. Until 2010, New York Fashion Week was also held here twice a year, before it moved to Lincoln Center.

script_body: Grand Central Terminal is a Beaux Arts masterpiece that embodies the romanticism of train travel. Its annual Holiday Laser Light Show, a Christmas-themed display projected onto the ceiling of the main hall, begins on November 30 and runs for six weeks. It is very impressive.

The Holiday Laser Light Show projects on the main hall ceiling from November 30 for six weeks

script_body: The Chrysler Building is the crowning achievement of auto-industry giant Walter P. Chrysler. Designs of hubcaps and fenders are worked into the building inside and out, and you'll find waterspouts shaped like radiator caps. The 1,046-foot art deco monument opened in 1930 as the tallest building in the world, only to be dethroned one year later by the Empire State Building.

physical_cues.cue: Hubcap and fender motifs and radiator-cap-shaped waterspouts on the facade

source_passage: The Chrysler Building is the crowning achievement of auto industry giant Walter P. Chrysler. Designs of hubcaps and fenders have been incorporated into the building both inside and out. You'll also find waterspouts in the shape of radiator caps. The 1,046-foot-tall (319 meters) building is a unique art deco monument. When it opened in 1930, the Chrysler Building was the tallest building in the world. One year later, it was dethroned by the Empire State Building.

script_body: The wonderful collection at The Morgan Library & Museum came from the private holdings of wealthy banker and art collector John Pierpont Morgan. In 1924, eleven years after his death, it was opened as a public institution. The collection includes manuscripts, drawings, books, and old Middle Eastern tablets, among other things.

script_body: The Empire State Building was the result of a race between the chairmen of General Motors and Chrysler to see who could build the world's tallest building first; General Motors "won." The pencil-shaped tower opened in 1931 and, until 1971, was indeed the tallest building in the world. The view from the 86th floor is as phenomenal as ever.

script_body: Gramercy Park is the only non-public park in New York; only residents living in the area hold a key. In the 19th century most apartments here were intended for the poor, so the apartments at 34 Gramercy Park East were called "French flats" to set them apart from the working-class buildings nearby. Go for a drink on the beautiful terrace of the Gramercy Park Hotel.

Vendors offer organic fruits and vegetables, bread, cheese, and organic wine, and you can catch cooking demonstrations from famous local chefs and sample their creations.

Be sure to also check out the cooking demonstrations from famous local chefs and sample their creations.

trigger_address: 47-49 E 65th St, between Madison and Park avenues
script_body: The Roosevelt House is actually two houses with one shared entrance. Sarah Delano Roosevelt gave the house to her son Franklin and his new bride, Eleanor, and the dominating mother lived at number 47. In 1921 and 1922, FDR and his wife lived at number 49 while he was recovering from polio. The house always remained their home base whenever they were in New York. Following Sarah's death in 1941, the house was sold.

script_body: The 7th Regiment Armory, also known as Park Avenue Armory, seems a bit like a fort. The large brick building, dating back to 1880, was once the headquarters of the seventh regiment of the New York National Guard. The interior is beautifully decorated, but after 120 years the building had grown dilapidated. In 2006 the Park Armory Conservancy began significant renovations to transform it into a unique place for unconventional art.

script_body: The neoclassical Naumburg Bandshell was built in Central Park in 1923. Since then, artists of all ilk have performed here. Famous people such as Martin Luther King Jr. and John Lennon have also stood on this stage. The Mall runs through the middle of the park, from the Bethesda Terrace down to 66th Street, lined with benches where you may have to compete with street artists, roller skaters, and skateboarders for a seat.

script_body: Hard as it is to imagine today, up until the 19th century this part of New York City was considered the wilderness. The area wasn't built up until after 1880, when construction began on its first apartment complex — the Dakota. As more train lines were laid, it became easier for New Yorkers to live farther from their work downtown. Thus the Upper West Side was born.

poi_name: General Ulysses S Grant National Memorial
script_body: The 18th president, General Ulysses S. Grant, and his wife Julia were laid to rest at the General Grant National Memorial — but not technically buried in the tomb. Thus an old student's riddle asks, 'Who is buried in Grant's Tomb?' The answer, of course, is nobody. A Civil War hero, Grant was hugely popular in his time, which explains why his is the largest mausoleum in North America.

source_passage: Standing 392 feet tall (120 meters), Riverside Church, which was completed in 1930, is the tallest church in the United States. The building was modeled on the Gothic cathedral of Chartres in France. Inside the church hangs a carillon with 74 bells—the heaviest in the world. The largest bell weighs 18 tons, and the smallest just 11 pounds.

script_body: Columbia University is one of the oldest, wealthiest, and largest universities in the country, and a prestigious Ivy League school. In 1897 the university moved to its current location in Morningside Heights. A mix of classic and modern architecture and an abundance of green space make this a truly urban campus. Among its famous alumni you'll find Theodore Roosevelt, John Jay, and Barack Obama.
key_claims: Columbia is an Ivy League school
It moved to Morningside Heights in 1897
Alumni include Theodore Roosevelt, John Jay, and Barack Obama
source_passage: Columbia University is one of the oldest, wealthiest, and largest universities in the country, not to mention it's a prestigious Ivy League school. In 1897, the university moved to its current location in Morningside Heights. The hustle and bustle here, combined with a mix of classic and modern architecture and an abundance of green space make this a truly urban campus. Among the impressive list of famous Columbia alumni, you'll find Theodore Roosevelt, John Jay, and Barack Obama.

script_body: The most photographed item on the Columbia campus is probably the bronze Alma Mater statue. With her outstretched arms and an open book on her lap, she seems to welcome students and visitors. Hidden among the folds of her robe is an owl, the symbol of wisdom. Legend has it that the first student of each incoming class to find the owl will graduate at the top of the class.

Legend has it that the first student of each incoming class to find the owl will graduate at the top of the class.

script_body: Low Memorial Library is a classical building dating to 1895, set in the middle of the Columbia campus with a dome-shaped roof and a row of columns out front. Despite the name, the building has not housed a library since 1934. Instead it holds school offices and the Visitors Center, and the lobby displays a collection of artifacts from the university's history.

key_claims: Low Memorial Library dates to 1895

source_passage: Low Memorial Library is a classical building dating back to 1895. The building, with its dome-shaped roof and row of columns in front, is located in the middle of the Columbia University campus. Despite the name, the building has not housed a library since 1934. Instead, it is home to a number of school offices as well as the Visitors Center (office 213), where you can pick up a map of campus. For those interested in the university's rich history, there is a collection of artifacts on display in the building's lobby.

script_body: If bigger is indeed better, you may never find a better cathedral than the Cathedral Church of Saint John the Divine. Construction of this colossus began in 1891 and is still not complete — a truly time-consuming affair. Every April dozens of cyclists come to the church for the traditional blessing of the bikes.

Construction of this colossus, which began in 1891 and is still not complete, has been a truly time-consuming affair. script_body: When the Studio Museum opened in 1968, it was the first museum in the country dedicated to promoting the work of African American artists. The space feels more like a gallery or studio, and you can see work from the 19th and 20th centuries by African American artists or artists influenced by black culture. Temporary exhibits have included historical photos of the 1920s Harlem Renaissance.

It shows 19th- and 20th-century African American art and Harlem Renaissance photos
source_passage: When Studio Museum opened in 1968, it was the first museum in the country dedicated to promoting the work of African American artists. In this museum, which actually feels more like a gallery or studio, you can check out artwork from the 19th and 20th centuries by African American artists or artists influenced by black culture. In addition to the permanent collection, the museum also has temporary exhibits, such as—for example—historical photos of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s.

script_body: Astor Row is the name for the 28 townhouses on the south side of West 130th Street in Harlem. Designed by Charles Buek and built between 1880 and 1883, the houses were very progressive for their time. Each is three stories, set back about 20 feet from the road, and has a beautiful wooden porch — though many porches are no longer original, due to necessary renovations.

Designed by Charles Buek and built between 1880 and 1883, the houses were very progressive for their time. Each one is three stories, set back about 20 feet (6 meters) from the road and has a beautiful wooden porch. However, many of the porches are no longer originals due to necessary renovations.

Others have made their debut during the famous Wednesday-night 'Amateur Night,' a true one-of-a-kind experience. The theater even has its own Walk of Fame.

script_body: There's nothing more American, more New York, or more typical of Harlem than jazz. Jazz lives in this borough, and the National Jazz Museum in Harlem captures it — a not-too-big collection that gives a great overview of jazz in New York.

script_body: Riverside Park runs along the west side of Manhattan, stretching about four miles — from 155th Street in the north down to 59th Street in the south — with great views of the Hudson. Around 91st Street there's a local plot called the People's Garden, wonderfully maintained by 40 diligent volunteers.

Views of the Hudson River along the park's length

key_claims: Riverside Park stretches ~4 miles from 155th to 59th Street
The People's Garden near 91st Street is maintained by 40 volunteers
source_passage: Riverside Park is located on the west side of Manhattan. It stretches about 4 miles (6.5 km), from 155th Street in the north to 59th Street in the south. This is a good alternative to Central Park if you are looking for someplace green to relax—it's also where residents of the Upper West Side and Harlem come. Here you can go for long walks and bike rides while enjoying a great view of the Hudson. Around 91st Street there is a local garden—the People's Garden—which is wonderfully maintained by 40 diligent volunteers.

script_body: North of the Upper West Side lies an important center of African American culture: Harlem. Here you'll find art galleries, churches often named after notable African American figures, the legendary Apollo Theater, and much more. In recent years Harlem has experienced a wave of gentrification, and the neighborhood's historical brownstones and wide streets have been drawing people from across the city.

In recent years Harlem has experienced a wave of gentrification, and the neighborhood's historical brownstones and wide streets have been attracting people from around the city.

script_body: Until the late 19th century, Williamsburg was mainly where Manhattan's elite came for a weekend away from the city. It didn't officially become part of New York City until 1898, when Brooklyn became a borough. Then the Williamsburg Bridge was completed in 1903, putting a crossing of the East River within reach of the average person. Newly arrived immigrants and people fleeing the packed tenements of the Lower East Side flooded into Brooklyn, and Williamsburg became one of the most densely populated neighborhoods in the city.
key_claims: Williamsburg became part of NYC in 1898 when Brooklyn became a borough
Williamsburg Bridge completed 1903
Immigrants from the Lower East Side made it one of the most densely populated neighborhoods
source_passage: Until the late 19th century, Williamsburg, in Brooklyn, was primarily a place where the Manhattan elite came for a weekend away from the big city. It didn't officially become part of New York City until 1898, when Brooklyn became a borough of New York City. The completion of the Williamsburg Bridge in 1903 made it possible for the average person to travel across the East River. Newly arrived immigrants and those escaping the packed tenement buildings of the Lower East Side soon flooded into Brooklyn, and Williamsburg became one of the most densely populated neighborhoods in the city.

script_body: Brooklyn has always been a melting pot, and that's still visible in Williamsburg. The neighborhood originated in what is now South Williamsburg, where there are significant populations of Hasidic Jews, Puerto Ricans, and Dominicans. The northern part, known as the North Side, is home to large Polish and Italian communities. In recent years many young Manhattanites have made the move across the water, and Williamsburg has become one of Brooklyn's hippest, most popular neighborhoods — artists and creative types were the trailblazers, but a growing influx of young professionals now lives in luxury waterfront apartments with a view of the city.
key_claims: South Williamsburg has Hasidic Jewish, Puerto Rican, and Dominican populations
The North Side has large Polish and Italian communities
Young Manhattanites moved in; artists were trailblazers, then young professionals
source_passage: Brooklyn has always been a melting pot of cultures, and this is still very visible in Williamsburg today. Williamsburg originated in what is now South Williamsburg. Here there are significant populations of Hasidic Jews, Puerto Ricans, and Dominicans. The north of Williamsburg, known as the North Side, is home to large Polish and Italian communities. Recent years have seen many young Manhattanites making the move across the water, and Williamsburg has become one of Brooklyn's hippest, most popular neighborhoods.

script_body: In creative Williamsburg, street art is a way of life. Nowhere else in New York City will you find so many murals, stickers, and stencils on walls, facades, lampposts, doors, mailboxes, curbs, or just about anywhere. Pay attention and you'll start to notice the recurring work of certain artists throughout the neighborhood.

Those who pay attention will notice the recurring work of certain artists throughout the neighborhood.

script_body: The Williamsburg Bridge connects Manhattan and Williamsburg, carrying cars and trucks but also a separated path for cyclists and pedestrians. The view of eastern Manhattan from the Williamsburg side is amazing, and because foot and bike traffic is kept apart from vehicles, crossing is both safe and pleasant.

script_body: The Williamsburg Art & Historical Center is housed in the original Kings County Savings Bank — an ornate 1860s building that still stands as a New York City landmark. Today it is the best-known gallery in the neighborhood, with exhibits that change regularly and range from paintings and sculptures to installations and modern art by both American and international artists.

script_body: The tiny City Reliquary Museum is definitely not your average museum — it's packed with rare artifacts tied to the history of New York City. There's a replica of the Bay Ridge Barbershop, which operated in Brooklyn for 50 years, along with a collection of items from the 1964 World's Fair held in New York. The gift shop carries fun, interesting pieces by local artists.

There is a replica of the Bay Ridge Barbershop, which operated in Brooklyn for 50 years, as well as a collection of items from the 1964 World's Fair held in New York.

script_body: Republic of Booza was the first shop in the United States to sell booza, an ice cream invented about 500 years ago in the eastern Mediterranean. Ice cream as we know it descends from booza, but booza is more elastic and creamier, with a richer taste. The ancient recipe arrives here in a hypermodern, almost Japanese interior, alongside experimental flavors like Chinese pepper with Oreo cookies.

Booza ice cream was invented about 500 years ago in the eastern Mediterranean. Ice cream as we know it, is based on booza, but booza is more elastic and creamier and has a richer taste.

The company had its roots in Australia, where owner Toby Smith started roasting his own coffee, and years later it opened its first American location here in Williamsburg. Partners still pours "short blacks" and "flat whites" alongside small-batch roasted beans.

script_body: Since 1952 the United Nations headquarters has stood on this spot beside the East River. The buildings' simple geometric shapes, glass walls, and deliberate lack of cultural references are characteristic of the International Style in which they were built — an architecture meant to belong to no single nation. The Visitors Centre is free and regularly hosts exhibits, and you can also take a guided tour inside.

Its permanent collection spans art from world cultures alongside paintings and sculptures, but it's the temporary exhibitions in particular that draw the crowds. You won't see everything in a single day here, so you'll have to make some choices.

At its head sits Grand Army Plaza with the Soldiers & Sailors Monument, forming the formal entrance to the park. Around the plaza you'll find the Brooklyn Library, the Brooklyn Museum, and Flatbush Avenue, which separates Prospect Park from the Brooklyn Botanical Garden. It's a place with lots to do.

At the point is Grand Army Plaza, with the Soldiers & Sailors Monument, which forms the entrance to the park. Around this plaza you'll find the Brooklyn Library, the Brooklyn Museum, and Flatbush Avenue that separates Prospect Park from the Brooklyn Botanical Garden. It's a place with lots to do.

script_body: Hudson River Park stretches some 4.5 miles along the water, from Battery Park up to 57th Street. It's full of activity: come here for kayaking, ice skating, tennis courts, boat clubs, and playgrounds, with events organized throughout the year. There's a scenic two-mile walking route that starts at Battery Park; in summer the grassy field fills with sunbathers, and there are even outdoor showers to cool down when it gets too hot.

Come here for kayaking, ice skating, and playing in the playgrounds. There are also tennis courts and boat clubs. Throughout the year many events are organized in the park. Tip: there's a scenic 2-mile walking route along the Hudson River that starts at Battery Park. Afterward, have a refreshing drink at Pier 45. In the summer the grassy field fills up with sunbathers—there are even outside showers to help you cool down when it gets too hot.

script_body: The Museum at FIT, part of the Fashion Institute of Technology, is a slice of heaven for fashion lovers. It holds the world's largest collection of garments and accessories, with fashion and haute couture spanning the 18th century to the present, plus regular exhibitions from big names in the field. During New York Fashion Week a visit here is a must — you might even run into a famous designer or blogger.

script_body: Governors Island lies less than half a mile off the coast of lower Manhattan. For nearly 200 years it was closed to civilians as a military base, but since 2006 it has been open to the public, with ferries shuttling visitors across the water in just seven minutes. Come for the military history, a festival, a picnic near the Statue of Liberty, or simply the greenery and the view of the NYC skyline — a good way to explore is by bike, your own or one rented from Bike and Roll on arrival.

physical_cues.cue: View of the NYC skyline across the water

source_passage: Governors Island is a small island less than half a mile off the coast of lower Manhattan. For nearly 200 years Governors Island was not accessible to civilians, but since 2006 it has been open to the public. Ferries shuttle visitors across the water to this former army base in just seven minutes. Come here for the military history, for a festival, to picnic near the Statue of Liberty, or simply to enjoy the greenery and the awesome view of the NYC skyline. script_body: For the more than twelve million immigrants who crossed the Atlantic between 1892 and 1954, the first glimpse of their new home was a one-hundred-and-sixty-five-foot copper woman, green from oxidation, holding a torch of liberty. Etched on the pedestal are the famous lines from Emma Lazarus's poem: "Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free."

script_body: Since 1886 this statue — broken shackles at her feet and a tablet bearing the date of independence in her hand — has stood as an inspiration for Americans. A museum in the pedestal tells the story of sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi's creation, which was built with money donated by the French public and shipped across the Atlantic. The statue arrived in New York Harbor in 1886 in three hundred and fifty pieces, then was reassembled and dedicated in October of that year.

script_body: One of Manhattan's oldest buildings, this tavern was by the 1760s a popular meeting place for patriots known as the Sons of Liberty. Here, in 1783, George Washington bade farewell to the officers of the Continental Army. script_body: Federal Hall is all about George Washington and "firsts." The bronze statue on the front steps marks the spot where Washington was inaugurated as president in 1789. This was the first capitol building of the new nation, where the first U.S. Congress met, and it was also the original City Hall of New York. The current building — an early example of Greek Revival architecture — was finished in 1842, and the broad steps outside still offer a great view of the narrow historic streets of the nation's first capital.

script_body: This historic church was founded by Anglicans in 1697 and destroyed twice — by fire in 1776 and after heavy snow in 1839. The current Gothic Revival church dates from 1846. Among the congregation's prominent members was the Federalist Alexander Hamilton, who is buried in the churchyard.

script_body: It would be impossible to imagine New York without its immigrant populations, visible in the Lower Manhattan enclaves of Little Italy and Chinatown. Every group that settled here — like the Italian stonemasons and Eastern European tailors of the nineteenth century — added to America's cultural heritage. The familiar "melting pot" term came from a 1908 play of the same name by the Anglo-Jewish activist and writer Israel Zangwill, though for New York it is somewhat misleading: the ethnic groups did not meld but clustered in neighborhoods that preserved their language, culture, food, and customs.

script_body: Lower Manhattan technically takes in everything below Houston Street, between the Hudson and East Rivers, and its historic role founded New York City and turned it into a commercial power. Later, in 1785, New York became the first capital of the new nation following the Revolutionary War.

script_body: The Tredwells' 1832 Federal-style row house is reportedly Manhattan's most haunted house. Each month from January to October it presents Candlelight Ghost Tours, in which Gertrude Tredwell — the last family owner, who died in 1933 — is summoned from the great beyond. By day, eight rooms over three floors keep the family's fixtures, furnishings, decorative arts, and personal possessions exactly as they left them, the city's only 19th-century home to retain its original interior and exterior.

script_body: This slimline park sits 30 feet above the ground, created along 1.45 miles of disused freight track. script_body: New York's literary roots trace to Washington Irving, considered the first American to make a living from writing. Famous for the short story "Rip Van Winkle," Irving was born and raised in post-colonial Manhattan. In 1807 he launched the satirical literary magazine Salmagundi, in which he coined the term "Gotham" as a pseudonym for New York — a nickname that has clung to the city ever since.

script_body: Once an immigrant neighborhood, the East Village acquired its distinctive feel in the 1960s as the haunt of artists, musicians, and hippies, and as the center of America's counterculture. It was home to writers of the Beat Generation in the 1950s; with the rise of 1960s counterculture, hippies moved in where immigrants had once settled. Gentrification has since erased some of the area's grittiness, but its artsy vibe survives in graffiti-covered walls and independent stores.

script_body: During the 1950s and '60s, the Chelsea Hotel became a bohemian commune where artists, musicians, and writers hung out. The famed venue played host to musical luminaries including Bob Dylan, Patti Smith, Jimi Hendrix, and Janis Joplin, as well as writers such as Arthur Miller and Gore Vidal. Songs, stories, and novels were written both in and about the hotel — Arthur C. Clarke penned 2001: A Space Odyssey while staying here.

script_body: The triangular sliver of land formed by the intersection of Fifth Avenue, Broadway, and 23rd Street dictated the foundation for this oddly shaped structure, completed in 1902. Designed by Daniel H. Burnham and Co., of Chicago World's Fair fame, and originally named the Fuller Building, this early skyscraper's three-sided configuration led to its current name. A National Historic Landmark, it was one of the first structures built with a steel frame that formed a strong foundation for its exterior walls — a principle employed in many later skyscrapers.

Today, benches sit among shady trees, historic statuary, and year-round public art.

script_body: Financier Pierpont Morgan amassed an extraordinary collection of rare artwork, literature, and music memorabilia. script_body: Oil fortune heir John D. Rockefeller, Jr., hatched the idea of a grand cultural, commercial, and entertainment complex on a large Midtown property he was leasing from Columbia University. The task of creating this 'city within a city' was handed to Wallace K. Harrison, whose team helped construct nineteen buildings, ranging from immensely tall to surprisingly short, fronted by a plaza that would become a New York icon in its own right. The center's 'front door' is on Fifth Avenue, with the stubby Maison Française on the left and a mirror-image British Empire edifice on the right; the flower-filled Channel Gardens in between provide a route into the heart of the center, culminating in Rockefeller Plaza. Soaring straight up from the plaza, the seventy-story General Electric Building reflects both the art deco vibe of the 1930s, when most of Rockefeller Center was built, and the boxy modernism of the postwar period. Affectionately called '30 Rock' by those who work within, the skyscraper was originally home to the Radio Corporation of America, RKO Pictures, and NBC television, and its lobby flaunts massive murals by Spanish artist José Maria Sert.

Although the church was consecrated in 1879, construction continued through the turn of the 20th century. Its twin spires were the tallest landmark along Fifth Avenue until the early 1930s... The 108-foot-high (34 m) nave can seat 2,500 people, and a number of its exceptionally rich stained-glass windows were made in Chartres, France.

script_body: A masterpiece of beaux arts design, this steel, granite, and limestone building opened in 1913 as the city's state-of-the-art train depot. Outside, beneath the massive central window, a statue commemorates railroad tycoon Cornelius Vanderbilt. In the Main Concourse the vaulted ceiling is decorated with the constellations of the zodiac, and as light streams through the cast-iron windows and shadows move across the Tennessee marble floor, the space looks more like an ancient temple than a hub for transportation.

script_body: Art deco's fusion of the utilitarian with the artistic reaches its peak in the Chrysler Building. Automobile magnate Walter P. Chrysler funded the structure himself, working closely with architect William Van Alen. Although the 1,050-foot building kept its 'world's tallest' tag for only a year, its artistic merit has continued to soar. Many of Van Alen's details were inspired by car motifs, including the stainless steel gargoyles modeled after the radiator caps of a 1929 Chrysler. The building is best viewed from the Empire State Building's observation deck, but visitors can also explore the art deco lobby, once a Chrysler showroom.

script_body: A standout along this part of the East River, the United Nations complex still looks as modern today as it did upon its completion in 1952. American architect Wallace K. Harrison had overall design control, but consulted other maestros including Brazil's Oscar Niemeyer and France's Le Corbusier, who devised the winning plan. The 39-story Secretariat Building dominates the complex, and directly below it sits the futuristic General Assembly building with its swayback roof and trademark dome. Guided tours start from the Public Lobby of the General Assembly building.

script_body: The robust lines and soaring spires of the Chrysler and Empire State Buildings epitomize New York's love affair in the 1920s and '30s with the streamlined design of art deco. The style acquired official recognition at a 1925 exhibition in Paris, the 'Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs,' and the shorthand term 'art deco' stuck. Its sunbursts, chevrons, zigzags, and other geometric patterns could be applied to diners and jewelry, elevators and comic books, planes, trains, and automobiles, and New York transformed itself into a science-fiction metropolis of silvery skyscrapers.

script_body: Stretching from 59th to 110th Streets between Central Park and the East River, the Upper East Side has been the neighborhood of choice for the city's wealthy elite since the late 1880s. That pedigree accounts for the town houses, mansions, and upscale shops that line the placid blocks from Fifth to Lexington Avenues. East of Third Avenue the scene shifts to newer high-rise apartments, though older brownstones still turn up on the side streets. Now gentrified, these blocks were once German and Hungarian immigrant neighborhoods, and many of the churches and purveyors here still remind visitors of that heritage.

script_body: Steel magnate Henry Clay Frick, who lived from 1849 to 1919, commissioned this mansion from the prestigious Carrère and Hastings architecture firm. Completed in 1914, it lets you appreciate art in an intimate residential setting rather than a gallery. Frick filled his home with eighteenth-century French furniture and porcelain, Oriental rugs, paintings, sculpture, and an exceptional assortment of small bronzes. Holdings have been added and the building enlarged since his death, but it has never lost its highly personal feeling — the paintings are hung not by period, but much as they were when Frick lived here.

script_body: In the paneled Living Hall at the heart of the house hang masterpieces by Hans Holbein, Titian, and El Greco. The sweeping West Gallery holds a late Self-Portrait by Rembrandt, Diego Velázquez's King Philip IV of Spain, and Johannes Vermeer's Mistress and Maid. Two more Vermeers wait in the South Hall — Girl Interrupted at Her Music and Officer and Laughing Girl — tracing Frick's fascination with that enigmatic artist. The East Gallery mingles Francisco de Goya and Anthony van Dyck with Édouard Manet and Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin. Finally, linger in the skylit Garden Court, an oasis of greenery.

script_body: One of the world's most preeminent organizations devoted to strengthening ties between Asian countries and the United States, the Asia Society was founded in 1956 by John D. Rockefeller III, and now keeps offices around the world. The crown jewel of its New York headquarters is the Asia Society Museum, whose permanent collection — the Mr. and Mrs. John D. Rockefeller 3rd Collection — includes several hundred masterpieces of Asian art dating as far back as the eleventh century B.C. Rotating exhibitions have ranged across Korean ceramics, Himalayan sculpture, Buddhist art, and Islamic calligraphy.

script_body: The largest art collection in the United States, the Met can be overwhelming, so it pays to decide what to see before you go. It has stood on its current site in Central Park since 1880. Founded in 1870 with the mission of collecting works that represent the broadest spectrum of human achievement at the highest level of quality, it is one of the world's premier encyclopedic art museums. Its sprawling galleries span four city blocks, with a collection drawn from six continents and covering eight millennia of world history — ancient Mesopotamia, nineteenth-century Paris, and 1960s New York all just yards and minutes apart.

script_body: Designed around 1479 to 1482 for Federico da Montefeltro, duke of Urbino, the Gubbio studiolo — a study — is a triumph in woodworking, on view in Gallery 501 on the first floor. The duke used it as a personal haven in his palace at Gubbio, where he could study and think in peace. Using only wood inlay, its maker created a room lined with trompe l'oeil bookshelves and cabinets, and filled the shelves with the duke's favorite books, musical instruments, and scientific tools — all of them, too, rendered in wood inlay.

script_body: The colorful cubiculum — Latin for bedroom — in Gallery 165 on the first floor comes from a place near Pompeii. Painted around 50 to 40 B.C., its frescoes show deities, altars heaped with offerings, and objects such as trompe l'oeil glass vases. The eruption of Vesuvius in A.D. 79 buried the cubiculum in lava and ash, and that burial is exactly what preserved the frescoes until they were excavated in the early twentieth century.

script_body: Without question, the Guggenheim's most famous exhibit is its own landmark building, designed by the American architect Frank Lloyd Wright and as stunningly modernistic today as when it was completed in 1959. Wright's spiraling ramps show off art as few settings can, and the exhibits hung along them have ranged from masterworks to motorcycles. The best way to see it: take the elevator to the top of the Rotunda, then view the collections as you descend the gently sloping ramp.

script_body: Founded in 1904, this museum chronicles the diversity of Jewish culture, both religious and secular. Since 1947 its collections have been housed in the French Gothic-style mansion of philanthropist Felix Warburg, twice expanded over the years and given a sculpture court to hold the vast holdings — nearly 30,000 objects spanning paintings, sculpture, photography, archaeological artifacts, and ceremonial objects. Its two-floor permanent exhibit, Culture and Continuity: The Jewish Journey, follows the Jewish experience over four thousand years through art, artifacts, video, photos, and TV excerpts.

script_body: In 1798, Archibald Gracie, a Scottish-born shipping magnate who lived from 1755 to 1829, bought property here for a country retreat, and built his elegant mansion the following year. His parties drew illustrious guests, among them President John Quincy Adams and the future French king Louis-Philippe. In 1891 the city acquired the former Gracie estate, folding it into the adjoining East River Park. The last of the country mansions that once lined Manhattan's East River shore, Gracie Mansion is New York's oldest wooden building and a model of early American style.

script_body: Journalist Frederick Law Olmsted and architect Calvert Vaux designed the country's first landscaped park here in 1858 to meet a need for urban greenery. As ordinary New Yorkers searched for respite from the nineteenth-century city, members of high society pressed for a dedicated public space in which to socialize, and where the lower classes would benefit from fresh air. After a lengthy debate, an area of Manhattan unsuitable for commercial buildings was chosen as the site. Twenty thousand workers spent twenty years turning swamps into lakes, redesigning the rocky landscape, planting more than 270,000 trees and shrubs, and transforming the whole area into an idyllic pastoral oasis.

script_body: More than 150 species from around the world live in the Central Park Zoo, including red pandas, grizzly bears, and rare snow leopards. The modern five-acre facility was first established as a makeshift menagerie in 1860, expanded in the 1930s, and refurbished in 1984. Among its highlights are the octagonal sea lion pool in the central courtyard, where daily feedings take place, and the Tisch Children's Zoo, which opened in 1997, where kids get the chance to pet and feed goats, alpacas, Vietnamese pot-bellied pigs, and more.

script_body: The Mall is a long, tree-lined pedestrian walkway where New Yorkers once came to stroll in their Sunday best, and it remains a great place for people-watching. It is flanked by benches and rows of giant American elms forming a leafy canopy that entices photographers to attempt the perfect Central Park shot. The Mall's majestic trees form one of the largest remaining collections of American elms in the country — the rest of the population having been largely wiped out by Dutch elm disease.

script_body: The memorial to musician and songwriter John Lennon is a 2.5-acre, tear-shaped garden across the street from the Dakota building, where Lennon and his wife, Yoko Ono, lived at the time of his murder in 1980. The couple often visited this peaceful stretch of the park, which today draws thousands of fans on the anniversaries of Lennon's birth, October 9, and death, December 8 — many staying late into the night singing his favorite songs. Beautifully landscaped and secluded, it has a twisting, ascending path dotted with rustic wooden benches and bronze plaques inscribed with quotations from the Bard. The garden is especially spectacular in spring, when crocuses, hyacinths, and roses bloom.

script_body: This six-acre garden is a popular spot for weddings, thanks to its fairy-tale-like setting, and is composed of three distinct sections: Italian, French, and English. Circular pathways meander around the English-style garden, where magnolias and Japanese lilac trees perfume the air in spring and summer.

script_body: New York's towering buildings and colorful characters have inspired filmmakers since the 1890s, and more than 200 films feature scenes set in Central Park alone — from the sinister assault on Dustin Hoffman and his girlfriend in 'Marathon Man' to the task-force penguins digging a tunnel to escape the Central Park Zoo in 'Madagascar.' New York was first captured on the silver screen in William Heise's 1896 motion picture 'Herald Square,' but many early Manhattan-set movies were actually shot on California sets — a habit that changed with the 1960s 'New Hollywood' era, when Martin Scorsese, Francis Ford Coppola, and Woody Allen found success with stories shot in the city itself.

It is considered polite to run counterclockwise around the park's lake.

script_body: Created by Frederick Law Olmsted, co-designer of Central Park, Riverside Park is much prized by local residents for its tranquility and superb facilities. Begin exploring at 70th Street, where you can also rent bicycles; Pier 1 at 70th Street is an ideal spot for fishing and relaxing, and a summer venue for free concerts and kids' shows. At the 79th Street Boat Basin you can glimpse yachts and sailboats or grab a snack at the Boat Basin Café. Of the park's 15 playgrounds, the River Run Playground at 82nd Street, with its miniature Hudson River, is one of the best. From 83rd Street, the half-mile Serpentine Promenade — a bike and running path — snakes past the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial to New Yorkers who died in the Civil War and the 91st Street Garden, its flowerbeds tended by die-hard volunteers.

source_passage: Created by Frederick Law Olmsted, co-designer of Central Park, Riverside Park is much prized by local residents for its tranquility and superb facilities. Begin exploring at 70th Street, where you can also rent bicycles. Pier 1 at 70th Street is an ideal spot for fishing and relaxing, and a summer venue for free events such as concerts and kids' shows. At the 79th Street Boat Basin you can glimpse yachts and sailboats, or grab a snack at the Boat Basin Café. Of the park's 15 playgrounds, the River Run Playground (82nd St.), with its miniature Hudson River, is one of the best. From 83rd Street, the half-mile (0.8 km) Serpentine Promenade, a bike and running path, snakes past the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial to New Yorkers who died in the Civil War and the 91st Street Garden, its lovely flowerbeds tended by die-hard volunteers.

script_body: No residential building in New York City is more iconic than the aptly named brownstone — long rows of these narrow, three-to-six-story homes distinguish neighborhoods on the Upper West Side and beyond. In New York, the term "brownstone" refers to any kind of row house, whether of brick, limestone, or marble. Beginning in the 1850s, brownstone quarried in Connecticut and New Jersey became the building material of choice, and everyone from middle-class families to the city's elite aspired to live in one — including the railroad magnate William H. Vanderbilt, who owned a $2 million pair at 640 and 642 Fifth Avenue.

script_body: While much of the city had filled with densely packed brownstones by the late 1870s, the Upper West Side remained largely undeveloped until an elevated train arrived in 1879 and kicked off a period of huge growth. The architectural styles of that era — Queen Anne, Romanesque, and Renaissance Revival — encouraged unusual artistic freedom and eclecticism. On the Upper West Side, the houses were visually distinct from one another, often with different colored bricks and stone on a single facade, much to the taste of their socially competitive residents.

script_body: At the top end of Fifth Avenue's Museum Mile, in East (Spanish) Harlem—El Barrio—this museum started life modestly in 1969 as a place to curate and display the art and history of New York's Puerto Rican community. Today its collection of more than 6,500 paintings, sculptures, photographs, and other works of art spans at least 800 years of Latino, Latin American, and Caribbean culture, from pre-Columbian Taino artifacts to late 20th-century pieces. Signage on the exhibits is in both English and Spanish.

script_body: One of the world's largest cathedrals has a floor area of 121,000 square feet and a 232-foot-high vault. Built in fits and starts beginning in 1892, in a mixture of Gothic, Romanesque, and Byzantine styles, it is still only two-thirds complete. On Wednesdays and Fridays at noon and on Saturdays at noon and 2 p.m., you can climb 124 feet up spiral staircases to the top of the cathedral to study the architecture and stained-glass windows.

poi_name: General Ulysses S Grant National Memorial
script_body: A grand, granite mausoleum overlooking the Hudson River in the north of Riverside Park is the final resting place of President Ulysses S. Grant and his wife, Julia. The tomb—the largest in North America—was completed in 1897 and is engraved with the words "Let us have peace," a line from Grant's speech to the 1868 Republican Convention that became his campaign slogan. When the former Civil War general died in 1885, around 90,000 people donated more than $600,000 to build his tomb—then the largest public fundraising effort in U.S. history.

script_body: Starting at the turn of the century, African Americans from across the country, especially the South, moved north to seek better lives, settling in Harlem beginning around 1910. Over time many made their voices heard as poets, intellectuals, and musicians in what became known as the Harlem Renaissance. One of the most successful authors of the period was Langston Hughes; with poems such as "The Negro Speaks of Rivers," he wrote about what it was like to be black in America and encouraged others to do the same. Zora Neale Hurston was the leading black female writer of the period, best known for Their Eyes Were Watching God, one of the first novels based on a black woman's voyage of self-discovery. In 1925, African-American professor Alain Locke edited a collection of poems and essays by black writers called The New Negro; the book shattered stereotypes and was key to defining the Harlem Renaissance. Locke wrote that in Harlem, "Negro life is seizing upon its first chances for group expression and self-determination."

script_body: Artists from Walt Whitman to Spike Lee have drawn inspiration from Brooklyn. The Dutch settled it in 1636 and named it Breuckelen, and it stayed an independent city until 1898, when it was incorporated as a borough of New York. In the years that followed, everyone from New England farmers to European immigrants put down roots in what was then a rural swath of land, now covering around seventy-one square miles. Brooklyn still draws immigrants from all over the world, making it one of the most diverse places in the United States.

script_body: One of the engineering marvels of the nineteenth century, the Brooklyn Bridge was the world's first steel suspension bridge, completed in 1883, and it overawed onlookers with its sheer size. Awe-inspiring it was, but also serviceable: in 1884, circus-founder P. T. Barnum paraded over it with twenty-one elephants to demonstrate that it was safe. Today the bridge inspired both architect Frank Lloyd Wright and artist Georgia O'Keeffe, and crossing it on foot takes about forty-five minutes over its six-thousand-foot span.

script_body: The Brooklyn Bridge was the first-ever bridge to link Manhattan Island to a populous outer borough, and like so many fabled structures, it is supposed to be cursed. Designer John Augustus Roebling died from injuries sustained while taking measurements for the towers. His son Washington was crippled by the bends while overseeing underwater work, but, determined to continue, he supervised the project from afar by watching through a telescope. Opened in 1883, it was the world's longest span for more than twenty years.

script_body: Few New York neighborhoods rival Brooklyn Heights for its historic buildings. Some of the borough's first brick houses and brownstones were built here after 1814, when regular ferry service between Manhattan and Brooklyn was established. Designated New York's first historic district in 1965, the neighborhood has since been protected from invasive development, and a walk down Willow Street reveals some of the handsomest and most architecturally diverse buildings in the city.

script_body: One of the most picturesque and romantic spots in the city, this promenade is perched high above the East River and the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, with lovely views of the harbor, Lower Manhattan, and the Brooklyn Bridge. Stretching for a third of a mile between Remsen and Orange Streets, it draws everyone from tourists and old-timers to teenage couples and families. Completed in 1950 under the influential city builder Robert Moses, the promenade was created in part to appease residents who opposed the construction of the BQE. The design works surprisingly well; even the noise of cars whizzing below is soothing, calling to mind rushing water more than traffic.

script_body: A horticultural triumph, the fifty-two-acre Brooklyn Botanic Garden has been one of the borough's great attractions since 1910. Immaculately maintained and home to wild rabbits, ducks, and turtles, it seems instantly to induce a state of calm. Among its highlights are more than two hundred cherry trees, which blossom in April. Set among rolling hills, the Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden incorporates traditional elements such as a Shinto shrine by the pond, overhung with evergreen trees that make it a truly meditative spot.
