These recordings were at the forefront of the hard-bop movement. The LPs documented two different saxophone-bass-drums trios. Rollins had shown an interest in smaller ensembles as early as 1955; in Paradox, he exchanged four-measure phrases with drummer Max Roach, with no other instrument taking part. In the Vanguard recordings we hear similar styles in arrangements. In the song "Old Devil Moon", Rollins is accompanied only by a bassist and a drummer. Musically, this song set the standard for the piano-less trio.

script_body: A skating rink in this corner of the park was first proposed in 1945. Four years later, in 1949, philanthropist Kate Wollman donated six hundred thousand dollars to build it and commemorate her family. She was the great-aunt of Henry and Richard Bloch, co-founders of H&R Block. One of her brothers was William J. Wollman, who ran the W.J. Wollman & Co. stock exchange firm, originally in Kansas City and later in New York. After he died in 1937, she helped administer his estate.

script_body: The rink had to be closed in the winter of 1980 when its concrete floor buckled. At the time, the renovation was estimated to cost up to 4.9 million dollars and take two years. Instead, the need to solicit bids for three separate contracts, a series of planning errors, construction mishaps, and flooding caused by heavy rains meant the work had not been completed by May 1986. By that point, 12.9 million dollars had been spent, with another two to three million estimated to finish the job by the winter of 1987.

By that time, $12.9 million had been spent, with an additional $2 to $3 million estimated to complete the work by the winter of 1987.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The 1980 closure, $4.9M / two-year original estimate, the multi-contract / planning-error / flooding overrun, and $12.9M spent by 1986 are all corroborated by contemporary reporting recapped in Snopes and HeraldNet.

script_body: Donald Trump then publicly offered to complete the renovations at his own expense within six months, in return for leases to operate the rink and an adjacent restaurant in order to recoup his costs. Instead, Mayor Ed Koch agreed to reimburse Trump for any costs up to an agreed limit, and Trump agreed to donate the profits of the rink and restaurant to charity and public works. Trump convinced the primary contractor, HRH Construction, to do the work without making a profit, telling them that their work would pay for itself with the publicity. However, in the press conferences that Trump held at every incremental milestone in the four-month effort, he never mentioned HRH. Adrian Benepe, then the Parks Department's spokesperson and later its commissioner, stated the project was largely complete by the time Trump entered the picture, and that the city, not Trump, had paid the contractors for the actual reconstruction. The work was completed two months ahead of schedule and 750,000 dollars under the estimated costs.

script_body: In January 2021, New York City mayor Bill de Blasio announced that the city would sever all contracts with the Trump Organization, citing Trump's involvement in the previous week's storming of the United States Capitol. The cancellation of the contracts to operate Wollman Rink, Lasker Rink, and the Central Park Carousel was supposed to take effect on February 26, but the city later allowed the rinks to stay open until the scheduled end of the skating season. The Trump concession expired in April 2021.
source_passage: In January 2021, New York City mayor Bill de Blasio announced that the city government would be severing all contracts with the Trump Organization, citing Trump's involvement in the previous week's storming of the United States Capitol. The cancellation of the Trump Organization's contracts to operate Wollman Rink, Lasker Rink, and the Central Park Carousel was supposed to go into effect on February 26. The city later allowed the rinks to stay open until the scheduled end of the skating season. The Trump concession expired in April 2021.

source_attribution.section: History: Cancellation of Trump Organization contracts

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions for the period this beat covers. de Blasio announced the severance on Jan 13, 2021, naming Wollman Rink, Lasker Rink and the Central Park Carousel (plus Ferry Point Golf Course), with a Feb 26 effective date, later extended to season's end; Trump concession expired April 2021. Subsequent (post-2021) developments — Wollman Park Partners taking over and the Oct 2025 selection of WPP II for a 2027 concession — are outside this beat's scope and do not contradict it.

script_body: From 1966 to 1980, music festivals of 30 to 50 concerts each were held at the rink, named after their main sponsors: Rheingold Beer in 1966 and 1967, the F. & M. Schaefer Brewing Company from 1968 to 1976 in what was called the Schaefer Music Festival, and Dr Pepper from 1977 to 1980 in the Dr Pepper Central Park Music Festival. Among the biggest rock groups who played here were The Jimi Hendrix Experience, The Who, Led Zeppelin, The Beach Boys, and the Patti Smith Group.

script_body: What you're standing near is a not-for-profit social service agency on the Lower East Side that provides social services, arts programs and health care services to New Yorkers of all ages. It was founded under the name Nurses' Settlement in 1893 by progressive reformer and nurse Lillian Wald.

It was founded under the name Nurses' Settlement in 1893 by progressive reformer and nurse Lillian Wald.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions

script_body: In 1892, Lillian Wald was a 25-year-old nurse enrolled in the Women's Medical College when she volunteered to teach a class on home health care for immigrant women at the Louis Down-Town Sabbath and Daily School on the Lower East Side. One day, a young girl approached her, repeating "mommy ... baby ... blood". Wald gathered some sheets from her bed-making lesson and followed the child to her home, a cramped two-room tenement apartment. Inside, she found the child's mother, who had recently given birth and was in need of health care. The doctor tending to her had left because she could not afford to pay him. This was Wald's first experience with poverty; she called the episode her "baptism by fire" and dedicated herself to bringing nursing care, and eventually education and access to the arts, to the immigrant poor on Manhattan's Lower East Side. The next year she founded the Nurses' Settlement, which later changed its name to the Henry Street Settlement.
entities: Louis Down-Town Sabbath and Daily School

script_body: The Settlement's administrative offices are still located in its original federal row houses, dating to about 1832, at 263, 265 and 267 Henry Street. Those three buildings became New York City designated landmarks in 1966. Along with the Neighborhood Playhouse building at 466 Grand Street, they were collectively added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1974 and designated a National Historic Landmark in 1989.

The year before, the Settlement had added new facilities, including a gymnasium at 299, 301 and 303 Henry Street.

script_body: In 1927, the Henry Street Music School began operation, with its formal opening in November 1928. Early supporters of this addition to the settlement included Aaron Copland and Walter Damrosch. In 1937, the school premiered the play-opera The Second Hurricane, which featured music by Copland, a libretto by Edwin Denby, direction by Orson Welles, and orchestral conduction by Lehman Engel. The director at the time, Grace Spofford, initially suggested the idea of a play-opera for school performers, and was largely responsible for bringing the production together. Alumni of the music school include violinists Berl Senofsky, Stuart Canin, Isidor Lateiner, and Helen Kwalwasser; pianists Martin Canin and Jacob Lateiner; and singer Billie Lynn Daniel. Faculty have included violinist Ivan Galamian, pianist Isabelle Vengerova, and composers Paul Creston, Roy Harris, and Robert Starer.

In 1937, the school premiered the play-opera The Second Hurricane, which featured music by Copland, libretto by Edwin Denby, direction by Orson Welles, and orchestral conduction by Lehman Engel. The director at the time, Grace Spofford, initially suggested the idea of a play-opera for school performers, and was largely responsible for bringing the production together. Alumni of the music school include violinists Berl Senofsky, Stuart Canin, Isidor Lateiner, and Helen Kwalwasser (who later became a faculty member); pianists Martin Canin and Jacob Lateiner; and singer Billie Lynn Daniel. Faculty have included violinist Ivan Galamian, pianist Isabelle Vengerova, bassoonist Stephen Maxym, conductor Arnold Gamson, and composers Paul Creston, Roy Harris, and Robert Starer.

script_body: By combining the three townhouses at 263, 265 and 267, the Settlement preserved part of the 1820s streetscape amid what later became a crowded tenement district. The block of Henry Street between Montgomery Street and Grand Street, which also includes St. Augustine's Church, gives an impression of uptown Manhattan as it would have looked in the 1820s and 1830s. Number 263 Henry Street was restored in 1989 and number 265 in 1992.

script_body: Henry Street is known for pioneering efforts in social service and health care delivery. Its innovations included one of New York City's first off-street playgrounds in 1902, funding the first public school nurse that same year, and starting the Visiting Nurse Service. It opened one of the nation's first mental health clinics in 1946, one of the first transitional housing facilities for the homeless in 1972, and the city's first Safe Haven shelter for homeless women in 2007.

Its innovations included the establishment of one of New York City's first off-street playgrounds (1902); funding the first public school nurse (1902); starting the Visiting Nurse Service, which became independent as the Visiting Nurse Service of New York in 1944; opening one of the nation's first mental health clinics (1946), one of the first transitional housing facilities for the homeless (1972), the first Naturally Occurring Retirement Community (NORC) in public housing (1994) and the city's first Safe Haven shelter for homeless women (2007).

script_body: In 2021, the New York State Historic Preservation Office approved Henry Street Settlement's headquarters at 265 to 267 Henry Street as an LGBT historic site. The designation is founded upon Lillian Wald's romantic and platonic relationships with the women she affectionately called "The Family," who provided an essential support network for her from the 1890s until her retirement in the 1930s.

script_body: The entrance sits on Central Park West at West 72nd Street, near where John Lennon was murdered outside The Dakota, the apartment building in which he lived. The memorial is a triangular piece of land falling away on two sides of the park, and its focal point is a circular pathway mosaic of inlaid stones bearing a single word, the title of Lennon's most famous song, "Imagine". The mosaic is laid in the style of Portuguese pavement.

Along a path toward the southeast, a plaque on a low glaciated outcropping of schist lists the nations that contributed to building the memorial. Lennon's widow Yoko Ono, who long lived in The Dakota, contributed over a million dollars toward the landscaping and the upkeep endowment.

At the farthest northern tip of the upper lawns enclosed by woodland stand three dawn redwood trees, which lose their needles but regain them every spring, an emblem of eternal renewal. script_body: In April 1981, a patch of land in Central Park near the Dakota Apartments, where Lennon had lived with Ono, was officially named Strawberry Fields in his memory. That August it was announced that the site would be completely renovated and landscaped, since at the time it sat in an isolated median between West Drive and two slip roads of 72nd Street. Yoko Ono requested that the rebuilt memorial be a living memorial rather than a statue; according to NYC Parks landscape architect Arne Abramowitz, Ono believed that there are enough statues in Central Park.

Speaking on behalf of the United Nations at the dedication was Marcela Pérez de Cuéllar, the UN first lady.

script_body: The memorial is often covered with flowers, candles in glasses, and belongings left behind by Lennon's fans. On his birthday, October 9, and on the anniversary of his death, December 8, people gather to sing songs and pay tribute, staying late into what is often a cold night. Impromptu gatherings have also marked the deaths of other musicians, including Jerry Garcia and George Harrison, and in the days following the September 11 attacks, candlelight vigils were held at the Imagine Circle to remember those killed.
source_passage: The memorial is often covered with flowers, candles in glasses, and other belongings left behind by Lennon's fans.  On Lennon's birthday (October 9) and on the anniversary of his death (December 8), people gather to sing songs and pay tribute, staying late into what is often a cold night. The tributes usually run all night, but for a period through the late 1990s and early 2000s, mayor Rudy Giuliani enforced a curfew, which prohibited people from being inside Central Park after it closed each day at 1:00 a.m. Gatherings also take place on the birthdays of other Beatles. Impromptu memorial gatherings for other musicians, including Jerry Garcia and George Harrison, have occurred at the memorial. In the days following the September 11 attacks, candlelight vigils were held at the Imagine Circle to remember those killed.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Annual gatherings on Oct 9 and Dec 8, tributes for Jerry Garcia and George Harrison, and post-9/11 candlelight vigils at the Imagine Circle reflect the cited revision and are well documented.

script_body: One of the memorial's best-known visitors was Gary dos Santos, a devoted Beatles fan who decorated this spot in circles of different flowers and objects, often in the shape of a peace symbol. Born Ayrton "Gary" Ferreira dos Santos Jr., he was a performance artist who, for 19 years, installed flower designs around and within the "Imagine" mosaic here. His work was documented in The New York Times, and his income came from tips he received from tourists, drawn by his work and by the three-minute monologue he delivered describing it and the life of John Lennon and his family. Santos became the subject of a documentary film, The Mayor of Strawberry Fields, directed by Torre Catalano and distributed by Nehst Studios. For almost twenty years he came to the memorial daily with his girlfriend of fifteen years, Lisa Page, and their dog, Mary Jane, and was well known by many long-time local residents. In September 2013 he was diagnosed with leukemia, and after about nine weeks in the hospital, he died in November 2013.

script_body: In 1960, Fidel Castro came to New York for the opening session of the United Nations. He had first been staying at the Hotel Shelburne on Lexington Avenue in Midtown Manhattan, but he left after the management demanded a twenty-thousand-dollar deposit. Instead, he and his entourage came here to the Theresa, where they rented eighty rooms for eight hundred dollars a day. Malcolm X and other civil rights leaders arranged for their stay. According to The New York Times, Castro felt that 'Negroes would be more sympathetic' to his cause, and indeed he drew enthusiastic crowds of supporters, along with some protesters. While Castro was here, he was visited by Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev, activist Malcolm X, poets Langston Hughes and Allen Ginsberg, President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt, Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru of India, and the radical sociologist C. Wright Mills. In a repudiation of segregationist policies, Castro also thanked the hotel's all-black staff by hosting them at a steak dinner held in the hotel's own banquet room. And subsequent to Castro's visit, other Third World leaders, such as Patrice Lumumba of the Belgian Congo, chose to stay at the Theresa as well.

script_body: In April 1934, the War Department announced its opposition to the Narrows Bridge's construction. The War Department's opposition was based on the fact that a bridge could create a blockage during wartime, a rationale it gave for opposing a Brooklyn–Battery Bridge connecting Red Hook, Brooklyn, with Lower Manhattan. The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey did not have a public position regarding the Narrows Bridge plan, other than a request that it be allowed to operate the future bridge. Following the War Department's announcement that they would oppose the Narrows bridge, private interests began studying the feasibility of a tunnel under the Narrows.

script_body: Three men died during the construction of the bridge. The first fatality was 58-year-old Paul Bassett, who fell off the deck and struck a tower in August 1962. Irving Rubin, also 58 years old, died in July 1963, when he fell off of the bridge approach. The third worker who died was 19-year-old Gerard McKee, who fell into the water in October 1963, after slipping off the catwalk. After McKee's death, workers participated in a five-day strike in December 1963. The strike resulted in temporary safety nets being installed underneath the deck. These nets had not been provided during the four years prior to the strike.

script_body: On June 26, 1976, to celebrate the United States' 200th anniversary, workers placed a very large U.S. flag on the side of the bridge. The flag, which measured 193 by 366 feet, was described in The New York Times as being the size of a football field and a half, and billed as the world's largest flag. It was supposed to withstand wind speeds of 30 miles per hour, but it ripped apart three days later, when there was a wind speed of just 16 miles per hour. The flag had been stuck against the bridge's suspender cables, so any slight wind would have caused the cables to make tears in it.

script_body: In June 2016, St. Francis College student Robert Nash started a petition to spell Giovanni da Verrazzano's name on the bridge correctly, with two "z"s. A bill to formally change the bridge's name passed the New York State Senate in 2017 before being defeated in the New York State Assembly in early 2018. On June 6 of that year, the Senate unanimously passed a bill to change the spelling of the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge. The Assembly passed the bill on June 21, and on October 1, 2018, Cuomo signed the bill into law, effectively changing the legal spelling to the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. The first signs with the corrected spelling were installed in February 2020.
source_passage:
In June 2016, St. Francis College student Robert Nash started a petition to spell Giovanni da Verrazzano's name on the bridge correctly, with two "z"s. The petition gained support from politicians including New York state senators Martin Golden and Andrew Lanza. In December 2016, Golden and Lanza sent letters to the Metropolitan Transportation Authority CEO Thomas F. Prendergast, in which they recommended that the bridge's name be spelled correctly. An MTA spokesperson said the agency was reviewing the letter.
A bill to formally change the bridge's name passed the New York State Senate in 2017 before being defeated in the New York State Assembly in early 2018. In mid-2018, Golden sponsored a State Senate bill to change the bridge's spelling to "Verrazzano" with two "z"s. On June 6 of that year, the Senate unanimously passed a bill to change the spelling of the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge, sending the measure to the New York State Assembly and the office of New York governor Andrew Cuomo for approval. If the bill was passed, the MTA would modify nearly a hundred road signs at a cost of $350,000. The Assembly passed the bill on June 21, sending the measure to Cuomo with a minor modification. As a cost-saving measure, existing signs would retain the one-"z" spelling, and only new signs would contain the double-"z" spelling. On October 1, 2018, Cuomo signed the bill into law, effectively changing the legal spelling of the bridge to the "Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge". The first signs with the corrected spelling were installed in February 2020.

script_body: The Met very nearly ended up somewhere else entirely. Planning for a new home began as early as the mid-1920s, when the backstage facilities of the former house were becoming vastly inadequate for growing repertory and advancing stagecraft. As part of the development of the present-day Rockefeller Center site, there was to be a development with a new 4,000-seat opera house at its center. But financial problems and the following stock market crash of 1929 postponed the relocation of the Metropolitan Opera, and the complex became more commercially based. John D. Rockefeller Jr. replaced the opera house development with the Rockefeller Center complex, which included a 66-story skyscraper, the RCA Building, that opened in 1933.

script_body: Some twenty years after the Rockefeller Center plan fell through, Wallace Harrison — by then a Rockefeller Center veteran — was approached by officers of the New York Philharmonic Society and the Met to develop a new home for both institutions. As chief architect again for the development of Lincoln Center, Harrison was chosen to design the new opera house as the centerpiece of the complex: a twenty-five-acre, eighteen-block site on the Upper West Side, chosen by Robert Moses as a major urban renewal and slum-clearance project. It was not a smooth process. After a long sequence of redesigns, revisions, and opposing interests — the Met wanting a more traditional design, and the architects of the other Lincoln Center venues pulling in other directions — construction of Harrison's forty-third design of the Metropolitan Opera House began in the winter of 1963, making it the last of the three major Lincoln Center venues to be completed. Construction delays tied to finishing the neighboring New York State Theatre, in time with the opening of the 1964 World's Fair, left an excavation site that workers nicknamed "Lake Bing" after then-Met General Manager Rudolf Bing.

script_body: The building's debut came in two stages, and the first was anything but conventional. Although the house would not officially open for several more months, the first public performance at the new Metropolitan Opera House was Giacomo Puccini's La fanciulla del West on April 11, 1966, with Beverly Bower as Minnie, Gaetano Bardini as Dick Johnson and Cesare Bardelli as Jack Rance. The production was attended by 3,000 high school students, and it began with the playing of the National Anthem and a series of sound tests that included a loud chord from the orchestra — and a blast from a shotgun. The new building officially opened on September 16, 1966, with the world premiere of Samuel Barber's Antony and Cleopatra, directed and designed by Franco Zeffirelli and choreographed by Alvin Ailey, starring Leontyne Price as Cleopatra with Thomas Schippers conducting.

Each is roughly 30 feet by 36 feet. The south wall holds The Triumph of Music, while the north wall contains The Sources of Music. In 2009, the Met's board of directors decided to use the paintings as collateral for a long-term loan that had previously relied on cash for backing. Some sources estimate the value of the paintings at twenty million dollars; by 2026, when the Metropolitan Opera contemplated selling the murals to cover a funding deficit, Sotheby's had appraised them at fifty-five million dollars.

script_body: The multi-story lobby is dominated by a concrete and terrazzo cantilevered stairway that connects the main level with the lower-level lounges and the upper floors. Its centerpiece is an array of eleven crystal chandeliers described as resembling constellations, with sparkly moons and satellites spraying out in all directions; the auditorium contains 21 matching chandeliers, the largest measuring 18 feet in diameter. Here is the surprising part: those chandeliers were donated by the government of Austria as repayment for American help during the Marshall Plan following World War II, and were designed by Dr. Hans Harald Rath of J. & L. Lobmeyr of Vienna. Twelve of the auditorium chandeliers sit on motorized winches and are raised to the ceiling before performances so as not to obstruct the sight lines of the audience on the upper levels. In 2008 the lobby chandeliers were dismantled and sent back to the J & L Lobmeyr workshop in Vienna to be refurbished prior to the Met's 125th anniversary season, where workers re-wired the pieces and replaced any of the 49,000 crystals that were broken or missing.

script_body: The building in front of you has a complicated origin story. In 2015 the award-winning architect David Adjaye — whose firm Adjaye Associates designed the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture — was commissioned to design a new home for the Studio Museum, one that would let it expand its exhibition schedule. In 2021, the museum announced it had raised $210 million for the construction, endowment and operating fund for the new building. But by 2023, the museum had severed its relationship with Adjaye in response to allegations of sexual harassment and misconduct against the architect. Work continued anyway, and the building opened on November 15, 2025, at a cost of $160 million. In advance of the official opening, the museum hosted a gala at the new building, raising over $3.7 million.

script_body: Andy Feltz became the Beacon's manager in 1986. That February, the theater's owners announced plans to convert the Beacon into a nightclub and restaurant with a discotheque. At the time, the Beacon was the only mid-sized live-concert venue in Manhattan; the two other similarly sized venues in the borough, Avery Fisher Hall and Carnegie Hall, were largely used for classical music. The operator of the planned nightclub, Olivier Coquelin, said he and his architect Charles A. Platt, a former LPC commissioner, had chosen the Beacon Theatre for conversion specifically because of its landmark status. The nightclub would be built as a freestanding structure within the auditorium, thus reducing the need to modify the protected interior spaces. Area residents expressed concerns that the renovations would damage the landmarked design features. Preservationists and community groups, including the Committee to Save the Beacon Theatre, organized in opposition to the plans.

script_body: The rock band the Allman Brothers Band was at one point the most frequent performer at the Beacon, appearing there nearly every year from 1989 to 2014. After their first performance in 1989, the band returned in 1992, 1994, and annually after 1996; a New York Times article in 2002 called the band's performances "as sure a sign of spring as the reappearance of robins and bellybuttons". The band recorded a live album at the theater in March 2000, releasing Peakin' at the Beacon that November. In 2009, the Allman Brothers Band celebrated its 40th anniversary at the Beacon with shows dedicated to the band's founder and original frontman, Duane Allman. The band could not perform at the Beacon in 2010 because the theater was hosting an extended run of a Cirque du Soleil production, but the band was invited back in 2011. The band played the final show of its career at the Beacon Theatre on October 28, 2014, after 238 total concerts at the theater.

script_body: This was the first suspension bridge to use a Warren truss in its design. It has a main span of 1,480 feet between two 350-foot suspension towers, and its deck carries seven vehicular lanes—four on an upper level and three on a lower level—along with four subway tracks, two each flanking the lower-level roadway. The span is carried by four main cables, which travel between masonry anchorages at either side, and 1,400 vertical suspender cables. The bridge's use of light trusses influenced the design of other long suspension bridges in the early 20th century.

The span is carried by four main cables, which travel between masonry anchorages at either side of the bridge, and 1,400 vertical suspender cables. Carrère and Hastings designed ornamental plazas at both ends of the bridge, including an arch and colonnade in Manhattan that is a New York City designated landmark. script_body: The bridge's debut was a rolling, unfinished affair. One hundred prominent Brooklyn citizens walked over it on December 4, 1909, at a time when the subway tracks were unfinished and there was still uncertainty over which company would use the streetcar tracks. Outgoing mayor George B. McClellan Jr. toured the span on December 24. It officially opened on December 31, 1909, at a final cost of $26 million, although work was still incomplete. Empty commercial vehicles tended to use the Manhattan Bridge, while trucks with full loads used the Brooklyn Bridge, since the Manhattan Bridge's wood-block pavement was less sturdy than the Brooklyn Bridge's plank pavement.

script_body: There's an idea buried in this deck. The Manhattan Bridge was the first suspension bridge to employ Josef Melan's deflection theory for deck stiffening. The theory held that the weight of a suspension bridge's deck, and the downward forces created by vehicles, provided stability to the deck—so such a bridge could use lighter trusses. As such, it was the first suspension bridge in the world to use a lightly-webbed, weight-saving Warren truss. The trade-off showed itself in motion: as built, the bridge sagged by as much as 3 feet when a train crossed it, and it took about 30 seconds for the deck to return to its normal position after a train had passed.

script_body: The uneven weight of subway trains exacted a long, slow toll. Their weight caused deep and widespread cracks to form in the bridge's floor beams, prompting the city to replace 300 deteriorated beams during the late 1970s. The deck twisted up to 8 feet every time a train passed by, and trains had to slow down on the bridge. The condition was blamed on the imbalance in the number of trains crossing, as well as deferred maintenance during the New York City fiscal crisis of the 1970s. One engineer estimated in 1988 that the bridge would cost $162.6 million to repair.

script_body: Now turn to the Manhattan plaza, where the bridge meets the city through a triumphal gateway. The arch and colonnade are made of white, fine-grained Hallowell granite, decorated with two groups of allegorical sculptures by Heber and a frieze called "Buffalo Hunt" by Rumsey. The design references the fact that the Manhattan Bridge continues into Brooklyn as Flatbush Avenue, which runs south to the Atlantic Ocean—so the arch signified the bridge's role as an ocean "gateway." The arch itself was based on Paris's Porte Saint-Denis, and it is one of the city's three remaining triumphal arches, the others being the Washington Square Arch and the Soldiers' and Sailors' Arch. Its opening measures 36 feet high and 40 feet wide. On the northern side, the opening is flanked by carvings of classical ships, masks, shields, and oak leaves; the western pier contains the sculptural group Spirit of Commerce, depicting a winged woman flanked by two figures, while the eastern pier contains Spirit of Industry, depicting the god Mercury flanked by two figures. The arch's keystone contains a depiction of a bison, and above it the "Buffalo Hunt" frieze depicts Native Americans hunting animals while on horseback. The relief is topped by dentils and egg-and-dart ornamentation. The cornice of the arch contains modillions as well as six lion heads, and the interior of the arch contains a coffered ceiling, with rosettes on the arch's soffit. The southern side, facing Brooklyn, is less ornately decorated but has rusticated stone blocks indicative of a Parisian or Florentine bank, with carved lions at the bases of each pier.

script_body: The whole place began as a bequest after the 1801 death of Revolutionary War soldier and ship master Captain Robert Richard Randall. His will set aside much of his estate for public use. His country manor, in what is now Greenwich Village in Manhattan, was reserved as an institution for "aged, decrepit and worn-out sailors", which he called "Sailors' Snug Harbor" — the phrase "snug harbor" meaning a comfortable retreat. That 21-acre tract, which Randall had acquired in 1790, had been assembled from the land grants of two 17th-century Dutch colonists.

US Founding Father Alexander Hamilton and later US Vice President Daniel D. Tompkins are sometimes credited with having written Randall's will, though the extent of their involvement is disputed. The will bequeathed much of his estate for public use. His country manor in what is now Greenwich Village, Manhattan, was reserved as an institution "aged, decrepit and worn-out sailors", which he called "Sailors' Snug Harbor"; the phrase "snug harbor" referred to a comfortable retreat. The 21-acre (8.5 ha) tract, which Randall had acquired in 1790, was assembled from the land grants of two 17th-century Dutch colonists.

script_body: Randall's gift didn't go unopposed. As early as 1817 Manhattan's northward growth had the trustees looking elsewhere for a site, and several challenges to the will delayed any progress. One came from a Stephen Brown, who claimed Randall had been derelict as executor of Brown's grandfather's estate; the trustees refused to acknowledge it. Another was launched in 1826 by Anglican Bishop John Inglis of Nova Scotia, a distant cousin of Randall's who claimed to be an heir. Inglis's lawsuit was eventually escalated to the Supreme Court of the United States, which ruled in favor of the trustees.

script_body: Once the trustees settled on Staten Island, they set out to build the first of what would become five Greek Revival buildings. Work on the first structure, now building C, had begun by September 1831, with a cornerstone laid that October or November. Minard Lafever was involved with the original design but departed abruptly, leaving Samuel Thomson & Son to finish the work. Building C was completed in August 1833, initially housing 37 retired sailors, and John Whetten was appointed the institution's first governor that year. Snug Harbor may have been one of the country's first retirement homes, though it was patterned after older institutions abroad, such as the Greenwich Hospital in London.

script_body: The men who lived here had their own culture. Nineteenth-century sources called them "inmates", a term dropped by the 20th century, but locally they were known as "snugs" or "snuggies". Staff addressed every resident as "captain" regardless of his real rank, even though an implicit hierarchy ran on actual rank and service. There were few rules — be well-behaved, keep your room tidy, obey a curfew — and outside curfew hours men came and went as they pleased, even staying with family or friends for long stretches. At first the only exception was Sunday, when on-site church was required, but even that was no longer compulsory by the 1890s.

There were relatively few rules, other than that residents be well-behaved, keep their rooms tidy, and abide by a curfew. Outside of curfew hours, residents were welcome to come or go as they pleased, and they could stay with families or friends for extended periods. Initially, the only exception was Sunday, when they were required to attend church on-site, though even this was no longer compulsory by the 1890s.

script_body: In 1867 the third governor of Snug Harbor was retired sea captain Thomas Melville — brother of Moby-Dick author Herman Melville. Under his tenure the trustees began paying residents to help with chores, and he oversaw construction of the final two Temple Row buildings, finished in 1879 and 1880. He was also accused of embezzlement during his time here, though later exonerated. Melville ran the place as a strict disciplinarian, frequently punishing rule-breakers by putting them on the "taboo list": men on the list lost their tobacco ration and could not leave the premises. During his governorship, black residents were required to sleep and eat in segregated areas but were allowed to mix with others elsewhere.

script_body: You're standing in the fourth-largest public park in New York City, a 897-acre expanse in the northern part of Queens. Until the 19th century this site was wetlands straddling the Flushing River, which traverses the region from north to south. Then, starting in the first decade of the 20th century, it was used as a dumping ground for ashes, since at the time the land was so far away from the developed parts of New York City as to be considered almost worthless. New York City Parks commissioner Robert Moses first conceived the idea of developing a large park here in the 1920s. The park was created as the site of the 1939 New York World's Fair, and it also hosted the 1964 New York World's Fair.

Starting in the first decade of the 20th century, it was used as a dumping ground for ashes, since at the time, the land was so far away from the developed parts of New York City as to be considered almost worthless. script_body: Beginning in 1910, contractor Michael Degnon set out to fill this land using household coal ash and street sweepings from Brooklyn. He contracted the Brooklyn Ash Removal Company, owned by Fishhooks McCarthy, a member of the corrupt Tammany Hall political machine. Residential ash was collected via trolleys, loaded onto freight trains, and hauled to Corona. The operation was referred to as a citywide refuse "conveyor belt," while the trains were nicknamed the "Talcum Powder Express" because they often ran uncovered and deposited soot onto the surroundings.

script_body: During nearly 30 years of filling, around 50 million cubic yards of ash and waste were dumped onto the meadows site. One particular mound of ash rose 90 feet high and was called "Mount Corona," while the average thickness of the ash was 30 feet. The dumps drew the ire of local residents, due to strong odors and increasing rat infestations, and the meadows were considered one of the worst breeding grounds for mosquitoes in the city. The dump was famously characterized as "a valley of ashes" in F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby. Fitzgerald meanwhile described the Flushing River, now polluted from the dumps, as "a small foul river."

The dumps drew the ire of local residents, due to strong odors and being deemed unsightly, along with increasing rat infestations in the local neighborhoods. Much of the "street sweepings" collected consisted of horse manure from horse-drawn carriages. In addition, many residents simply threw out normal garbage along with the coal ashes. The meadows were also considered one of the worst breeding grounds for mosquitoes in the city. The dump was famously characterized as "a valley of ashes" in F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby. script_body: In 1935, the site, now planned as "Flushing Meadow Park," was selected for what would become the 1939 World's Fair. Houses in Corona east of 111th Street, adjacent to the dumps, were condemned and added to the site, displacing residents. The plans were drafted by Parks Department landscape architect Gilmore David Clarke and his partner Michael Rapuano, designed in Beaux-Arts style. Work on the World's Fair site began on June 16, 1936. The project primarily involved leveling the ash mounds, with the leftover material used to fill other areas of the meadow. Two sites were excavated to create Meadow and Willow Lake, while much of the Flushing River was diverted into underground culverts. The project was an around-the-clock job, with 450 workers operating on three daily shifts. Workers had to combat the effects of high tide, and dust storms created by the ash. Thousands of trees were transplanted to the fair site in order to create a natural landscape. Meanwhile, thousands of 100-foot Douglas fir timbers were driven into the ground to act as pilings for the foundations of the fair structures. The pedestrian plan called for numerous wide tree-lined pathways, including a central "Cascade Mall" leading to the Trylon and Perisphere.
source_passage: In 1935, the site, now planned as "Flushing Meadow Park", was selected for what would become the 1939 World's Fair. Two sites were excavated to create Meadow and Willow Lake, while much of the Flushing River was diverted into underground culverts. A floodgate was built to prevent tidal flow from flooding the lakes. In addition to recreation, the lakes would serve as repositories for excess storm runoff. The dirt from the lake sites was used as additional topsoil for the park. The project was an around-the-clock job, with 450 workers operating on three daily shifts. Workers had to combat the effects of high tide, and dust storms created by the ash. The work significantly changed the topography of the meadows, differing from that created by glaciation. Thousands of trees were transplanted to the fair site in order to create a natural landscape. Meanwhile, thousands of 100-foot (30 m) Douglas fir timbers were driven into the ground to act as pilings for the foundations of the fair structures. The pedestrian plan called for numerous wide tree-lined pathways, including a central "Cascade Mall" leading to the Trylon and Perisphere, many of which would be retained for the park.

script_body: Some of the buildings from the 1939 Fair were used for the first temporary headquarters of the United Nations beginning in 1946. The former New York City Building was used for the UN General Assembly during this time. Robert Moses attempted to sell Flushing Meadows as a permanent headquarters for the UN, which would have required new structures and a complete redesign of the fair ground layout. The proposal was rejected, however, due to concerns over the strength of the former marshland for building construction, the lack of "scenic beauty" in the meadows, and the distance from Manhattan. The UN moved to their now-permanent headquarters in 1951.

Now, when there is something beautiful to be seen, there is no mention of the name Corona."

script_body: Long before it was one place, this was two. In 1857, Michael P. Holland bought land here and named the area after himself. Soon after, Louis Hammel, an immigrant from Germany, bought a tract just east of Holland. In 1878 Hammel gave portions of his land to the New York, Woodhaven and Rockaway Railroad to build a station for the peninsula, and the area around it became known as "Hammels." On June 11, 1897, Hammels merged with Holland and incorporated as the Village of Rockaway Beach.

script_body: In the 1930s, Robert Moses rose to power as New York City's Parks Commissioner, and his road and transportation projects were both a benefit and a disaster for this neighborhood. As commissioner, Moses ordered the construction of the Marine Parkway Bridge and the Cross Bay Veterans Memorial Bridge, completed in 1937 and 1939 respectively. The Marine Parkway Bridge was built further west on the peninsula, between Jacob Riis Park and Breezy Point, linking the isolated communities to Brooklyn. The Cross Bay Bridge landed in the middle of Rockaway Beach itself. That new bridge made the community the peninsula's gateway to Queens, since it provided the only direct car access to the borough. The construction of the two bridges began to transform the neighborhood and the rest of the peninsula into a more year-round residential area, or commuter town, as people had a more convenient way to travel to and from work. The conversion of the Rockaway Beach LIRR branch to the Rockaway subway line also brought an increase in Rockaway's permanent residents.

script_body: The community was devastated by Hurricane Sandy in late 2012. Reconstruction of Rockaway Beach began with Phase One, a $10 million contract from the Army Corps of Engineers to restore 600,000 cubic yards of sand along the beach in August 2013. The second phase put nearly 3.5 million cubic yards of sand in 2014 at a cost of about $37 million, paid by the federal government through the Hurricane Sandy relief bill.
source_passage: The community was devastated by Hurricane Sandy in late 2012. Rockaway Beach reconstruction began with Phase One, a $10 million contract provided by the Army Corps of Engineers to restore 600,000 cubic yards (460,000 m3) of sand along Rockaway Beach in August 2013. The second phase put nearly 3.5 million cubic yards (2,700,000 m3) of sand in 2014 at a cost of about $37 million. Phase Two was paid by the federal government through the Hurricane Sandy relief bill.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions for the post-Sandy reconstruction described. Hurricane Sandy (late October 2012) devastation, Phase One ~600,000 cubic yards of sand (completed Fall 2013, Army Corps), and Phase Two ~3.5 million cubic yards in 2014 at ~$37M (Army Corps figure ~$36.5M, federally funded via Sandy relief) are confirmed. Subsequent larger projects (the $336M Atlantic Shorefront Resiliency Project) post-date this beat but do not change its accuracy.

script_body: As more people moved to the city, the Rockaways became a destination for day trippers. Out-of-towners started to call the beach "Williamsburg on the Rockaways" because some surfers from the Brooklyn neighborhood spend whole summers out here.
source_passage:
With more and more people moving to the city, the Rockaways became a destination for day trippers. The area appears in New York magazine's 2007 spring travel issue as a place for "Surfing" and to "scuba dive for sunken ships".
Out-of-towners start to call the beach "Williamsburg on the Rockaways" because some surfers from the Brooklyn neighborhood spend whole summers out in the Rockaways.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The 'Williamsburg on the Rockaways' nickname reflects the documented mid-2000s-onward influx of Brooklyn (Williamsburg) surfers/day-trippers and the area's reinvention as a surf destination, consistent with multiple feature articles on the Rockaways' surf revival. This is a colloquial/cultural nickname appropriately framed as such.

script_body: Woody Allen's Radio Days, a 1987 movie highlighting the goings-on of a working-class family during the 1930s and '40s, was filmed on location right here in Rockaway Beach.
source_passage: Woody Allen's Radio Days, a 1987 movie highlighting the on goings of a working-class family during the 1930s and '40s, was filmed on location in Rockaway Beach.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Woody Allen's 'Radio Days' (1987), about a working-class family in 1930s-40s Rockaway Beach, was filmed on location there (the family home at 180 Beach 115th St still stands; other locations included a Beach 97th St shop and Rockaways' Playland, demolished 1987 shortly after filming).

script_body: What you are standing on is an artificial island. Little Island is a public park within Hudson River Park, just off the western coast of Manhattan, designed by Heatherwick Studio near the intersection of West Street and West 13th Street in the Meatpacking District and Chelsea neighborhoods. It sits atop Hudson River's Pier 55, connected to the rest of Hudson River Park by footbridges at 13th and 14th Streets. Compact as it is, it packs in two concession stands, a small stage, and a 687-seat amphitheater.

physical_cues.cue: the footbridges connecting the island to the shore at 13th and 14th Streets

source_passage: Little Island at Pier 55 (stylized as Little Island @Pier55) is an artificial island and a public park within Hudson River Park, just off the western coast of Manhattan in New York City. Designed by Heatherwick Studio, it is near the intersection of West Street and West 13th Street in the Meatpacking District and Chelsea neighborhoods of Manhattan. It is located atop Hudson River's Pier 55, connected to the rest of Hudson River Park by footbridges at 13th and 14th Streets. Little Island has two concession stands, a small stage, and a 687-seat amphitheater.

script_body: Look at the pot-shaped structures holding the park aloft. There are 132 of them, known as "tulips", suspended above the water and varying in height, sitting between 15 and 62 feet above the mean waterline. That variation is not just for looks. The design was meant to protect the park from a 500-year flood, during which the water level in the river could rise as much as 11 feet. And the heights of the pots were intended to give the appearance of a floating leaf or a wave.

physical_cues.cue: the tulip-shaped concrete pots rising at varying heights above the water

The tulips vary in height, sitting between 15 and 62 ft (4.6 and 18.9 m) above the mean waterline. The design was meant to protect the park from a 500-year flood, during which the water level in the river could rise as much as 11 ft (3.4 m). The heights of the pots were intended to give the appearance of a floating leaf or a wave.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions
unverified_claims: Exact figure that a 500-year flood would raise the river as much as 11 ft is a specific engineering design parameter not independently corroborated beyond the source; not contradicted by any source.

script_body: Each of those pots is made of four to six lightweight concrete sections called "petals", precast to resist erosion and corrosion. They were manufactured by the Fort Miller Company at their factory in Easton in Upstate New York. To do it, the company hired a partner to create foam molds using a laser cutter, then cleared out a 600-foot-long building to hold the foam pieces. Thirty-nine types of molds were fabricated. As the company's president put it, "A full one-third of our annual production capacity was displaced by this project."
source_passage: Each pot has four to six lightweight concrete sections, referred to as "petals", which are designed to reduce the load on the pilings. The precast concrete is also meant to be resistant to erosion and corrosion. The concrete pots were manufactured by the Fort Miller Company at their factory in Easton in Upstate New York. The Fort Miller Company hired a partner to create foam molds for the pieces of the pots using a laser cutter, then cleared out a 600-foot-long building for these foam pieces. Thirty-nine types of molds were fabricated. According to the company's president, "A full one-third of our annual production capacity was displaced by this project."

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions
unverified_claims: 600-foot-long building cleared for foam molds is a specific construction detail not independently corroborated; not contradicted.

script_body: The whole island stands on a forest of concrete pilings driven into the riverbed, each one three feet in diameter and reaching at most 200 feet down into the bottom of the Hudson River. There were either 267 or 280 of them, and they were not designed in a vacuum. The pilings' design was deliberately intended to evoke the exposed pilings under the old Pier 54, which had previously occupied this very site. Some of those original pilings still exist here today, and are now used as marine habitats.

physical_cues.cue: the old exposed wooden pilings of former Pier 54 still standing in the water

source_passage: The pots stand on 267 or 280 concrete pilings, which extend at most 200 ft (61 m) into the bottom of the Hudson River. Each piling measures 3 ft (0.91 m) in diameter and can handle loads of 250 to 350 short tons (220 to 310 long tons; 230 to 320 t). The pilings were hollowed at their cores, with metal guide rails to allow the pots to be installed without the pilings tipping over. The edges of the pots are placed 9 ± 3 in (229 ± 76 mm) apart. The pilings' design was intended to evoke the design of the exposed pilings under Pier 54, which had previously occupied the site. Some of the pilings still exist and are used as marine habitats.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Note: the beat's physical cue describes the surviving pilings as Pier 54's; some sources describe surviving wood piles as remnants of Pier 54 (and adjacent Pier 56) preserved as marine habitat — consistent with the cue.

script_body: This place began at a party. By 2011 Hudson River Pier 55 was deteriorating, and the next year Hurricane Sandy made it worse. At a 2011 party for donors of the High Line park, Diana Taylor of the Hudson River Park Trust approached Barry Diller to gauge his interest in rebuilding the pier. Diller liked the idea but said he wanted to be "ambitious" about the space. His initial concept was a $35 million amoeba-shaped structure "with a few trees". After Sandy's 2012 storm surges, he decided to raise the structure about 13 feet compared with the original plans, to make it less vulnerable to flooding.
source_passage: By 2011, Hudson River Pier 55 was deteriorating, a situation that was worsened by Hurricane Sandy in New York the next year. At a 2011 party for donors of the High Line park, Diana Taylor of the Hudson River Park Trust approached Diller to determine his interest in rebuilding the pier. Diller supported the idea of rebuilding the pier but said he would like to be "ambitious" about the space. His initial concept called for a $35 million amoeba-shaped structure "with a few trees". Following storm surges caused by Hurricane Sandy in 2012, Diller decided to raise the structure about 13 feet (4.0 m) compared with the original plans, making the park less vulnerable to flooding.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions
unverified_claims: The specific 2011 High Line donor party where Diana Taylor approached Diller, and the $35M amoeba-shaped 'with a few trees' concept, are reported narrative details corroborated only by the source; not contradicted.

script_body: Getting to the design you see took some false starts. Diller had cold-called Heatherwick to design a park here, and by Diller's own account the first plan was "completely unbuildable" and resembled "Noah's Ark in stainless steel". Heatherwick's subsequent plan for the raised concrete pots was designed over a year and a half, while it took Signe Nielsen a year to engineer the individual pots to hold dirt. Diane von Fürstenberg had tried to convince Diller not to build the park, saying it was vulnerable to rising sea levels, but he insisted the plans were safe from a thousand-year flood. The project was nicknamed Diller Island, and as von Fürstenberg put it, the plans were all "Barry's dream".
source_passage: Diller had cold-called Heatherwick to design a park at the site. According to Diller, the first plan was "completely unbuildable" and resembled "Noah's Ark in stainless steel". Heatherwick's subsequent plan for the raised concrete pots was designed over a year and a half, while it took Nielsen a year to engineer the individual pots to hold dirt. Von Fürstenberg had tried to convince Diller not to build the park, saying it was vulnerable to rising sea levels, but Diller said the plans were safe from a thousand-year flood. The project was nicknamed Diller Island because of Diller's close association with the project. According to von Fürstenberg, the park plans were all "Barry's dream".

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions
unverified_claims: Direct quotes ('completely unbuildable', 'Noah's Ark in stainless steel', 'Barry's dream') and the year-and-a-half / one-year design timeline are attributed narrative details corroborated only by the source; not contradicted.

script_body: The park was nearly killed by a feud between two real-estate billionaires. While appealing the City Club of New York's lawsuit, Diller claimed that developer Douglas Durst was financing it. Durst, once a supporter of Hudson River Park, had given up his chairmanship with the Hudson River Park Trust over various disagreements. Early in 2017 he confirmed he had funded the City Club's suit, though he said he had stepped back half a year earlier. In an interview with The Villager, Durst said he did not want to personalize the dispute, then added: "I have nothing against Diller—except he said he wishes I had been killed by my brother", businessman Robert Durst, who at the time had been accused of murder. Diller subsequently apologized for the comments.
source_passage: While appealing the City Club's lawsuit, Diller claimed that developer Douglas Durst was financing the lawsuit against Pier 55. Durst, once a supporter of Hudson River Park, had given up his chairmanship with the Hudson River Park Trust over various disagreements. Early in 2017, Durst confirmed that he had funded the City Club's suit against the project, though he said he had not been involved with the lawsuits for half a year. In an interview with The Villager newspaper, Durst said that he did not want to personalize the dispute over Pier 55. Durst claimed, "I have nothing against Diller—except he said he wishes I had been killed by my brother", businessman Robert Durst. At the time, Robert Durst had been accused of murder, and Diller subsequently apologized for the comments.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Robert Durst was convicted of murder in 2021 and died in January 2022; the beat correctly frames the 2017-era statement as 'had been accused of murder' at the time, so it is not stale.

script_body: For forty-three days, this island did not exist. Plans for the park were scrapped in September 2017 amid continuing legal disputes and cost overruns that had pushed the budget past $200 million. Diller said he had already invested $45 million of his foundation's money, and on the day the project was canceled he was scheduled to order $80 million in cement. Von Fürstenberg and the couple's children had advised him to stop and "go where you're wanted". Then on October 25, 2017, Governor Andrew Cuomo brokered an agreement to complete it, and in exchange the City Club's lawyers dropped their lawsuits.
source_passage: Plans for the park were scrapped in September 2017 due to continuing legal disputes. The park also experienced cost overruns as its budget had exceeded $200 million by then. According to Diller, he had already invested $45 million of his foundation's money. On the day the project was canceled, he was scheduled to order $80 million in cement. After his lawyers advised him that the City Club's lawyers may request an injunction on the project, von Fürstenberg and the couple's children advised Diller to stop the project and "go where you're wanted". The City Club's lawyers expressed excitement over the park's cancellation. Among the disappointed supporters of the project were the Hudson River Park Trust, de Blasio, New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, and U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The underlying facts are correct: project scrapped Sept 13, 2017 amid legal disputes/cost overruns past $200M; Cuomo brokered the revival deal Oct 25, 2017 and the City Club dropped its suits.

disputes.claim: 'For forty-three days, this island did not exist.'
disputes.issue: Cancellation was Sept 13, 2017 and revival Oct 25, 2017, which is 42 days (exclusive count). 'Forty-three days' is correct only if both endpoint days are counted inclusively. This is a narrative framing in the beat header, not in the cited source_passage (which gives no exact span).
disputes.recommendation: LOW impact. Optionally soften to 'for about six weeks' to avoid the off-by-one ambiguity, or leave as-is since inclusive counting yields 43.

script_body: This park rose during a shutdown. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Little Island's construction was allowed to proceed even as most other projects were forced to stop. Work was temporarily halted for three weeks to disinfect the worksite, but the park was otherwise classified as an "essential project".

Work was temporarily halted for three weeks to disinfect the worksite, but the park was otherwise classified as an "essential project".

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions
unverified_claims: The three-week disinfection halt and 'essential project' classification during the 2020 COVID shutdown are construction-history details corroborated only by the source; not contradicted by any source (NY State did deem certain infrastructure construction essential in 2020).

script_body: At the western end of the island is a 687-seat amphitheater nicknamed "The Amph", set on the north side of the park's tallest hill, where a flat pier holds public restrooms and actors' changing rooms. Keeping it accessible was written into the deal. The low or free admission fees were a term of Diller's lease agreement from the Hudson River Park Trust, which operates Hudson River Park. Under that agreement, at least 51 percent of tickets must be under 30 dollars, including tickets provided for free.

At the park's opening in 2021, most events at the Amph were free but, for ticketed shows, thirty percent of tickets were to be sold online. script_body: Wave Hill is a 28-acre estate in the Hudson Hill section of Riverdale in the Bronx. It now consists of public horticultural gardens and a cultural center, all situated on the slopes overlooking the Hudson River, with expansive views across the river to the New Jersey Palisades. The estate includes two houses and a botanical garden. The oldest part of the main house, Wave Hill House, dates to 1843; Glyndor House dates from 1927 and contains a multi-room art gallery.

script_body: The original Wave Hill House was a gray fieldstone mansion, built in 1843 by the lawyer William Lewis Morris. It was owned from 1866 to 1903 by the publisher William Henry Appleton, who enlarged the house between 1866 and 1869 and again in 1890, and who added greenhouses and gardens to the grounds. During these years, the house was visited by Thomas Henry Huxley, the man who helped Charles Darwin bring evolution by natural selection to the public's attention.

script_body: The house was purchased in 1903 by George Walbridge Perkins, a partner of J. P. Morgan, along with adjacent property. That property included Glyndor, a house built by the Harriman family in 1888, which later burned down and was rebuilt in 1927. In 1910, Perkins added an underground building for recreation which included a bowling alley. Perkins performed extensive landscaping on the site and leased Wave Hill House to an eminent ichthyologist, Bashford Dean of the American Museum of Natural History, who built a stone addition to the building as a private museum, Armor Hall.

disputes.claim: Glyndor was 'a house built by the Harriman family in 1888, which later burned down and was rebuilt in 1927.'
disputes.issue: Wave Hill's own published history conflicts with these dates. It states the Perkins family purchased the house (then called 'Nonesuch') from Oliver Harriman in 1895 (rather than the Harrimans building it in 1888), and that the house was struck by lightning and severely damaged in 1926 (not 'burned down'), then rebuilt as Glyndor II — consistent with the beat's 1927 rebuild. The Harriman connection itself is corroborated; only the 1888 build year and 'burned down' framing diverge from the official source.
disputes.recommendation: Low-stakes for a tour. Sources genuinely differ on the build year; do not rewrite. If trimmed, the safe phrasing is 'an earlier Harriman-era house that was damaged and rebuilt as Glyndor in 1927.' The Perkins/Morgan, Bashford Dean, and Armor Hall facts in this beat are solid.

script_body: Chelsea takes its name from the estate and Georgian-style house of retired British Major Thomas Clarke, who obtained the property when he bought the farm of Jacob Somerindyck on August 16, 1750. The land was bounded by what would become 21st and 24th Streets, from the Hudson River to Eighth Avenue. Clarke chose the name "Chelsea" after the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London. He passed the estate on to his daughter, Charity, who, with her husband Benjamin Moore, added land on the south of the estate, extending it to 19th Street.

script_body: The house was the birthplace of Charity and Benjamin Moore's son, Clement Clarke Moore, who in turn inherited the property. Moore is generally credited with writing "A Visit From St. Nicholas" and was the author of the first Greek and Hebrew lexicons printed in the United States.

script_body: In 1827, Moore gave the land of his apple orchard to the Episcopal Diocese of New York for the General Theological Seminary, which built its brownstone Gothic campus south of the manor house. Despite his objections to the Commissioner's Plan of 1811, which ran the new Ninth Avenue through the middle of his estate, Moore began the development of Chelsea with the help of James N. Wells, dividing it into lots along Ninth Avenue and selling them to well-heeled New Yorkers. Covenants in the deeds of sale forbade stables, manufacturing and commercial uses, and specified architectural details of the buildings.

script_body: The industrialization of western Chelsea brought immigrant populations from many countries to work in the factories, including a large number of Irish immigrants, who dominated work on the Hudson River piers that lined the nearby waterfront and the truck terminals integrated with the freight railroad spur. With the immigrant population came the political domination of the neighborhood by the Tammany Hall machine, as well as festering ethnic tensions: around 67 people died in a riot between Irish Catholics and Irish Protestants on July 12, 1871, which took place around 24th Street and Eighth Avenue.
