script_body: In the early 1940s, tons of uranium for the Manhattan Project were stored in the Baker & Williams Warehouse at 513–519 West 20th Street. The uranium was removed and a decontamination project at the site was completed during the early 1990s.

physical_cues.cue: the Baker & Williams Warehouse at 513-519 West 20th Street

source_passage: In the early 1940s, tons of uranium for the Manhattan Project were stored in the Baker & Williams Warehouse at 513–519 West 20th Street. The uranium was removed and a decontamination project at the site was completed during the early 1990s.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Uranium stored at Baker & Williams Warehouses (513-519 W 20th St) ~1942-43; radioactive contamination found in 1989, remediation by Bechtel under FUSRAP 1991-1993, certified complete November 1995. Beat's 'completed during the early 1990s' is slightly early (certification was 1995) but within LOW tolerance and not misleading. The warehouse buildings still stand at 513-519 West 20th Street beneath the High Line.

script_body: Hotel Chelsea, built between 1883 and 1885 and designed by Hubert, Pirsson & Co., was New York's first cooperative apartment complex and was the tallest building in the city until 1902. After the theater district migrated uptown and the neighborhood became commercialized, the residential building folded, and in 1905 it was turned into a hotel. It attracted attention as the place where Dylan Thomas had been staying when he died in 1953 at St. Vincent's Hospital in Greenwich Village, and for the 1978 slaying of Nancy Spungen for which Sid Vicious was accused. The hotel has been the home of numerous celebrities, including Brendan Behan, Thomas Wolfe, Mark Twain, Tennessee Williams and Virgil Thomson, and the subject of books, films, and music.

physical_cues.cue: Hotel Chelsea, the tallest building in the city until 1902

source_passage: Hotel Chelsea, built 1883–1885 and designed by Hubert, Pirsson & Co., was New York's first cooperative apartment complex and was the tallest building in the city until 1902. After the theater district migrated uptown and the neighborhood became commercialized, the residential building folded and in 1905 it was turned into a hotel. The hotel attracted attention as the place where Dylan Thomas had been staying when he died in 1953 at St. Vincent's Hospital in Greenwich Village, and for the 1978 slaying of Nancy Spungen for which Sid Vicious was accused. The hotel has been the home of numerous celebrities, including Brendan Behan, Thomas Wolfe, Mark Twain, Tennessee Williams and Virgil Thomson, and the subject of books, films (Chelsea Girls, 1966) and music.

fact_check.omission_check: Minor omission of context: the Hotel Chelsea reopened in 2022 after a roughly decade-long renovation/ownership saga, but this does not affect any historical claim in the beat. Construction 1883-1885, Hubert/Pirsson & Co. design, cooperative apartment origin, tallest-until-1902 claim, 1905 conversion to a hotel, Dylan Thomas (died 1953, St. Vincent's), and 1978 Nancy Spungen death all corroborated.

script_body: The Chelsea Piers were the city's primary luxury ocean liner terminal from 1910 until 1935, when the growing size of ships made the complex inadequate. The RMS Titanic was headed to Pier 59 at the piers, and the RMS Carpathia brought survivors to Pier 54 in the complex.

physical_cues.cue: the Chelsea Piers along the Hudson waterfront

source_passage: The Chelsea Piers were the city's primary luxury ocean liner terminal from 1910 until 1935, when the growing size of ships made the complex inadequate. The RMS Titanic was headed to Pier 60 at the piers and the RMS Carpathia brought survivors to Pier 54 in the complex, which was destroyed in 2018 although ironwork remains.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions for the narrative. (Wikipedia's surrounding sentence notes Pier 54 was largely demolished in 2018 with ironwork remaining; the beat already drops that, and the Hudson River piers/waterfront remain visible to the west, so the 'view' cue holds.)

corrections.original_text: The RMS Titanic was headed to Pier 60 at the piers
corrections.corrected_text: The RMS Titanic was headed to Pier 59 at the piers
corrections.reasoning: The White Star Line operated both Pier 59 and Pier 60 at the Chelsea Piers, but independent sources (Encyclopedia Titanica, Untapped New York, RMS Titanic Trail, atlanticliners.com) consistently identify Pier 59 as the Titanic's intended/assigned berth. The Carpathia later dropped Titanic's lifeboats at Pier 59 before unloading survivors at Pier 54. Pier 60 is a less-attested figure; the broadcast-safe, well-corroborated number is Pier 59.

script_body: Above 23rd Street, by the Hudson River, the neighborhood is post-industrial, featuring the elevated High Line viaduct, which follows the river all through Chelsea. The elevated rail line was the successor to the street-level freight line originally built through Chelsea in 1847, which was the cause of numerous fatal accidents, so it was elevated in the early 1930s by the New York Central Railroad. It fell out of use in the 1960s through 1980 and was originally slated to be torn down, but in the early 2000s it was redesigned and converted into a highly used aerial greenway and rails-to-trails park.

physical_cues.cue: the elevated High Line viaduct above the street

source_passage: Above 23rd Street, by the Hudson River, the neighborhood is post-industrial, featuring the elevated High Line viaduct, which follows the river all through Chelsea. The elevated rail line was the successor to the street-level freight line original built through Chelsea in 1847, which was the cause of numerous fatal accidents, so it was elevated in the early 1930s by the New York Central Railroad. It fell out of use in the 1960s through 1980 and was originally slated to be torn down, but in the early 2000s, it was redesigned and converted into a highly used aerial greenway and rails-to-trails park.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Street-level freight line authorized 1847, dangerous ('Death Avenue'), elevated by New York Central Railroad in the early 1930s (built 1929-1934, opened 1934), disused from the 1960s through 1980, slated for demolition, then converted to an elevated greenway park (opened in stages from 2009). The elevated High Line viaduct is still present above the street in Chelsea.

script_body: The building you stand before still serves as a Quaker Meeting, with worship every Sunday. It is recognized as the oldest house of worship in the state of New York. Because Quakers did not call their buildings churches, it usually holds the title of oldest religious building or oldest house of worship rather than oldest church. It is also the second-oldest Quaker meeting house in the United States.
source_passage: Today, it still serves as a Quaker Meeting, with meetings for worship taking place every Sunday. It is recognized as the oldest house of worship in the state of New York. Because Quakers did not refer to their buildings as "churches," it often holds the title of "oldest religious building" or "oldest house of worship" rather than "oldest church." It is also the second-oldest Quaker meeting house in the United States.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions

script_body: This meeting house began as a small frame structure, built in 1694 on land acquired in 1692 by John Bowne and John Rodman. The first recorded meeting held there was on November 24, 1694. That original structure is now only the easterly third of what you see today, the rest expanded between 1716 and 1719. The Flushing meeting house was the second meeting house to be built on Long Island, the first having been built in Oyster Bay in 1672, which no longer stands.

physical_cues.cue: Look at the easterly third of the building, the oldest part still standing

source_passage: The Flushing Friends Quaker Meeting House was built in 1694 as a small frame structure on land acquired in 1692 by John Bowne and John Rodman in Flushing, New York.  The first recorded meeting held there was on November 24, 1694. This original structure is now the easterly third of the current structure, which was expanded 1716-1719. According to one source, the original structure was renovated in 1704 and then demolished in 1716. The Flushing meeting house was the second meeting house to be built on Long Island, the first one being built in Oyster Bay in 1672, which no longer stands.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The easterly-third / 1716-1719 expansion and the Oyster Bay 1672 first-on-Long-Island detail are corroborated by the meeting's own history and reference sources.
unverified_claims: Precise 1692 land-acquisition date by John Bowne and John Rodman and the November 24, 1694 first-meeting date are stated in Quaker/Wikipedia accounts but not independently corroborated to the day; not contradicted by any source.

script_body: Before this house was built, the Quakers had to meet in secret. They had come from the Netherlands and settled in the area in 1657, holding meetings in people's homes until the Meeting House was built. Henry Townsend offered his home for meetings, but was fined for harboring pestilents, which was how the Quakers were regarded. The Quakers continued to meet in secret in the woods until John Bowne offered his home for meetings. Bowne was banished to Holland for refusing to pay the fine, but returned two years later to combat the persecution that the Quakers faced. The group drafted the Flushing Remonstrance, and in Holland, Bowne pleaded before the Dutch West India Company to honor the cause of religious freedom. A letter was written in 1663 to Governor Stuyvesant to end the persecution of Quakers.
source_passage: The Quakers, coming from the Netherlands, settled in the area in 1657 and meetings were held in people's homes until the Meeting House was built.  Henry Townsend offered his home for meetings, but was fined for harboring “pestilents,” which was how the Quakers were regarded. The Quakers continued to meet in secret in the woods until John Bowne offered his home for meetings. Bowne was banished to Holland for refusing to pay the fine, but returned two years later to combat the persecution that the Quakers faced.  The group drafted the Flushing Remonstrance and in Holland, Bowne pleaded before the Dutch West India Company to honor the cause of religious freedom, and a letter was written in 1663 to Governor Stuyvesant to end the persecution of Quakers.

fact_check.omission_check: Minor chronology compression: the Flushing Remonstrance was signed in December 1657 (before Bowne's 1662 arrest/banishment), and independent sources note Bowne's exile trip took about three years total, returning to Flushing circa 1663-1664, rather than 'two years later.' The beat reflects the Wikipedia narrative ordering and asserts no specific wrong date, so no correction is made, but a visitor may infer the Remonstrance followed Bowne's banishment when it preceded it. Notably none of the Remonstrance's 30 signers were themselves Quakers.
unverified_claims: Henry Townsend being fined specifically for 'harboring pestilents' and Quakers meeting 'in the woods' are stated in the Quaker/Wikipedia account; the broader persecution and Townsend's fining are historically consistent but the exact wording is not independently corroborated.

script_body: Inside, the building contains a partition which can be lowered and raised, separating the men's from the women's side. Typically the business meetings would be conducted by each group independently, and then the partition would be raised for the religious meeting.

physical_cues.cue: the raised-and-lowered partition dividing the interior

source_passage: The building contains a partition which can be lowered and raised, and separates the men's from the women's side. Typically business meetings would be conducted by each group independently, then the partition would be raised for the religious meeting.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The raise/lower partition separating men's and women's sides is a standard feature of historic Quaker meeting houses and is documented for this building.

script_body: By 1976, repairs were recommended to the building that totaled an estimated seventy thousand dollars. After two and a half centuries, the wooden building suffered from dry rot and beetle teeth. A volunteer archeological crew from New York University and the New York State Division for Historic Preservation was formed to survey the site for stabilization work, funded by the Society of Friends and a grant from the National Park Service. Since no evidence of significant cultural or archaeological artifacts was found, it was determined that excavation for the stabilization work could continue.
entities: New York State Division for Historic Preservation
source_passage: In 1976, repairs were recommended to the building that totaled an estimated $70,000.  After two and half centuries, the wooden building suffered from “dry not rot and beetle teeth”.  A volunteer archeological crew from New York University and the New York State Division for Historic Preservation was formed to survey the site for stabilization work funded by the Society of Friends and a grant from the National Park Service.  The crew conducted tests to determine the nature of the surface below the Meeting House floor.  Since no evidence of significant cultural or archaeological artifacts were found, it was determined that excavation for the stabilization work could continue.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The 1976 ~$70,000 repair estimate, dry rot, and NYU / NY State Division for Historic Preservation archeological survey funded by the Society of Friends and a National Park Service grant are specific to the building's preservation record; consistent with the building's NPS/landmark documentation, not contradicted.
unverified_claims: The specific 1976 $70,000 figure and the NYU/NY State volunteer survey crew detail are from the building's own preservation account and were not independently re-confirmed by a second source; not contradicted.

script_body: Nearby lies a graveyard that contains hundreds of unmarked graves. In 2012, the Religious Society of Friends said it was dug into by a construction company working on an adjacent lot. The company erected a fence on disputed property and caused an outcry from the Quaker community about graves that may have been disturbed. After the Landmark Preservation Commission threatened a five thousand dollar fine, the company retreated, although it maintained that it did not disturb the grave site. Because of custom at the time, some graves do not display identifying headstones.

The company erected a fence on disputed property and caused an outcry from the Quaker community about graves that may have been disturbed.   After the Landmark Preservation Commission threatened a $5,000 fine, the company retreated, although maintained the claim that they did not disturb the grave site. Because of custom at the time, some graves do not display identifying headstones.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The 2012 dispute (construction company digging into the graveyard, fence on disputed property, ~$5,000 LPC fine threat, company's denial of disturbing graves) is corroborated. The adjacent historic graveyard with hundreds of unmarked graves is still present beside the meeting house.

script_body: Rosemary Vietor, vice president of the Bowne House Historical Society, said the contested area may have contained the remains of John Bowne and his successive wives. Although an archeological survey completed in 2010 approved the adjacent lot for construction, the Quaker community still feels that the issue is unresolved.

Although an archeological survey, completed in 2010 at the recommendation of the Landmarks Preservation Committee, approved the adjacent lot for construction, the Quaker community still feels that the issue is unresolved.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Rosemary Vietor (VP of the Bowne House Historical Society) and the 2010 archeological survey approving the adjacent lot are documented in the dispute coverage. Attributed-statement framing ('may have contained') is preserved.
unverified_claims: Rosemary Vietor's specific quoted attribution that the contested area may have held the remains of John Bowne and his successive wives is sourced from the dispute coverage and is presented as her stated view, not as established fact.

script_body: The Landmarks Preservation Commission noted that this is the oldest place of worship still standing in the city — and an example of medieval architecture.
source_passage: Further, the Commission noted that it is the oldest place of worship still standing in the city and is an example of medieval architecture.

The NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission characterization that it is the oldest place of worship still standing in the city and an example of medieval architecture ('a prime example of medieval survival in its proportions and framing system') is confirmed.

script_body: For all its outsized reputation, this is the most densely populated and geographically smallest of New York City's five boroughs. It is coextensive with New York County — the smallest county by area in the state, and one of the smallest in the United States. Sitting almost entirely on a single island near the southern tip of the state, it serves as the city's economic and administrative center, and has been described as the cultural, financial, media, and entertainment capital of the world.
source_passage: Manhattan is the most densely populated and geographically smallest of the five boroughs of New York City. Coextensive with New York County, Manhattan is the smallest county by area in the U.S. state of New York, and one of the smallest in the United States. Located almost entirely on Manhattan Island near the southern tip of the state, Manhattan is centrally located in the Northeast megalopolis and represents the urban core of the New York metropolitan area. Manhattan serves as New York City's economic and administrative center and has been described as the cultural, financial, media, and entertainment capital of the world.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions

script_body: The name itself is older than the city by far. It comes, most likely, from the local Munsee language of the Lenape — the word manahahtaan, in which manah- means 'gather,' -aht- means 'bow,' and -aan is used to form verb stems. Translated, it means 'the place where we get bows,' or 'place for gathering the wood to make bows.' According to a Munsee tradition recorded by Albert Seqaqkind Anthony in the 19th century, the island was named for a grove of hickory trees that was considered ideal for bowmaking. So the word you say every day may once have meant: come here for the good wood.
source_passage: The etymology of the name Manhattan is most likely – amongst other theories, and via loaning by Dutch — from the Lenape's local language Munsee, manaháhtaan (where manah- means "gather", -aht- means "bow", and -aan is used to form verb stems). The Lenape word has been translated as "the place where we get bows" or "place for gathering the (wood to make) bows". According to a Munsee tradition recorded by Albert Seqaqkind Anthony in the 19th century, the island was named for a grove of hickory trees that was considered ideal for bowmaking.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Note: the etymology is the leading theory among several; the beat correctly hedges with 'most likely'.

script_body: The island was first mapped during a 1609 voyage of Henry Hudson, who came across it and the native people living there before continuing up the river that would later bear his name. And the very first time the name was written down? It appears as Manna-hata, in the logbook of Robert Juet, an officer on that voyage.
source_passage: Manhattan was first mapped during a 1609 voyage of Henry Hudson. Hudson came across Manhattan Island and the native people living there, and continued up the river that would later bear his name, the Hudson River. Manhattan was first recorded in writing as Manna-hata, in the logbook of Robert Juet, an officer on the voyage.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Independent sources confirm Robert Juet's 1609 logbook on Hudson's Halve Maen recorded 'Manna-hata'.

script_body: Before the Dutch and long before the English, there was a Florentine. In April 1524, the explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing in service of Francis I of France, became the first documented European to visit the area that would become New York City. He entered the tidal strait now known as The Narrows and named the land around the upper harbor New Angouleme, after the family name of King Francis. He sailed far enough in to sight the Hudson River, and named the bay — now Upper New York Bay — Santa Margarita, after Marguerite de Navarre, the king's elder sister. Had those names stuck, you might be standing in New Angouleme today.
source_passage: In April 1524, Florentine explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano, sailing in service of Francis I of France, became the first documented European to visit the area that would become New York City. Verrazzano entered the tidal strait now known as The Narrows and named the land around Upper New York Harbor New Angoulême, in reference to the family name of King Francis I; he sailed far enough into the harbor to sight the Hudson River, and he named the Bay of Santa Margarita – what is now Upper New York Bay – after Marguerite de Navarre, the elder sister of the king.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. April 1524, Verrazzano in service of Francis I, New Angouleme (Land of Angouleme), The Narrows, and the Bay of Santa Margarita named for Marguerite de Navarre (king's elder sister) all corroborated independently.

script_body: In 1664, English forces conquered New Netherland and renamed it New York after the English Duke of York and Albany, the future King James II. Then came one of history's stranger trades. The Treaty of Breda, signed on July 31, 1667, ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War, and the Dutch ceded New Netherland to England in exchange for the territory of Suriname and control of the spice-producing Island of Run in the East Indies — an island known for its production of nutmeg and mace. In the calculus of the day, a nutmeg island looked like the better deal.
source_passage: In 1664, English forces conquered New Netherland and renamed it "New York" after the English Duke of York and Albany, the future King James II. The Treaty of Breda, signed on July 31, 1667, ended the Second Anglo-Dutch war. The Dutch ceded New Netherland (encompassing modern-day New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Delaware) to England in exchange for the territory of Suriname and control of the spice-producing Island of Run in the East Indies, known for its production of nutmeg and mace.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Treaty of Breda (31 July 1667) ending the Second Anglo-Dutch War, Dutch retaining Suriname and Run (nutmeg/mace) in exchange for England keeping New Netherland, all confirmed by Britannica and the NY Courts Historical Society.

script_body: The grid you walk was decreed on paper before most of it existed. The Commissioners' Plan of 1811 called for twelve numbered avenues running north and south, roughly parallel to the Hudson River, each one a hundred feet wide, with First Avenue on the east side and Twelfth Avenue on the west. The numbered cross streets run east to west, generally sixty feet wide, with about two hundred feet between them. The plan first laid out 155 numbered crosstown streets; later the grid was extended up to the northernmost corner of the island, where the last numbered street is 220th Street.
source_passage:
The Commissioners' Plan of 1811 called for twelve numbered "avenues" running north and south roughly parallel to the Hudson River, each 100 feet (30 m) wide, with First Avenue on the east side and Twelfth Avenue on the west side. There are several intermittent avenues east of First Avenue, including four additional lettered avenues running from Avenue A eastward to Avenue D in an area now known as Alphabet City. The numbered streets in Manhattan run east–west, and are generally 60 feet (18 m) wide, with about 200 feet (61 m) between streets. The address algorithm of Manhattan is used to estimate the closest east–west cross street for building numbers on north–south avenues.
According to the original Commissioner's Plan, there were 155 numbered crosstown streets, but later the grid was extended up to the northernmost corner of Manhattan Island, where the last numbered street is 220th Street, though the grid continues to 228th Street in the borough's Marble Hill neighborhood.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Twelve 100-ft avenues, ~60-ft cross streets, 155 original numbered streets, grid later extended to 220th St at the northern tip all confirmed (Museum of the City of NY 'Greatest Grid', Wikipedia).

script_body: There is a consequence of that strict grid that almost no planner intended. Because the grid is skewed about 28.9 degrees off true, there are days when the setting sun lines up perfectly with the street canyons. The phenomenon is sometimes called Manhattanhenge, by analogy with Stonehenge. On May 28 and July 12, the sunset aligns with the street grid lines, so the sun hangs visible at or near the western horizon from street level. A matching sunrise version happens on the eastern horizon on December 5 and January 8. Look west down any long cross street on the right evening, and the city becomes an instrument for catching the sun.

physical_cues.cue: Look west down a long cross street toward the horizon

source_passage: Another consequence of the strict grid plan of most of Manhattan, and the grid's skew of approximately 28.9 degrees, is a phenomenon sometimes referred to as Manhattanhenge (by analogy with Stonehenge). On May 28 and July 12, the sunset is aligned with the street grid lines, with the result that the sun is visible at or near the western horizon from street level. A similar phenomenon occurs with the sunrise on the eastern horizon on December 5 and January 8.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Grid skew of ~28.9 degrees and Manhattanhenge sunset dates of May 28 and July 12 confirmed for 2026 by AMNH/NYC Parks; the 'look west down a long cross street' cue remains accurate. Note: exact henge dates can shift by a day year-to-year, but the beat's May 28 / July 12 match the 2026 calendar.

script_body: During World War II, the borough gave its name to the Manhattan Project, the top-secret U.S.-led research program that developed the first nuclear weapons. The name came from here for an administrative reason: the project was named after the Manhattan Engineer District of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which was initially headquartered in Manhattan.
source_passage: During World War II, the borough gave its name to the Manhattan Project, the top-secret U.S.-led research program that developed the first nuclear weapons. The project was named after the Manhattan Engineer District of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which was initially headquartered in Manhattan.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The Manhattan Engineer District (created Aug 1942) was named for its initial NYC offices (270 Broadway / Columbia-area research); HQ later moved to Washington, D.C. This matches the beat's 'initially headquartered in Manhattan'.

script_body: Sometimes a city only learns to protect what it has by destroying it first. In 1961, the struggling Pennsylvania Railroad unveiled plans to tear down the old Penn Station and replace it with a new Madison Square Garden. Organized protests aimed to preserve the McKim, Mead & White-designed structure completed in 1910 — widely considered a masterpiece of the Beaux-Arts style and one of the architectural jewels of New York City. The protests failed; demolition began in October 1963. But the loss led directly to a 1965 law establishing the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission, and the preservation movement it triggered has been credited with the retention of some one million structures nationwide.
entities: New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission
source_passage: In 1961, the struggling Pennsylvania Railroad unveiled plans to tear down the old Penn Station and replace it with a new Madison Square Garden and office building complex. Organized protests were aimed at preserving the McKim, Mead & White-designed structure completed in 1910, widely considered a masterpiece of the Beaux-Arts style and one of the architectural jewels of New York City. Despite these efforts, demolition of the structure began in October 1963. The loss of Penn Station led directly to the enactment in 1965 of a local law establishing the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission, which is responsible for preserving the "city's historic, aesthetic, and cultural heritage". The historic preservation movement triggered by Penn Station's demise has been credited with the retention of some one million structures nationwide, including over 1,000 in New York City.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. 1961 PRR plan, McKim Mead & White Beaux-Arts station completed 1910, demolition begun October 1963, 1965 Landmarks Law / Landmarks Preservation Commission, and ~1 million structures preserved nationwide all confirmed (Museum of the City of NY, NYPAP). The replacement Madison Square Garden / Penn Station remains in place today.

script_body: The borough hides its history inside everyday phrases. The iconic Flatiron Building is said to be the source of 23 skidoo — meaning scram — from what cops would shout at men trying to glimpse women's dresses blown up by the winds the triangular building created. And the Big Apple? It dates back to the 1920s, when a reporter heard the term used by New Orleans stable-hands to refer to New York City's horse racetracks and named his racing column 'Around The Big Apple.' Jazz musicians then adopted it for the city as the world's jazz capital, and a 1970s tourism ad campaign made it stick.
entities: New York Convention and Visitors Bureau
source_passage: The iconic Flatiron Building is said to have been the source of the phrase "23 skidoo" or scram, from what cops would shout at men who tried to get glimpses of women's dresses being blown up by the winds created by the triangular building. The "Big Apple" dates back to the 1920s, when a reporter heard the term used by New Orleans stable-hands to refer to New York City's horse racetracks and named his racing column "Around The Big Apple". Jazz musicians adopted the term to refer to the city as the world's jazz capital, and a 1970s ad campaign by the New York Convention and Visitors Bureau helped popularize the term.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The Big Apple origin (racing writer John J. Fitz Gerald, who heard the term from New Orleans stable-hands ~1920, used it in his 'Around the Big Apple' Morning Telegraph column, later adopted by jazz musicians and revived by a 1970s NYC tourism campaign) is well documented by Popik/Cohen research. Both the Big Apple and 23 skidoo claims are correctly framed as legend/lore ('is said to be'); the 23 skidoo Flatiron etymology is folk and contested by lexicographers (the terms predate the 1902 building), but the beat's hedged 'said to be' phrasing is appropriate and does not assert it as fact.

script_body: There is a piece of Manhattan that is not on the island at all. Marble Hill was once part of the northern tip of Manhattan Island, until the Harlem River Ship Canal, dug in 1895 to better connect the Harlem and Hudson rivers, separated it from the rest. Then, before World War I, the old Harlem River channel that separated it from the Bronx was filled in, and Marble Hill became part of the mainland. After a 1984 court ruling tangled its status, the New York Legislature settled the matter for good that year, declaring the neighborhood part of both New York County and the Borough of Manhattan — an island borough's piece of dry mainland.
source_passage: Marble Hill was part of the northern tip of Manhattan Island, but the Harlem River Ship Canal, dug in 1895 to better connect the Harlem and Hudson rivers, separated it from the remainder of Manhattan. Before World War I, the section of the original Harlem River channel separating Marble Hill from the Bronx was filled in, and Marble Hill became part of the mainland. After a May 1984 court ruling that Marble Hill was simultaneously part of the Borough of Manhattan (not the Borough of the Bronx) and part of Bronx County (not New York County), the matter was definitively settled later that year when the New York Legislature overwhelmingly passed legislation declaring the neighborhood part of both New York County and the Borough of Manhattan.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Harlem River Ship Canal (1895), old channel filled before WWI making Marble Hill physically part of the mainland, the May 1984 court ruling (Judge McQuillan) and the 1984 NY Legislature statute declaring it part of New York County and the Borough of Manhattan are all corroborated.

script_body: You are standing in the central portion of Manhattan, the borough's primary central business district. Midtown is home to some of the city's most prominent buildings, several of which define the eastern side around you: the Chrysler Building, the headquarters of the United Nations, and Grand Central Terminal, alongside the Empire State Building, Rockefeller Center, and the Hudson Yards Redevelopment Project.
source_passage: Midtown Manhattan is the central portion of the New York City borough of Manhattan, serving as the city's primary central business district. Midtown is home to some of the city's most prominent buildings, including the Empire State Building, the Chrysler Building, the Hudson Yards Redevelopment Project, the headquarters of the United Nations, Grand Central Terminal, and Rockefeller Center, as well as several prominent tourist destinations, including Broadway, Times Square, and Koreatown.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Chrysler Building, UN headquarters, and Grand Central Terminal are correctly placed on Midtown's east side; Empire State, Rockefeller Center, and Hudson Yards are the broader Midtown landmark set as stated.

script_body: Where exactly does the eastern half of Midtown begin and end? One common answer draws the lines tightly. The term "Midtown East" can refer to the area between 42nd and 59th Streets, and between 5th Avenue and the East River.
source_passage: "Midtown East" can refer to the area between 42nd and 59th Streets, and between 5th Avenue and the East River.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The 42nd-59th Street / 5th Avenue-East River boundary is one commonly cited definition; the beat correctly frames it as 'one common answer' rather than the only one.

script_body: Midtown East is not one uniform grid of offices; it is stitched from smaller named enclaves between Sixth Avenue and the East River. There is Sutton Place, near the river between East 53rd and 59th Streets; Turtle Bay, from 53rd down to 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue to the river; and Tudor City, between 1st and 2nd Avenues from East 40th to 43rd Street.
source_passage:
Midtown East from around 6th Avenue to the East River, including (going from west to east, and north to south):
Sutton Place near the East River between East 53rd Street and East 59th Street
Turtle Bay from 53rd Street to 42nd Street and from Lexington Avenue to the East River
Tudor City from 1st Avenue to 2nd Avenue and East 40th Street to East 43rd Street

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Sutton Place (near the river ~E53rd-E59th), Turtle Bay (E42nd-E53rd, Lexington/Third to the river), and Tudor City (between 1st/2nd Ave, ~E40th-E43rd) are corroborated. Minor variance: independent sources commonly give Tudor City as E41st-E43rd rather than E40th-E43rd, a one-block, LOW-impact difference that also varies by source; beat faithfully reflects the cited Wikipedia revision.

script_body: Midtown is the original district in the United States to bear the name. It once included historical but now defunct neighborhoods, names that have largely vanished from the map. The Ladies' Mile ran along Fifth Avenue from 14th to 23rd Street. And the Tenderloin stretched from 23rd to 42nd Street and from Fifth Avenue to Seventh Avenue.
source_passage: Midtown is the original district in the United States to bear the name and included historical but now defunct neighborhoods such as the Ladies' Mile, along Fifth Avenue from 14th to 23rd Street; and the Tenderloin, from 23rd to 42nd Street and from Fifth Avenue to Seventh Avenue.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Ladies' Mile along Fifth Avenue 14th-23rd Street and the historic Tenderloin (roughly 23rd-42nd, Fifth to Seventh Avenue) are corroborated as historic, now-defunct district names.
unverified_claims: 'Midtown is the original district in the United States to bear the name' — plausible and widely repeated but not independently confirmable to a primary source; reflects the cited Wikipedia revision.

script_body: Midtown Manhattan is the largest central business district in the world, and it ranks among the world's most expensive locations for real estate. Fifth Avenue here has commanded the world's highest retail rents, ranked as the most expensive shopping street in the world before falling to second in 2024.
source_passage: Midtown Manhattan is the largest central business district in the world and ranks among the world's most expensive locations for real estate; Fifth Avenue in Midtown Manhattan has commanded the world's highest retail rents and had been ranked as the most expensive shopping street in the world before falling to second in 2024.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. 'Largest CBD in the world' is widely supported. The 2024 demotion of Fifth Avenue to #2 (Milan's Via Montenapoleone took #1 per Cushman & Wakefield, Nov 2024) is correctly captured and current as of 2026.

script_body: Real estate professionals carve out their own term for the costliest pocket of Midtown: the "Plaza District." It denotes the most expensive area of midtown from a commercial real estate perspective, lying between 42nd Street and 59th Street, from 3rd Avenue to 7th Avenue, about a square kilometer or half a square mile.
source_passage: The "Plaza District", a term used by Manhattan real estate professionals to denote the most expensive area of midtown from a commercial real estate perspective, lies between 42nd Street and 59th Street, from 3rd Avenue to 7th Avenue, about a square kilometer or half a square mile.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The 'Plaza District' (roughly 42nd-59th, 3rd-7th Avenue) is a standard Manhattan commercial-real-estate submarket term; boundaries and ~1 sq km / half sq mi area are consistent with the cited source.

script_body: The avenues here trade hands at record-breaking prices. When 450 Park Avenue was sold on July 2, 2007, for US$510 million, about US$1,589 per square foot, it broke the barely month-old record for an American office building of US$1,476 per square foot, set by the sale of 660 Madison Avenue.
source_passage: When 450 Park Avenue was sold on July 2, 2007, for US$510 million, about US$1,589 per square foot (US$17,104/m2), it broke the barely month-old record for an American office building of US$1,476 per square foot (US$15,887/m2) based on the sale of 660 Madison Avenue.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions to the narrative; the 660 Madison Avenue record at ~$1,476/sq ft (July 2007) is corroborated, and 450 Park's record-breaking 2007 sale is real.

disputes.claim: 450 Park Avenue sold July 2, 2007 for US$510 million, about US$1,589 per square foot, breaking 660 Madison Avenue's US$1,476/sq ft record.
disputes.issue: Sources conflict on the exact 450 Park figures. The beat (reflecting the cited Wikipedia revision / period NYT-style reporting) gives $510M and $1,589/sq ft. The current Wikipedia article on 450 Park Avenue and The Real Deal give $509M and $1,566/sq ft (one source cites $1,583/sq ft). The figures are the same transaction reported with rounding/closing-figure differences; the core narrative (a record-breaking 2007 sale at ~$1,500+/sq ft that topped 660 Madison's barely-month-old $1,476/sq ft record) is intact and corroborated.
disputes.recommendation: Keep the beat as-is (it faithfully reflects the cited revision and the narrative is sound), OR if conservatism is preferred, soften the precise figures to '$510 million, roughly $1,580 per square foot' and 'about $1,476 per square foot' to absorb the source variance. Do not present a single exact per-sq-ft figure as undisputed.

script_body: Two great railroad stations sit in Midtown, and the eastern one defines the district around it. Pennsylvania Station and Grand Central Terminal are the two major railroad stations located here. Grand Central serves the Metro-North Railroad, and also serves the Long Island Rail Road at Grand Central Madison.
source_passage: Pennsylvania Station and Grand Central Terminal are the two major railroad stations located in Midtown Manhattan. Penn Station serves Amtrak, NJ Transit, and the Long Island Rail Road (LIRR), while Grand Central serves the Metro-North Railroad and also serves the LIRR at Grand Central Madison.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Penn Station and Grand Central are Midtown's two major rail stations; Grand Central serves Metro-North; LIRR service via Grand Central Madison is correct (opened Jan 25, 2023 / fully Feb 2023). Penn Station serves Amtrak, NJ Transit, and LIRR (the beat names Penn but does not list its carriers, which is fine).

script_body: On real estate listings it shows up as Midtown West, but this neighborhood on the West Side of Midtown Manhattan is also known as Clinton, and most famously as Hell's Kitchen. It had long been a bastion of poor and working-class Irish Americans, and its gritty reputation held real-estate prices below those of most other areas of Manhattan. By 1969, the City Planning Commission's Plan for New York City reported that development pressures tied to its Midtown location were driving people of modest means from the area. Gentrification has accelerated since the early 1980s, and rents have risen rapidly.
source_passage:
Hell's Kitchen—also known as Clinton, or Midtown West on real estate listings—is a neighborhood on the West Side of Midtown Manhattan in New York City, New York, United States. It is generally bordered by 34th Street (or 41st Street) to the south, 59th Street to the north, Eighth Avenue to the east, and the Hudson River to the west.
Hell's Kitchen had long been a bastion of poor and working-class Irish Americans. Its gritty reputation has long held real-estate prices below those of most other areas of Manhattan. By 1969, the City Planning Commission's Plan for New York City reported that development pressures related to its Midtown location were driving people of modest means from the area. Gentrification has accelerated since the early 1980s, and rents have risen rapidly.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions

script_body: No one can pin down the exact origin of the label. Several explanations compete. Some point to a tenement on 54th Street as the first "Hell's Kitchen"; another version names an infamous building at 39th as the true origin, noting that a gang and a local dive took the name as well. Local historian Mary Clark traced the phrase to print: it first appeared on September 22, 1881, when a New York Times reporter went to the West 30s with a police guide to get details of a multiple murder. He called a particularly infamous tenement at 39th Street and Tenth Avenue "Hell's Kitchen" and said the entire section was "probably the lowest and filthiest in the city." By that account, 39th Street between 9th and 10th Avenues became known as Hell's Kitchen, and the name later expanded to the surrounding streets. Another version ascribes it to a German restaurant known as Heil's Kitchen, after its proprietors. But the most common version traces it to the story of "Dutch Fred the Cop," a veteran policeman who, with his rookie partner, was watching a small riot on West 39th Street near Tenth Avenue. The rookie supposedly said, "This place is hell itself," to which Fred replied, "Hell's a mild climate. This is Hell's Kitchen."
source_passage:

... first appeared in print on September 22, 1881 when a New York Times reporter went to the West 30s with a police guide to get details of a multiple murder there. He referred to a particularly infamous tenement at 39th Street and Tenth Avenue as "Hell's Kitchen" and said that the entire section was "probably the lowest and filthiest in the city." The rookie is supposed to have said: "This place is hell itself", to which Fred replied: "Hell's a mild climate. This is Hell's Kitchen."

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The competing-origins framing (54th St tenement, 39th St building, Heil's Kitchen restaurant, Dutch Fred the Cop, Mary Clark's 1881 NYT first-print citation) is faithfully and conventionally reproduced; these are accepted folk-etymologies that independent sources repeat without resolving.
unverified_claims: The verbatim 'Dutch Fred the Cop' dialogue ('Hell's a mild climate. This is Hell's Kitchen.') is an oft-repeated anecdote with no contemporaneous primary source; presented correctly here as 'the most common version' rather than fact.

script_body: Developers prefer to call the area "Clinton" or "Midtown West," but locals keep saying Hell's Kitchen. The "Clinton name", used by the municipality of New York City, originated in 1959 in an attempt to change the image of the neighborhood by linking the area to DeWitt Clinton Park at 52nd and Eleventh Avenue, named after the 19th century New York governor.
source_passage: Hell's Kitchen is frequently used to name the neighborhood, although real estate developers designate the area as "Clinton" and "Midtown West". The "Clinton name", used by the municipality of New York City, originated in 1959 in an attempt to change the image of the neighborhood by linking the area to DeWitt Clinton Park at 52nd and Eleventh Avenue, named after the 19th century New York governor, though The New York Times noted that those who live in the area "prefer Hell's Kitchen" as the name for the neighborhood.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. (The 1959 rebrand is widely tied to the August 1959 Capeman killings; that connection is covered in a separate beat and its omission here does not distort the claim.)

script_body: The neighborhood that would later be known as Hell's Kitchen started forming in the mid-19th century. Irish immigrants — mostly refugees from the Great Famine — found work on the docks and railroad along the Hudson River and established shantytowns there.
source_passage: The neighborhood that would later be known as Hell's Kitchen started forming in the southern part of the 22nd Ward in the mid-19th century. Irish immigrants – mostly refugees from the Great Famine – found work on the docks and railroad along the Hudson River and established shantytowns there.

script_body: After the American Civil War, an influx of newcomers crowded the tenements quickly, and many in this congested, poverty-stricken area turned to gang life. When Prohibition arrived in 1919, the district's many warehouses made ideal bootleg distilleries for the rumrunners who controlled illicit liquor. At the start of the 20th century the neighborhood was controlled by gangs, including the violent Gopher Gang led by One Lung Curran and later by Owney Madden. Early gangs like the Hell's Kitchen Gang transformed into organized crime entities around the same time that Madden became one of the most powerful mobsters in New York. The place became known as the "most dangerous area on the American Continent."
source_passage:
After the American Civil War, there was an influx of people who moved to New York City. The tenements that were built became overcrowded quickly. Many who lived in this congested, poverty-stricken area turned to gang life. Following Prohibition, implemented in 1919, the district's many warehouses were ideal locations for bootleg distilleries for the rumrunners who controlled illicit liquor. At the start of the 20th century, the neighborhood was controlled by gangs, including the violent Gopher Gang led by One Lung Curran and later by Owney Madden.

script_body: In 1959, an aborted rumble between rival Irish and Puerto Rican gangs led to the notorious "Capeman" murders, in which two innocent teenagers, mistaken for rival gang members, were killed. By 1965, Hell's Kitchen was the home base of the Westies, an Irish mob aligned with the Gambino crime family. In the early 1980s widespread gentrification began to alter the demographics of the long-time working-class Irish American neighborhood. The 1980s also saw an end to the Westies' reign of terror: the gang lost all of its power after the RICO convictions of most of its principals in 1986.

The 1980s saw an end to the Westies' reign of terror, when the gang lost all of its power after the RICO convictions of most of its principals in 1986.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. (The Capeman killer, Salvador Agron, struck on Aug 30, 1959, killing Anthony Krzesinski and Robert Young Jr., mistaken for rival gang members — fully consistent with the beat. The RICO downfall is sometimes dated to the 1986 indictments / 1988 convictions; '1986' as the year power was broken is well supported.)

script_body: As the pace of gentrification increased, there were numerous reports of trouble between landlords and tenants, and the most extreme example was the seven-story Windermere Apartments complex at the southwest corner of Ninth Avenue and 57th Street. Built in 1881, it is the second-oldest large apartment house in Manhattan. In 1980, the owner, Alan B. Weissman, tried to empty the building of its tenants. According to former tenants and court papers, rooms were ransacked, doors were ripped out, prostitutes were moved in, and tenants received death threats in the campaign to empty the building. All the major New York newspapers covered the trials that sent the Windermere's managers to jail. Although Weissman was never linked to the harassment, he and his wife made top billing in the 1985 edition of The Village Voice's annual list, "The Dirty Dozen: New York's Worst Landlords." Most tenants eventually settled and moved out. In May 2006, seven tenants remained, and court orders protecting the tenants and the building allowed it to remain in a derelict condition even as the surrounding neighborhood was experiencing a dramatic burst of demolition and redevelopment. In September 2007, the fire department evacuated the remaining seven residents, citing dangerous conditions, and padlocked the front door. In 2008, the New York Supreme Court ruled that the owners of the building, who include the TOA Construction Corporation of Japan, must repair it. The building was later sold and is being restored as a boutique hotel.

physical_cues.cue: Look to the southwest corner of Ninth Avenue and 57th Street for the eight-story Windermere

The most extreme example was the eight-story Windermere Apartments complex at the southwest corner of Ninth Avenue and 57th Street. fact_check.omission_check: Lie of omission / outdated: the beat ends at the 2008 court ruling and leaves the Windermere as a derelict, padlocked shell. In 2009 the building was sold (to developer Mark Tress for ~$13M) and has since undergone a landmark facade restoration and conversion toward a boutique hotel (~175 rooms); it is no longer the abandoned ruin the narrative implies. The historical facts through 2008 remain accurate; the building still stands at the corner so the physical cue is valid, but a visitor today sees a restored/under-renovation landmark, not a derelict one.

'Eight-story' is incorrect; this descriptor also appears in the physical cue a visitor would use to identify the building.

The building itself is still present at the southwest corner of Ninth Ave and 57th St, but it now reads as a restored / under-renovation landmark rather than the derelict structure the beat describes.

script_body: Ninth Avenue is noted for its many ethnic restaurants. The Ninth Avenue Association's International Food Festival stretches through Hell's Kitchen from 42nd to 57th Streets every May, usually on the third weekend of the month; it has been going on since 1974 and is one of the oldest street fairs in the city. And Restaurant Row, so called because of the abundance of restaurants, runs along West 46th Street between Eighth and Ninth Avenues, with more restaurants and food carts and trucks on Tenth Avenue between 43rd and 47th Streets.

physical_cues.cue: Restaurant Row lines West 46th Street between Eighth and Ninth Avenues

source_passage:
Ninth Avenue is noted for its many ethnic restaurants. The Ninth Avenue Association's International Food Festival stretches through Hell's Kitchen from 42nd to 57th Streets every May, usually on the third weekend of the month. It has been going on since 1974 and is one of the oldest street fairs in the city. There are Caribbean, Chinese, French, German, Greek, Italian, Irish, Mexican, and Thai restaurants as well as multiple Afghan, Argentine, Ethiopian, Peruvian, Turkish, Indian, Pakistani, and Vietnamese restaurants.
Restaurant Row, so-called because of the abundance of restaurants, is located on West 46th Street between Eighth and Ninth Avenues. There are more restaurants and food carts and trucks on Tenth Avenue between 43rd and 47th Streets.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. The Ninth Avenue International Food Festival is sometimes dated to 1973 rather than 1974, but it celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2024, consistent with a 1974 start; the 1-year variance is immaterial. Restaurant Row on West 46th St between Eighth and Ninth Avenues confirmed current.

script_body: Hell's Kitchen's gritty reputation kept its housing prices lower than elsewhere in Manhattan, and that, combined with its proximity to Broadway theatres, made the neighborhood a haven for aspiring actors. Many famous actors and entertainers have resided there, including Burt Reynolds, Rip Torn, Charlton Heston, James Dean, Bob Hope, Madonna, Jerry Seinfeld, Larry David, Alicia Keys, and Sylvester Stallone. This is due in large part to the Actors Studio on West 44th, at which Lee Strasberg taught and developed method acting.
source_passage: Hell's Kitchen's gritty reputation had made its housing prices lower than elsewhere in Manhattan. Given the lower costs in the past and its proximity to Broadway theatres, the neighborhood is a haven for aspiring actors. Many famous actors and entertainers have resided there, including Burt Reynolds, Rip Torn, Timothée Chalamet, Bob Hope, Charlton Heston, James Dean, Madonna, Jerry Seinfeld, Larry David, Alicia Keys, and Sylvester Stallone. This is due in large part to the Actors Studio on West 44th at which Lee Strasberg taught and developed method acting.

fact_check.omission_check: No significant omissions. Core claims confirmed: low historic housing prices + proximity to Broadway theatres made the neighborhood a haven for aspiring actors, and the Actors Studio (432 West 44th St) is where Lee Strasberg taught and refined method acting.
unverified_claims: The famous-residents roster is a soft-sourced list. Burt Reynolds, James Dean, Bob Hope, Madonna, Jerry Seinfeld, Larry David, Alicia Keys, and Sylvester Stallone are commonly cited as Hell's Kitchen residents, but independent corroboration that Rip Torn and Charlton Heston specifically lived in the neighborhood was not found (not refuted either). Several named figures are living people (Madonna, Seinfeld, David, Keys, Stallone) — the claim is only that they resided there, which is the standard, repeated attribution.

script_body: Solomon R Guggenheim made his money in mining, and did not start buying abstract art until his sixties. The person who got him started was his adviser, a German baroness called Hilla Rebay, described here as eccentric. In 1939 the two of them opened a temporary museum on 54th St and called it the Museum of Non-Objective Painting, with Rebay running it. The rooms were lined in grey velour, classical music was piped in, and incense burned while you looked at the pictures. Four years after that, they went to Frank Lloyd Wright for somewhere permanent.
key_claims: Guggenheim was a mining magnate who began collecting abstract art in his 60s
His adviser was a German baroness, Hilla Rebay
1939 temporary museum on 54th St: the Museum of Non-Objective Painting
It had grey velour walls, piped-in classical music, burning incense
source_passage: The Guggenheim came out of the collection of Solomon R Guggenheim, a New York mining magnate who began acquiring abstract art in his 60s at the behest of his art adviser, an eccentric German baroness named Hilla Rebay. In 1939, with Rebay serving as director, Guggenheim opened a temporary museum on 54th St titled the Museum of Non-Objective Painting. (Incredibly, it had grey velour walls, piped-in classical music and burning incense.) Four years later, the pair commissioned Wright to construct a permanent home for the collection.

script_body: Getting the building up took nearly thirteen years. Money ran short, the Second WWII arrived, and the neighbours objected loudly — the book's phrase for what they thought was landing among them is a giant concrete spaceship. It was finished in 1959, by which point neither the architect nor the man whose collection it was built for was alive to see it.

physical_cues.cue: The concrete exterior of the museum from Fifth Ave

key_claims: Construction was delayed almost 13 years
Causes: budget, WWII, outraged neighbors
Completed 1959 after both Wright and Guggenheim had died
source_passage: Like most developments in New York City, the project took forever to come to fruition. Construction was delayed for almost 13 years due to budget constraints, the outbreak of WWII and outraged neighbors who weren't all that excited to see a giant concrete spaceship land in their midst. Construction was finally completed in 1959 - after both Wright and Guggenheim had passed away.

script_body: The shape is an inverted ziggurat, and it split opinion before the doors ever opened — some critics mocked it, others took to it immediately. It has been on postcards, television and film ever since.

physical_cues.cue: The inverted ziggurat form of the building, widening as it rises

key_claims: Inverted ziggurat
Derided by some critics, hailed by others before opening
source_passage: A sculpture in its own right, this building by architect Frank Lloyd Wright almost overshadows the collection of 20th-century art inside. Even before it opened, the inverted ziggurat structure was derided by some critics but hailed by others, who welcomed it as a beloved architectural icon. Since its opening, this unusual structure has appeared in countless postcards, TV programs and films.

script_body: Doors opened in October 1959 and admission cost fifty cents. Hanging that first day were Alexander Calder and Wassily Kandinsky, along with two painters out of abstract expressionism: Willem de Kooning and Franz Kline.
key_claims: Opened October 1959
Ticket price 50c
Kandinsky, Calder, Kline, de Kooning on view
source_passage: When the Guggenheim opened its doors in October 1959, the ticket price was 50c and the works on view included pieces by Wassily Kandinsky, Alexander Calder and abstract expressionists Franz Kline and Willem de Kooning.

script_body: The New York Times tore the building apart. Other voices were calling it one of the most beautiful things in the country almost as quickly. Whether or not that was Wright's aim, the city ended up with a landmark people recognise instantly.
key_claims: The New York Times savaged the structure
Others called it one of the country's most beautiful buildings
source_passage: The structure was savaged by the New York Times, but others quickly celebrated it as one of the country's most beautiful buildings. Whether Wright intended to or not, he had given the city one of its most recognizable landmarks.

script_body: An eight-storey tower went up on the east side in the early 1990s, adding fifty thousand square feet of gallery. Those rooms take work from the permanent collection; the spiral itself is kept for temporary shows.

physical_cues.cue: The eight-story tower on the east side of the building

key_claims: Early 1990s renovation added an eight-story tower to the east
50,000 sq ft of extra exhibition space
source_passage: A renovation in the early 1990s added an eight-story tower to the east, which seamlessly provided an extra 50,000 sq ft of exhibition space. These galleries feature rotating exhibitions from the permanent collection, while the ramps of the Rotunda are occupied by temporary exhibits.

script_body: What hangs here now runs well past the abstract art Guggenheim started with. Kandinsky, Picasso and Jackson Pollock are here. So are paintings by Degas, by Van Gogh, by Monet; sculpture from Constantin Brancusi; photographs taken by Robert Mapplethorpe. The surrealist works came as a gift from his niece Peggy.
key_claims: Holdings include Kandinsky, Picasso, Pollock, Monet, Van Gogh, Degas, Brancusi, Mapplethorpe
Surrealist works donated by niece Peggy
source_passage: The museum's holdings include works by Kandinsky, Picasso and Jackson Pollock. Over time, other key additions have included paintings by Monet, Van Gogh and Degas, sculpture by Constantin Brancusi, photographs by Robert Mapplethorpe, and key surrealist works donated by Guggenheim's niece Peggy.

script_body: Wright wanted you to ride to the top and walk down the spiral. One cramped lift makes that hard to do, so the shows are hung the other way round — from the bottom upward, against the architect's intention.

physical_cues.cue: The spiral ramp rising through the rotunda

key_claims: Wright intended visitors to descend from the top
A single cramped elevator makes that difficult
Exhibitions are installed bottom to top
source_passage: The museum's ascending ramp displays rotating exhibitions of modern and contemporary art. Though Wright intended visitors to go to the top and wind their way down, the cramped single elevator makes this difficult. Exhibitions, therefore, are installed from bottom to top.

script_body: The Met opened in 1870 and now holds more than two million objects, running from Egyptian temples to American painting. Seventeen acres of galleries draw over six million people a year, which makes it the busiest single site in the city. The book's advice is simply to allow time.
key_claims: Founded 1870
More than two million objects
17 acres of galleries
Over six million visitors a year
Largest single-site attraction in NYC
source_passage: This sprawling, encyclopedic museum, founded in 1870, houses one of the world's largest and most important art collections, with more than two million individual objects, from Egyptian temples to American paintings. 'The Met' attracts over six million visitors a year to its 17 acres of galleries, making it the largest single-site attraction in NYC. In other words: plan on spending some time here.

script_body: 39 Egyptian galleries begin north of the Great Hall, and they open on the Tomb of Perneb — an Old Kingdom burial chamber cut from limestone around 2300 BCE. Past it the rooms fill up with funerary stelae, carved reliefs and pieces of pyramid. Gallery 105 holds the clay figures from the Tomb of Meketre, small models made to be useful to their owner after death.

Clay figurines from the Tomb of Meketre in Gallery 105

Tomb of Perneb, c 2300 BCE, Old Kingdom limestone burial chamber

source_passage: Located to the north of the Great Hall, the 39 Egyptian galleries open dramatically with one of the Met's prized pieces: the Tomb of Perneb (c 2300 BCE), an Old Kingdom burial chamber crafted from limestone. From here, a web of rooms is cluttered with funerary stelae, carved reliefs and fragments of pyramids. Don't miss the intriguing models from the Tomb of Meketre, clay figurines meant to help in the afterlife, in Gallery 105.

The skylights above them were being replaced when this was written, to give the pictures better light.

source_passage: On the museum's 2nd floor, the European Paintings galleries display a stunning collection of masterworks. This includes more than 1700 canvases from the roughly 500-year period starting in the 13th century, with works by every important painter from Duccio to Rembrandt. At the time of writing, the skylights in these galleries were being replaced to improve the quality of light within.

script_body: Fifteen rooms in the southeastern corner of the second floor hold art from the Middle East and from Central and South Asia. Among the garments, manuscripts and decorative objects is a mihrab, a prayer niche, made in Iran in the fourteenth century and faced in patterned blue, white and yellow tile — Gallery 455. Nearby are Ottoman textiles in 459, a Moroccan court done in medieval style in 456, and an eighteenth-century room from Damascus in 461.

In addition to garments, secular decorative objects and manuscripts, you'll find a magnificent 14th-century mihrab (prayer niche) from Iran, lined with elaborately patterned blue, white and yellow tile work (Gallery 455). There's also a superb array of Ottoman textiles (Gallery 459), a medievalstyle Moroccan court (Gallery 456) and the 18th-century Damascus Room (Gallery 461).

script_body: In Gallery 111 there is a small hippopotamus glazed blue, put into an Egyptian tomb three thousand nine hundred years ago so that he would look after the person buried there. Somebody nicknamed him William, and he has become the museum's mascot without ever being made official. The shop on the first floor sells him as a figurine, a plush toy, a tie, a T-shirt, a magnet and a children's book.

Nicknamed 'William,' he's the Met's unofficial mascot. If you'd like your own guardian hippo, head to the museum shop on the 1st floor, where you can buy bright-blue William figurines, plush toys, ties, T-shirts, magnets and children's books.

script_body: Two floors in the northwestern corner hold American decorative and fine art, from colonial portraits through the Hudson River School, and Emanuel Leutze's enormous Washington Crossing the Delaware hangs in Gallery 760. What the permanent holdings lack is any serious body of Native American work. In 2018-19 the museum showed a hundred and sixteen pieces from over 50 indigenous cultures of North America — sculpture, painting, textiles and regalia — given, donated or lent out of the Diker Collection, reckoned the most significant private holding of its kind in the country.

source_passage: In the northwestern corner, the two-floor American Wing showcases a wide variety of decorative and fine art from throughout US history. These include everything from colonial portraiture to Hudson River School art - not to mention Emanuel Leutze's massive canvas of Washington Crossing the Delaware (Gallery 760). What the permanent collection lacks, though, is a serious body of Native American art. In 2018-19 a landmark exhibition showcased 116 works of sculpture, painting, textiles and regalia from more than 50 indigenous North American cultures. The works were gifts, donations and loans from the Diker Collection, considered to be the most significant private collection of Native American art in the US.

script_body: Twenty-seven galleries are given to classical antiquity. Leaving the Great Hall you pass down a barrel-vaulted room with Greek torsos along both sides, and come out in the sculpture court, Gallery 162 — one of the airiest rooms in the building, full of marble gods and marble men. The Hercules there, bearded, a lion's skin over his shoulders, was carved somewhere between 68 and 98 CE.

source_passage: The 27 galleries devoted to classical antiquity are another Met doozy. From the Great Hall, a passageway takes you through a barrel-vaulted room flanked by the chiseled torsos of Greek figures. This spills right into one of the Met's loveliest spaces: the airy Greek and Roman sculpture court (Gallery 162), full of marble carvings of gods and historical figures. The statue of a bearded Hercules from CE 68-98, with a lion's skin draped about him, is particularly awe-inspiring.

Crowds are rare here except during a popular show, which leaves the place feeling private in a way few museums manage. There is a fountain trickling in the indoor courtyard, gardens you cannot walk in, and a quiet Portico Gallery of sculpture and decorative work. Nobody under ten gets in.

Ronald Lauder, who made his money in cosmetics, bought it for the museum at a hundred and thirty-five million dollars. How it travelled from Vienna to this room is the subject of the 2015 film Woman in Gold.

script_body: A merchant named Archibald Gracie put this Federal-style house up in 1799 as somewhere to go outside the city. Since 1942 it has been where New York's mayors live with their families — with one exception. Michael Bloomberg stayed in his own Upper East Side apartment, which he preferred. The building has been added to and done over repeatedly since Gracie's day.

Its promenade looks out across the East River to several islands and the Triborough Bridge, and the book counts it among the parts of the Upper East Side that visitors miss.

script_body: At the far end of Museum Mile, in a Georgian Colonial Revival building, is the one museum here concerned with nothing but this city — its past, its present and what comes next. On the ground floor a film called Timescapes runs for twenty-eight minutes and tracks the place from a small trading post used by Native Americans to the metropolis outside.

Don't miss the 28-minute film Timescapes (on the ground floor), which charts NYC's growth from a tiny trading post for Native Americans to burgeoning metropolis.

script_body: Most of this neighbourhood is people's homes. What visitors come for sits in a line along Fifth Ave between 70th and 93rd Sts — the stretch known as Museum Mile, studded with old mansions and the institutions that took them over. Central Park runs the length of it on the other side of the avenue, behind a low stone wall, so a day here can alternate between galleries and grass.

Central Park runs along the western side of Fifth Ave, bordered by a low stone wall. If the weather's fine, you can spend a very pleasant day alternating museum stops with a stroll through some greenery.
